pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which 1000 wh power station can run a microwave and for how long". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which 1000 wh power station can run a microwave and for how long?
pages.why_used: The cited pages work out microwave minutes from an assumed 85% of rated capacity, and some say they did no testing. Backup Power Finder lists OutdoorGearLab's usable-Wh figures, but it doesn't give the test load or turn them into microwave time. This page uses energy measured at about 80% of each unit's rated output (a load the size of a microwave's draw) and The Solar Lab's timed 1,479 W run. It converts those into minutes and reheats per charge. It also notes that boost modes (BLUETTI Power Lifting, EcoFlow X-Boost) don't raise the ceiling for a microwave.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's 2,700 W 'Power Lifting' figure, on both the AC180 and the Elite 100 V2, is the maker's limit for pure resistive loads only ('devices consisting of heating elements only'), while the rated output 'remains 1800W'. A microwave is not a heating-element load, so the only number that counts for one is the continuous rating: 2,000 W on the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, 1,800 W on the BLUETTI and EcoFlow units, 1,500 W on the Jackery.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 pick rather than changing it. Once boost modes are set aside, the C1000 Gen 2's 2,000 W is the highest continuous rating among the four mainstream picks (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, AC180, EcoFlow DELTA 3, Jackery 1000 v2). The only higher ones are the DJI Power 1000 V2 at 2,600 W and the ALLPOWERS S2000 Pro at 2,400 W. BLUETTI's 2,700 W is a resistive-only mode, so it gives no headroom for a 1,580 W over-the-range microwave. Our Elite 100 V2 row needs one fix: change '1,800 W / 2,700 W' to '1,800 W (2,700 W Power Lifting, heating loads only)' and add a footnote.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns measured usable AC energy into microwave minutes. Using OutdoorGearLab's discharge tests (July 2026), every 1 kWh candidate gives 35–36 minutes at a 1,500 W draw and 17–18 two-minute reheats. The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 also has one test at a microwave-like 1 kW load: The Technology Man measured 907 Wh. These numbers show runtime does not separate the candidates, so inverter headroom decides the pick.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick and does not change it. Measured usable AC energy puts every candidate at 34.8–36.4 minutes at a 1,500 W draw and 17–18 two-minute reheats, so battery size can't pick a winner. Inverter headroom decides. The C1000 Gen 2 (2,000 W continuous per Anker) and DJI Power 1000 V2 have margin above a 1,500 W draw. DELTA 3 and Elite 100 V2 (1,800 W) have about 300 W of margin. The Explorer 1000 v2 (1,500 W per OutdoorGearLab's spec table) has no margin, which makes it the one to steer away from even though it measured the most usable Wh (910). One extra data point: The Technology Man saw the C1000 Gen 2 overheat after 26 minutes at 2 kW, with the heater placed too close to the unit. That supports staying well under the inverter's limit.

Anker lists the C1000 Gen 2 (ChatGPT's top pick) as not expandable, so it is limited to its one 1,024 Wh battery (about 35 minutes at 1,500 W).

It also shows that neither it nor the DELTA 3 Classic can go past roughly 35 minutes of 1,500 W cooking per charge. A shopper who wants more microwave time should buy the EcoFlow DELTA 3 (1,024 Wh, not the Classic) or the DELTA 3 Plus and add an extra battery. The cheaper Classic cards ChatGPT showed can't be expanded. Separately, ChatGPT's $998 price for the BLUETTI AC180 at BLUETTI-US is the two-unit option; a single AC180 is $499.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 'boost' ratings on 1 kWh stations are reduced-voltage modes and not extra continuous power. EcoFlow's X-Boost (2,200 W on the DELTA 3) 'marginally reduces voltage', and BLUETTI limits the AC180's 2,700 W Power Lifting mode to 'pure-resistive heating devices', so for a microwave the continuous AC rating is the real ceiling. Only the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 has 2,000 W of continuous output with no boost mode involved.
angles.decides: This confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick for full-size microwaves drawing about 1,600–2,000 W. Its 2,000 W is a plain continuous rating. The BLUETTI AC180's 2,700 W covers resistive heating devices only, so the AC180 stays capped at 1,800 W for a microwave. The DELTA 3's 2,200 W comes only in X-Boost, which runs at reduced voltage. EcoFlow lists a 1,300 W microwave as an X-Boost example, but that is already below the DELTA 3's 1,800 W continuous rating. So the boost figures should not be used to move the line for the microwave sizes each station can run.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a runtime measured at a microwave-sized load: The Solar Lab ran the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at a steady 1,479 W and it lasted 37.5 minutes, and OutdoorGearLab's usable-energy figures, taken at about 80% of each unit's rated output, work out to about 35–36 minutes at 1,500 W for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (890 Wh each) and about 35 minutes for the EcoFlow DELTA 3 (870 Wh).

Runtime per charge is therefore effectively a tie at about 35–36 minutes or about 17 two-minute reheats at 1,500 W, so the deciding factor is inverter headroom: the Anker's rated 2,000 W against 1,800 W. A 1,000 W-cooking microwave that draws about 1,500 W would leave it no margin. That supports the current page's verdict that it suits only a 700–900 W microwave.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which 1000 wh power station charges fully from the wall in under an hour". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which 1000 wh power station charges fully from the wall in under an hour?
pages.why_used: The rival pages, and our own earlier version, repeat Anker's 1,600 W UltraFast figure and the 49-minute claim. None of them reads Anker's US nameplate of 120 V, 12 A max (1,440 W), which is also the code limit for one plug-in device on a standard 15 A circuit. None sets that against EcoFlow's 15 A rating or DJI's 13 A. This page checks each fast mode against what a US 120 V outlet can supply and shows the arithmetic, so it explains why the 49 minutes still fits under an hour at 120 V and why 1,200 W units can't.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the US Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is rated for at most 12 A at 120 V. That is 1,440 W, less than the 1,600 W UltraFast input Anker advertises. On the same 120 V basis the DJI Power 1000 V2 is rated for 13 A (1,560 W) and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 for 15 A (1,800 W). So the model with the highest advertised input has the lowest rated current from a US outlet.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker as the pick and changes how the page should explain it. The 49-minute claim needs only about 1,254 W on average into a 1,024 Wh battery, which is under the 1,440 W nameplate limit. The Solar Lab timed 47 minutes in Ultra-Fast mode (outlet voltage not stated). So the time is believable, but the '1,600 W' headline is not what Anker's US nameplate allows at 120 V. Our '≈13 A at 120 V' circuit warning should be rewritten around the 12 A rating. The EcoFlow is the only one of the three makers I checked whose 120 V rating (15 A) is above its charge wattage (1,500 W). It also had the highest measured charging speed in OutdoorGearLab's test, which favours it as the runner-up.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much wall energy a full charge takes or what that does to the fastest possible time. StorageReview measured 1,180 Wh from the wall to fill the 1,024 Wh EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, about 87 % efficient. Because charging stops at 100 % but the losses still come out of the wall, the fastest possible full charge, with no slow-down near full, is 1,180 Wh ÷ max AC input. That works out to about 44 min for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 at 1,600 W and 47 min for the DELTA 3 Plus at 1,500 W. It would be about 59 min for a 1,024 Wh unit capped at 1,200 W, such as the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, which leaves no room to finish in under an hour.
angles.decides: It backs the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick. It has the most headroom: about 44 min is its fastest possible time, against a 49 min claim and a 60 min target, so about 11 min of its claimed charge goes to slowing near full. The DELTA 3 Plus can't beat about 47 min and claims 56. A 1,024 Wh unit capped at 1,200 W (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 TurboBoost) can't beat about 59 min even if it never slowed near full. That rules it out as an under-an-hour answer and explains why BLUETTI only claims 80 % in 45 min. The same check should be run on the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh), whose input cap I couldn't source: unless its charger is better than 89 % efficient, 1,200 W could not fill it in under an hour.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's US page says to wall-charge the SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 only with the standard Anker SOLIX AC charging cable, warning that third-party cables may cause damage. The same page rates the AC input at '120V~ 12A Max' while advertising 1,600 W UltraFast, which works out to about 13.3 A at 120 V.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick and adds two conditions to the 49-minute claim: (1) use the supplied Anker SOLIX AC cable, not a spare cord; (2) the maker's own input rating is 12 A at 120 V, yet UltraFast at 1,600 W draws about 13.3 A. Either way, a US shopper needs the station on a 15 A outlet with nothing heavy sharing the circuit. This doesn't change the ranking.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own US spec caps the SOLIX C1000 Gen 2's wall input at '120V~ 12A Max' (1,440 W at 120 V), which is below its advertised 1,600 W UltraFast rate and equals the electrical code's 12 A limit for a single plug-in device on a standard 15 A circuit (NEC 210.23(A)(1)); a US outlet therefore cannot supply the full 1,600 W behind the 49-minute claim.
angles.decides: The finding keeps the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick but changes how its claim should be read on a US outlet. Its 12 A input label and the code limit both point to about 1,440 W at 120 V, not 1,600 W. Holding that draw flat would stretch the 49-minute claim to about 54 minutes, which is still under an hour but closer to the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus's 55–56 minutes. The 47-minute measured time was taken on UK mains and doesn't carry over to 120 V. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus's 1,500 W is about 12.5 A at 120 V, also over the 12 A limit; StorageReview says that rate suits a 20 A circuit and that the app's charge-speed limit is for 15 A plugs. The energy arithmetic sets the floor: StorageReview measured 1,180 Wh from the wall to fill the 1,024 Wh DELTA 3 Plus. A full charge inside 60 minutes therefore needs an average draw of at least about 1,180 W across the whole charge, including the slow final stretch. Modes capped at 1,200 W, such as Anker's normal mode, ALLPOWERS P1800 fast mode and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 Turbo, have almost no margin. That fits the reviews where those modes take about an hour or longer.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that OutdoorGearLab (Kenji Mowrey, 2026-07-23) timed the EcoFlow DELTA 3 at a full 0–100 % wall charge in 50 minutes at an average 1,299 Wh/hr, with no app fast mode mentioned, while the same lab timed the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 at 56 minutes in its default mode.
angles.decides: This confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the fastest pick. Two named reviewers each measured 47 minutes with UltraFast on: The Technology Man at about 20 °C, and The Solar Lab. It also sets up a clear second choice for shoppers who won't switch on an app mode. In OutdoorGearLab's single lab, the DELTA 3 filled in 50 minutes on its default charger, which beats the Anker's 56-minute default run there. So the Anker is only fastest with UltraFast enabled. The DJI Power 1000 V2 is borderline: The Technology Man measured under 53 minutes and OutdoorGearLab measured 59 minutes. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 fails the under-an-hour test in OutdoorGearLab's run (almost 2 hours at 563 Wh/hr, mode not stated).

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got lists the Jackery HomePower 1000 v2 (1,024 Wh). Jackery's own US store sells it for $549 today and says it is 'Fully Charged in Just 50 Minutes'. That beats the 56-minute EcoFlow and DJI claims and comes close to the Anker C1000 Gen 2's 49 minutes, which costs $799 at Anker's own US store.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the fastest maker-claimed full wall charge (49 min, UltraFast enabled in the app). It also makes the price trade-off visible. At maker-store prices the Anker costs $799. The DELTA 3 costs $579 for a 56-minute claim. The Jackery HomePower 1000 v2 costs $549 for a 50-minute claim, but its black version is sold out. The BLUETTI AC180 and Elite 100 V2 cost $499 but are only claimed to reach 80 % in 45 minutes, so they don't meet the 'fully in under an hour' test. The page should add the HomePower 1000 v2 as the value alternative and state its charge conditions once they are sourced.

pages.query: 1000 wh power station bundled with a 400 w solar panel
pages.why_used: The rival pages give only rated Wh and their own 75–85% assumptions. None prints a named lab's delivered-energy figure for any of the 1 kWh kit stations. This page ranks the kits on lab-measured AC energy (BLUETTI AC180 980–1,030 Wh against 850–910 Wh for the EcoFlow, Jackery and Anker units) and adds the low-load result of 530–620 Wh at about 34 W.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the stations' 'max solar input' watts are not comparable: the BLUETTI AC180 is capped at 10 A, so its 2 × 200 W kit reaches 400 W only if the array runs at 40 V or more (series wiring). The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 drops to 8.2 A below 29 V, which allows about 230 W at most, and only Anker's 48 V PS400 panel gets the full 400 W through it, with its 57.6 V open-circuit voltage 2.4 V under the 60 V ceiling.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. Each maker's own 400 W kit gets the whole 400 W (AC180 if wired in series, C1000 Gen 2 with the PS400). The finding matters for shoppers who would put a station together with panels bought separately: low-voltage 200 W panels in parallel lose about half their output on the AC180 (10 A cap) and on the C1000 Gen 2 (8.2 A below 29 V). On cycle life, Anker's '4,000 cycles to at least 80%' is the only figure from a maker page I read that names its endpoint. The ALLPOWERS P1800 (cheapest kit, $698) gives no endpoint and its rating differs between stores (US store: 'over 3,000'; a search snippet of the EU page says 3,500+), so the table footnote should say its cycle count can't be compared.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's own store sells the AC180 with 400 W of its panels for less when bought as two parts ($769 AC180+200 W kit + $399 SP200L = $1,168, $1.01/Wh) than as its $1,232 'AC180+2*200W' bundle ($1.07/Wh). None states that the Anker C1000 Gen 2 only draws a full 400 W from a panel running at 29 V or more; below that its input tops out near 28 V × 8.2 A ≈ 230 W.
angles.decides: Confirms that both BLUETTI and Anker can take a full 400 W only under a voltage condition, and cuts the BLUETTI row's best price from $1,232 to $1,168 (still about $1.01/Wh against the ALLPOWERS kit's roughly $0.68/Wh on our page, which I could not re-verify today). The value pick stays the same. It adds a buying tip for BLUETTI and a check-the-panel-voltage warning for anyone pairing a 400 W panel with the Anker.

That cap means the AC180 + 2 × 200 W kit, which is in stock at $1,232, can only approach 400 W if its two SP200L panels are wired in series. BLUETTI's own AC180 manual gives no series or parallel instruction, and our page currently says the panels 'go in parallel'.

The AC180 + 2 × 200 W kit, priced at $1,232 on 2026-11-08, gets close to 400 W only when wired in series, and it is also the most expensive kit here. angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own 400 W panel for the C1000 Gen 2 kit (PS400, Voc 57.6 V) sits only 2.4 V (4.2%) under the C1000 Gen 2's 60 V solar-input ceiling. Open-circuit voltage rises as panels get colder, so this pairing has the least cold-weather headroom of the kits we list.
angles.decides: This confirms that every listed kit works electrically at the standard 25 °C rating and that no station limits current below its 400 W panel (PS400: 8.33 A at 48 V, within the C1000 Gen 2's 14.5 A high-voltage band). It does not rule out the Anker kit. It adds a winter caveat that applies only to the Anker kit: its panel runs 2.4 V below the input limit. I did not source Voc for the ALLPOWERS SP037 or the EcoFlow 400 W myself today. Rival pages give 45.3 V and 48 V, which would leave about 12–15 V of headroom. If those figures hold, the Anker kit is the one to flag for cold-climate buyers. Anker also lists the C1000 Gen 2 + 400 W bundle as shipping from early December for orders placed after Oct 30.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which 1 kwh power station takes 1000 w of solar through two inputs". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which 1 kwh power station takes 1000 w of solar through two inputs?
pages.why_used: The cited rival lists the DELTA 3 Plus only as 'two 500W MPPT inputs' and gives no volts or amps for either station. None of the results converts the 15 A and 20 A limits into the working voltage a panel string must hold (33.3 V per DELTA 3 Plus input, 50 V for the Elite 100 V2's one input), quotes EcoFlow's rule that a panel exceeding any one limit cannot be used, or carries Notebookcheck's finding that one input makes 1,000 W hard to reach on the Elite 100 V2. This page has all three.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's '1,000 W solar' comes through a single input capped at 20 A under a 60 V ceiling, so the panel string must run at 50 V or more to reach 1,000 W, while each of the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus's two 15 A inputs reaches its 500 W cap from about 33.3 V upward.
angles.decides: This confirms the DELTA 3 Plus as the pick. Its 1,000 W comes from two 500 W inputs, and an ordinary 400–500 W string on each input reaches the cap with room to spare. The Elite 100 V2 is the obvious single-input alternative. On paper it matches at 1,000 W and costs $499, but 1,000 W ÷ 20 A means the string must hold at least 50 V while its open-circuit voltage stays at or under 60 V. That is a narrow window, and Notebookcheck's reviewer said 1,000 W is hard to reach in practice. The page should tell shoppers that the two '1,000 W' figures are not equivalent.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's single 20 A solar input can only reach 1,000 W from a string working at 50 V or more under a 60 V ceiling (1,000 W ÷ 20 A = 50 V), while each EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus port needs only about 33 V for its 500 W (500 W ÷ 15 A).
angles.decides: This supports the DELTA 3 Plus as the answer. The Elite 100 V2 also claims 1,000 W, but on one input it only gets there with a string operating between 50 and 60 V, a narrow window that common portable panels and series pairs can easily miss. Each DELTA 3 Plus port reaches its 500 W anywhere from about 33 V to 60 V, so two ordinary strings can fill it. Before landed losses, both stations take about 1.0 h at a full 1,000 W.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the DELTA 3 Plus's car-charging cable plugs into one of the same two XT60i solar ports, so while it is charging from a car only one 500 W solar input is left. None of them says that each port stops at 15 A either, which means an array needs at least about 33.3 V working voltage, with open-circuit voltage at or under 60 V, to fill a port.
angles.decides: It confirms the DELTA 3 Plus as the pick and adds the conditions. Its two ports reach 1,000 W together only if each array works at 33.3 V or more and stays at or under 60 V open-circuit. Using one port for car charging takes away half the solar input. The single-input BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (12–60 V, 20 A, 1,000 W) only reaches 1,000 W from an array working at 50 V or more with open-circuit voltage at or under 60 V. That is a narrow range for real panels, so two inputs are the easier way to get 1,000 W of solar.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EcoFlow caps each DELTA 3 Plus input at 15 A, so each input reaches 500 W only from a panel string working at 33.3 V or more and staying under 60 V open-circuit. By the same arithmetic, the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's single 20 A input needs at least 50 V of working voltage under a 60 V ceiling to reach 1,000 W, which Notebookcheck says is difficult in practice.
angles.decides: This confirms the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus as the pick and sets what panels the plan needs. To get 1,000 W the shopper needs two separate strings of about 500 W, one per input. Each string must work at 33.3 V or more (500 W ÷ 15 A), have a cold-weather Voc of 60 V or less, and stay at 15 A or less. That rules out paralleling two 20 V-class panels into one input, since EcoFlow's own example (12.9 A × 2 = 25.8 A) is refused, and it rules out putting two 40 V-class panels in series. It also removes the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 as an equal alternative. Its one input needs at least 50 V at 20 A while staying under 60 V Voc, and Notebookcheck works out that two BLUETTI PV350s can't go in series (2 × 46.5 V = 93 V), leaving about 700 W.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured energy balance for the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus. StorageReview (Dylan Dougherty, Jan 2, 2025) drew 910 Wh out of the 1,024 Wh pack (88.9%) and needed 1,180 Wh in to refill it from 0 to 100% (86.8%). At the full 1,000 W of solar through its two ports, the input side works out to about 71 minutes, which matches EcoFlow's 70-minute claim. Separately, The Solar Lab reports getting 'really close to' 1,000 W with both 500 W ports in use.
angles.decides: This confirms the DELTA 3 Plus as the pick. It is the only candidate where a named tester actually drew close to 1,000 W through two inputs (The Solar Lab, both 500 W ports, Serious 415 W bifacial panels). Its measured efficiency (88.9% out, 86.8% in, StorageReview) means the 70-minute solar claim holds only if the full 1,000 W keeps coming in. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 tested similarly well on capacity (946 Wh at a 500 W load, Techreviewer.de). But it has one DC input (12–60 V, 20 A), so it fails the 'two inputs' requirement. No named reviewer I could open logged its solar watts. It also idles at about 16 W with the inverter on (The Solar Lab), and its AC charging drops to about 500 W below 20% charge.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, a 1,024 Wh station that takes 1,000 W of solar, sells for $499 on BLUETTI US today (2026-11-14), the same price as BLUETTI's 500 W AC180. Volt & Valley shows the two-input EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus at $949, so the second input costs about $450 more, unless the shopper can wire their panels into one 12–60 V string.
angles.decides: This confirms the DELTA 3 Plus for the question as asked. pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "best 2kwh portable power station for an rv under $900". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What's the best 2kwh portable power station for an rv under $900?
pages.why_used: The rival pages that were cited (RuntimeMath /compare, OutageReadyHQ under $1,000, OutdoorGearLab, BuyerSheet and our 2026-10-31 page) give no measured idle draw for any 2 kWh station, and every runtime table they offer assumes the same usable Wh for every model. This page sets out what named reviewers measured with the AC inverter left on: about 10 W on the Elite 200 V2 (The Gadgeteer), 17 W on the Jackery (The Solar Lab) and 27 W on the DELTA 3 Max (The Solar Lab). It turns each figure into the share of the battery lost per day. Because the AC200L is now discontinued at BLUETTI US, the pick moves to the in-stock Elite 200 V2, which is under $900 and has the best measured idle draw and usable capacity.

pages.why_used: The rival buyer's guides (invenio3d, TriMech's SHINING 3D guide, 3D Scanner Match) give only headline single-figure accuracies, or no figures at all. None applies the base + rate × length volumetric formula to a real part size, and none says which maker names a test standard. This page works out the error at 300 mm and at 1 m for each scanner from sourced specs, so a shopper can go from their tolerance to a scanner.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the scanners' stated volumetric accuracy into error over a real part length. At 1 m the EinScan Rigil's Laser HD spec (0.04 + 0.06 mm/m) works out to ±0.10 mm, and its IR Rapid spec (0.1 + 0.4 mm/m) to ±0.50 mm. The FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry (0.02 + 0.015 mm/m) works out to ±0.035 mm. That puts the Rigil's laser mode exactly at the '±0.1 mm mechanical fit' limit that ChatGPT's own filter offers, its IR mode far past it, and the UE Pro2 about 3× tighter.
angles.decides: This confirms the higher tier and sharpens the middle one. For parts around 1 m that need ±0.05 mm or better, only the UE Pro2 with photogrammetry meets it on its stated spec (±0.035 mm). The Rigil should only be recommended in Laser HD mode for ±0.1 mm work, and its IR Rapid mode (±0.30 mm at 500 mm) is shape-capture only. The budget picks (MetroX, MetroX Pro, Raptor, Raptor Pro) can only be placed once their mm/m figures come from the maker. Creality's US store pages publish no accuracy figure at all, so the page can't quote one from the store.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns a scanner's volumetric-accuracy formula (a mm + b mm/m) into the worst-case error on a part of a stated size; for example, the HandySCAN 3D PRO works out to 0.038 mm on a 300 mm part and 0.080 mm on a 1 m part, and the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry to 0.035 mm on a 1 m part.
angles.decides: It confirms the step-up pick for large parts. Over 1 m, the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry (0.035 mm) holds less than half the worst-case error of the HandySCAN 3D PRO without MaxSHOT (0.080 mm), even though their headline accuracies are about the same (0.02 mm vs 0.030 mm). For parts of about 300 mm or less, the two are within 0.014 mm of each other (0.0245 vs 0.038 mm). That difference matters only below a ±0.05 mm fit tolerance. The budget pick (MetroX vs Raptor) cannot be decided from this run, because their maker formulas could not be opened today (HTTP 429/404).

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which computers the budget picks need. Creality's CR-Scan Raptor manual lists macOS 11.7.7 or later on Apple M1/M2/M3 chips with 16 GB RAM, and on Windows 10/11 64-bit it suggests an i7 7th-gen CPU, an NVIDIA card with 6 GB VRAM and 16 GB RAM. Creality sells its Scan Bridge ($299) for the 'Sermoon S1 & Raptor Series' only, and Otter owners must buy a separate version.
angles.decides: For a Mac user, the Raptor is the budget pick that has a maker-documented Apple-silicon path (M1/M2/M3, 16 GB). For a Windows user, Creality suggests an NVIDIA GPU with at least 6 GB VRAM, which adds cost if the PC has integrated graphics. This confirms Raptor versus MetroX as the budget pair, but a full head-to-head needs MetroX's own requirements, which I could not open (see unsourced). On the Revopoint side, the maker's ball-plate listing says its Revo Metro measurement module is 'currently available only for MetroY Ultra and MetroY Ultra CMM models'. So a MetroX buyer gets no Revo Metro accuracy-verification software and should budget separately for inspection software.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the per-metre term in a handheld scanner's volumetric-accuracy spec is multiplied by the length of the object being scanned (Revopoint: 'L is the length of the object'). For a reverse-engineering part, the error to expect is therefore base + rate × part length: about 0.06 mm for MetroX vs 0.032 mm for MetroX Pro on a 300 mm part. Creaform measures its figure as sphere spacing on a calibrated length artefact; Revopoint gives no test conditions.
angles.decides: This lets the page turn the shopper's tolerance into a pick. With the claimed specs, a part up to about 300 mm can be held near ±0.03-0.04 mm by MetroX Pro (0.032 mm) or HandySCAN 3D PRO (0.038 mm). Standard MetroX at its originally published spec reaches 0.06 mm, which is fine for '±0.1 mm mechanical fit' but not '±0.05 mm precision'. At 1 m the gap widens: MetroX 0.13 mm, MetroX Pro 0.06 mm, HandySCAN PRO 0.08 mm, HandySCAN PRO with MaxSHOT 0.045 mm. On paper this favours MetroX Pro over standard MetroX for anyone at or below ±0.05 mm. It also tells larger-part buyers to add photogrammetry (MaxSHOT or Revopoint's Global Marker mode). One caution: only Creaform states how its figure is measured (sphere spacing on a calibrated length artefact). Revopoint's figure has no stated test method, so the two sets of numbers are not measured the same way.

pages.query: best 40gbps nvme ssd enclosure that doesnt throttle on long transfers
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages give peak speeds, maker claims or general warnings about throttling. None of them collects the named long-run tests with duration, room temperature, held write rate and SSD temperature. Those tests are the D1 SSD Plus's 2,550–2,600 MB/s AJA loop and its 15-minute stress test at 30 °C, OWC's one-hour run with no speed drop, the CM642's clean 450 GB write, and the CM850, which had to lose its sleeve to finish. Together they answer 'doesn't throttle on long transfers' directly and cover most candidates.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the long-copy rate next to the headline speed. Makers advertise 3,707–3,900 MB/s from short benchmarks. ASUS's own 30-minute claim for the PA40SU works out to about 1,644 MB/s. PCWorld's 450 GB write on the UGREEN CM642, ChatGPT's 'best for sustained transfers' pick, was slower than a couple of 20Gbps (about 2 GB/s) USB 3.2×2 SSDs, even though the enclosure 'never suffered any thermal related issues'.
angles.decides: The CM642 stays the pick for long copies, but for a narrower reason: in PCWorld's 450 GB test it finished without the thermal dropout that stopped the UGREEN CM850, not because it holds about 3.8 GB/s. On copies of hundreds of GB, the SSD's speed after its cache fills and the copy tool (PCWorld saw Explorer vs FastCopy differences on the PA40SU) limit speed more than the enclosure's fan does. The table should show three numbers for each enclosure: the maker's peak, the host-specific cap (Apple Silicon or Thunderbolt), and any long-copy figure. The footnote should say that a 'no throttle' long write lands around 1.6–2 GB/s.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Windows' default 'Quick Removal' write-cache policy cut the UGREEN CM642's single-queue sequential write from 2,523.54 to 1,375.07 MB/s in cdrinfo's test. On 1 TB that is about 12.1 minutes instead of about 6.6, a slowdown that has nothing to do with heat.
angles.decides: The UGREEN CM642 pick stands; only its own figures change. With Windows' Quick Removal setting on, a one-file copy runs at about half the enclosure's speed, so 'no throttling' is worth little unless the shopper switches the drive to Better Performance. This is one enclosure on one SSD (Crucial T710), so it does not rank the CM642 against the OWC Express 1M2 or TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus. PCWorld also says the CM642's 450 GB write time was slower than a couple of 20Gbps USB 3.2×2 SSDs it had tested. That fits ChatGPT's caveat that on long copies the SSD inside, not the 40Gbps link, sets the speed.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that OWC's own Express 1M2 manual says it runs at only USB 10Gb/s on Thunderbolt 3 hosts. Sabrent rates its fan-cooled EC-U4TN at 2,700 MB/s over Thunderbolt, against 990 MB/s in OWC's table for a 10Gb/s link. So on an Intel Thunderbolt 3 Mac or PC, ChatGPT's quiet fanless pick is about a third as fast as a fan model before any throttling starts.
angles.decides: This settles the pick for shoppers whose host is Thunderbolt 3 (Intel Mac or older PC): avoid the OWC Express 1M2, which OWC caps at USB 10Gb/s there. Prefer an enclosure whose maker states a Thunderbolt speed: Sabrent EC-U4TN says 2,700 MB/s over Thunderbolt and has a fan. It confirms the existing picks for Apple silicon and USB4/TB4 PCs (OWC: 3,189 MB/s on Apple silicon, 3,836 MB/s on a PC). Two caveats for every pick: use the 40Gbps cable in the box, and don't use an SSD with a heatsink in the 1M2.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that thermal throttling happens inside the SSD itself. The drive's own firmware drops to lower-power states once its composite temperature passes the drive's own thermal-management thresholds. The drive counts each of those events and the seconds spent in them in its standard NVMe health log (Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 transition count and total time). Comparing those counters before and after a long copy is how you tell real throttling from the SLC-cache slowdown that ChatGPT and itechguides could not separate.
angles.decides: This shifts the advice from which enclosure to which enclosure plus which SSD. No enclosure can switch off throttling. It can only keep the SSD under thresholds the SSD's maker sets, and on bus power it has a limited power budget. A Thunderbolt 4 port must supply at least 15 W to accessories, and a plain USB4 port is required to supply half that. That supports the fan model (UGREEN CM642) for multi-hundred-GB copies paired with an efficient Gen4 SSD rather than a Gen5 one. It also gives the page a test anyone can repeat, which rivals lack: log the drive's thermal-management counters during a long copy. If they don't move while speed drops, the cause is the SLC cache, not heat. Caveat: I did not confirm that every ASM2464PD enclosure passes the NVMe health log through to the host. One commenter saw a UGREEN CM850 show up as 'ASMT 2464 USB drive (UAS)' in USBView.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Macworld ran a one-hour Blackmagic test on the OWC Express 1M2 (Thomas Bergbold, Aug 19 2024): the transfer rate did not drop and the case reached about 40 °C. Hardware Busters ran a 15-minute stress test on the TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus in a 30 °C room (Sep 4 2025) and saw no thermal throttling, with a 54.8 °C maximum.
angles.decides: The finding backs the passive pick: the OWC Express 1M2 (one hour, no speed drop, about 40 °C) and the TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus (15 minutes at 30 °C ambient, no throttling, 54.8 °C maximum; NAS Compares 2,550–2,600 MB/s write in an AJA loop) both have named long-run tests with no throttling. That undercuts the 'mixed' and 'poor thermal' claims. The fan pick, the UGREEN CM642, still has PCWorld's 450 GB write with no thermal issues. Its sibling the CM850 lost the drive during that same write with its sleeve on, which shows enclosure cooling matters on the same chip. The page can then say that the one named failure under a long load went to the sleeved CM850 and the passive ZIKE Z666. The finned OWC and TerraMaster bodies and the fan-cooled CM642 held up in every named test.

pages.why_used: The QNAP spec page, Starry Hope and Notebookcheck all call each Intel box 'Quick Sync' and leave it there. None of them gives the iGPU size behind it. Intel ARK lists 80 execution units on the DXP6800 Pro's i5-1235U, 24 on both TVS-h674 CPUs and 16 on the TS-664's N5095. Intel's footnote adds that the 80-EU part is branded Iris Xe only with dual-channel memory, and the Pro ships with one stick. This page states all of that, along with QNAP's own prices for the 10GbE card each QNAP needs.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the QNAP TVS-h674's 'faster' desktop CPU (i5-12400 / i3-12100) has a 24-EU UHD 730 iGPU, against 80 EU on the i5-1235U (UGREEN DXP6800 Pro, TerraMaster F6-424 Max), 64 EU on the i3-1315U (TerraMaster F6-425 Pro) and 80 EU on the Core 5 120U (DXP6800 Ultra). The footnote: Intel's 'Iris Xe' name for the 80-EU part applies only with dual-channel memory, and Notebookcheck found the DXP6800 Pro ships with a single 8 GB module.
angles.decides: It supports the existing pick, DXP6800 Pro (or F6-424 Max) over the TVS-h674 for a Plex-first buyer. The $2,139–2,349 QNAP pairs its stronger CPU with the smallest iGPU in the group (24 EU vs 80), and it still needs a 10GbE card. Inference with no named source: EU count matters most for GPU-shader work such as HDR tone mapping, while basic decode/encode runs on the fixed-function Quick Sync media engine. The single-module footnote gives a cheap tweak, not a pick change: fill the second SO-DIMM slot so the i5-1235U runs dual-channel (Intel's Iris Xe condition). I found no named measurement of what single-channel memory costs Plex on these units.
products: UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Pro / TerraMaster F6-424 Max (Intel Core i5-1235U)

The TS-873A needs a QNAP-supported NVIDIA card that takes no power cable, in one of its two PCIe Gen3 x4 slots, set to QTS mode. It changes how the QNAP should be presented: the TS-873A can transcode, but only by giving one of its two PCIe slots to a graphics card, so a GPU plus 10GbE uses both slots. The DS1825+ stays a storage-only or direct-play pick: its single slot can hold a 10GbE card or nothing else, and no graphics card is listed for it.

At the EIA 2026 year-to-date US residential rate of 18.19¢/kWh and the makers' own power figures, that comes to $112.16/yr for the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus during drive access ($46.19 with drives hibernated), $95.77 ($29.22) for the Synology DS1825+, $86.15 ($40.90) for the QNAP TS-873A and $106.60 ($59.28) for the Asustor AS6508T.

The UGREEN costs about $16–17 a year more to run than the DS1825+ under both maker test states ($112.16 − $95.77 = $16.39 in access; $46.19 − $29.22 = $16.97 hibernated), or roughly $82–85 over five years. On the QNAP TS-873A, Plex hardware transcoding means buying a separate entry-level NVIDIA card with no power connector, running it in QTS mode (not shared with VMs), and depending on QNAP's NVIDIA driver packages. One Plex forum user reported GTX 1650 transcoding on a TS-873A failing after a QTS 5.2.3 update with no fix posted. The DXP8800 Plus has Quick Sync on the CPU, so it needs no card. For a media library with transcoding, the TS-873A only makes sense if the buyer accepts the card cost and driver risk. Several of them, and ChatGPT's answers, tell shoppers to pass the iGPU to a Docker VM, which is the layout Plex says won't work. This page uses Plex's and Proxmox's documentation to put Plex in a container on the host and keep the VMs off the GPU. It then compares all-in-one boxes by the RAM they ship with, since that decides whether two VMs fit under $800.

(1) Plex transcoding: for the branch where media drives go inside the box, the AMD boxes fall out (WTR Pro 5825U, WTR Max 8845HS, GMKtec K8 Plus) because Plex documents no hardware transcoding for them on Linux. That leaves Intel bay boxes: the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus at $619.99 with 8 GB included, or the Aoostar WTR Max Intel i5-1235U at $529 barebone with 6 HDD bays, 2× 10GbE and DDR5 up to 96 GB, before RAM. (2) Price on one basis: price every option as configured with 32 GB RAM and 1 TB NVMe, no hard drives. On that basis the 'cheap' $375 MS-01 SE barebone becomes $775 and the MS-01's DDR5 is costlier still: bitdoze priced a 32 GB DDR5 kit at $569.98. The Synology DS925+ has the lowest maker-stated draw with drives spun down, which supports the 'stay with Synology for photos and backup' caveat.

pages.why_used: StereoNET (cited in all three chats) lists the W-1200 only as having 'noise reduction'. Tape Lab gives no specs. Home Audio Advice says the W-1200 'includes Dolby B noise reduction', which implies it records with Dolby B. None of them says that both new decks have one shared record/play head and that their noise reduction works only on playback, so no tape they record carries Dolby encoding. Nor do they say that neither deck can record on metal tape, or that the vintage picks have separate record and playback heads with separate Dolby encode and decode circuits. That is the reason behind the 'buy new or buy vintage' split, and this page puts it into the table for six decks.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on the same WRMS scale the new TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII are rated at 0.25% wow and flutter. That is 11–13 times the 0.019% to 0.022% the Nakamichi Dragon and Sony TC-KA7ES are rated at. The new decks' frequency response is also quoted at a looser ±4 dB and stops at 15 kHz, while the vintage decks reach 22 kHz at ±3 dB.
angles.decides: It confirms the split pick and puts a number on it. For playback fidelity, a serviced vintage 3-head deck is in a different class: rated speed stability is 11–13 times better on the same WRMS basis. On paper, though, S/N is not the gap: the TEAC's 59 dB A-weighted and the TC-KA7ES's 57 dB with Dolby off are about the same. For the 'buy new' pick, the TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII have identical makers' deck specs (0.25% WRMS; 30 Hz–15 kHz ±4 dB on Type II tape; Dolby B-equivalent playback NR only). So the choice between them comes down to price, the remote, and rack mounting, not sound. Footnote for the table: the Revox B215's '0.1%' is a DIN 45507 peak-weighted maximum, not WRMS, so it can't be ranked against the 0.25% WRMS figures. Reviewers measured it at 0.01–0.042% RMS.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that how bright a laser looks equals its power times the eye's sensitivity at its wavelength. By the CIE 1988 photopic table, the eye's sensitivity is 0.710 at 520 nm and 0.885 at 532 nm (green) but 0.107 at 650 nm (red). That makes a green laser look about 6.6–8.3× brighter than a red laser of the same power. Because the laser class caps power (Class 2 at 1 mW, Class 3R at 5 mW), a green Class 3R laser can look about 5× brighter than a green Class 2 laser like the Klein 56074, and about 33× brighter than a 1 mW, 650 nm red Class 2 laser.
angles.decides: This confirms that the main pick should be a green Class 3R light (the US Wuben X5 3R or the US Olight ArkPro) for anyone who wants to point at things at a distance or in daylight. The arithmetic: the 5 mW Class 3R cap × 0.710 = 3.55 brightness-weighted mW. A Class 2 green like the Klein 56074 (<1 mW) gives under 0.71, and a 1 mW, 650 nm red Class 2 gives 0.107. So ChatGPT's 'Best for work' Klein 56074 has at most a fifth of a 3R laser's visible brightness, and its red budget picks (Hyper Tough, Coast PM50R, Fenix E06R, Klein 56040) are far dimmer still. The same arithmetic means a Class 1 green at the 0.39 mW our page lists for the Wuben X5 Class 1 (0.39 × 0.710 = 0.277) would still look about 2.6× brighter than a 1 mW, 650 nm red. That gives the X5 Class 1 a sourced reason to rank above red lasers for workplaces that ban Class 3R.

The Racks & Watts homelab guide, UGREEN's buying guides, Synology's data sheets and the Audiobookshelf and Calibre-Web docs list no watts or dB(A) measured with drives fitted, even though the box runs 24/7 in a family home. Neither sheet names the drives it used, and Synology's 'Access' and QNAP's 'typical operating' are not the same state.

On the makers' own sheets the DS225+ is cheaper to run than the QNAP TS-264-8G whether its disks are spinning or not. Arithmetic on the published figures: DS225+ at 16.98 W comes to about 149 kWh/yr, and Dong Knows measured about 100 kWh/yr with two HDDs. QNAP comes to 160 kWh/yr at disk standby and 255 kWh/yr at typical operating. That weakens the TS-264 as an alternative. For the DXP2800 I could only find a measurement with no hard drives, so the DS225+ vs DXP2800 comparison stays open on power. The pick between those two should still rest on RAM (8 GB vs 2 GB) and price.

The UGREEN DXP2800 family costs $11–$32 a year, depending on the idle draw a named reviewer measured. Over five years that is $50–$160, well below the gap in purchase price and RAM between the two.

Running costs for the DS225+ and DXP2800 are within about $5–$15 a year of each other, so electricity can't make up for the DS225+'s 2 GB RAM (6 GB maximum, and non-Synology RAM voids its warranty). pages.query: best nas for running frigate to record security cameras
pages.why_used: Frigate's hardware page states an AVX + AVX2 rule but names no NAS. The 0.17 FAQ links 'illegal instruction' crashes to missing AVX. No cited page checks the CPUs in the QNAP TS-464, Synology DS225+ and Asustor AS5402T against Intel's instruction-set listings, and Intel lists all three as SSE4.2 only. The pages still recommended the TS-464 as a Frigate box. This page checks each candidate's CPU on Intel's spec page and pairs it with a measured OpenVINO time for the pick's own CPU. Angle D has the fullest sourcing for this: the 0.17 FAQ, Intel spec pages, and maker CPU pages for QNAP, Synology and Asustor.

Frigate's hardware page names AVX + AVX2 as its CPU requirement, and the N100, N150 and Pentium Gold 8505 inside the UGREEN and TerraMaster picks all list AVX2.
angles.decides: The finding takes the QNAP TS-464, both Synology J4125 models and the Asustor AS5402T off any 'run Frigate on the NAS' shortlist. All of them say 'Intel x86 with UHD graphics' on the box, but none meets Frigate's stated CPU floor. A Frigate maintainer has also said Celeron is not officially supported for OpenVINO. That leaves the Intel AVX2 choices: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus (Pentium Gold 8505), N100 boxes such as the UGREEN DXP2800, and N150 boxes such as the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus. It supports keeping the DXP4800 Plus as the top pick. Our page's table needs fixing, because the TS-464 and AS5402T rows currently say 'OpenVINO'.

pages.query: best nas for streaming a flac music library with navidrome or plexamp
pages.why_used: The Plex, Navidrome and UGREEN pages shoppers see for this question say only 'very low resource usage' or 'CPU-intensive'. None of them turns any NAS's wattage into a yearly cost for a server that stays on all the time, and none warns that the makers test with different numbers of drives. This page converts each maker's access and hibernation watts into kWh and dollars per year and checks them against what reviewers measured with two drives.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers' disk-standby power figures can't be compared directly. Each maker tests differently: UGREEN measured the DXP2800 with one 2 TB HDD hibernating (5.24 W), QNAP measured the TS-264 with both bays full (18.288 W), and Synology (6.08 W) and Asustor (12.7 W) don't say which drives they used.
angles.decides: The finding supports the N100 UGREEN DXP2800 as the pick for an always-on Navidrome/Plexamp box. Its 5.24 W maker figure was measured with one 2 TB drive, and OCinside's two-HDD RAID 1 test came out at about 7 W idle (as reported by starryhope), so its low figure holds up with two drives. The QNAP TS-264 looks about 3x worse on paper (18.288 W against 6.08 W for the DS225+), but QNAP tested with both bays full and the others didn't, so part of that gap is the test, not the hardware. The page should show the spec-sheet numbers in one column and the footnoted conditions in the next, and should not rank on the raw figures. At the spec-sheet disk-standby figures, 24/7 use comes to about 46 kWh/yr (UGREEN), 53 kWh/yr (Synology), 111 kWh/yr (Asustor) and 160 kWh/yr (QNAP). That spread matters more than CPU speed for a FLAC server. Sonic Analysis needs x86 (Plex), which rules out the DH2300 and other ARM units for Plexamp's analysis features but doesn't choose between the four x86 units.

Using the makers' own access and hibernation wattages at the EIA's August 2026 US residential rate of 18.16¢/kWh, with 4 h/day of drive access and 20 h/day hibernated, that comes to about $8/yr for the UGREEN DH2300, $11/yr for the DXP2800, $13/yr for the Synology DS225+, $23/yr for the Asustor AS5402T and $32/yr for the QNAP TS-264. The TS-264 draws more with its disks asleep (18.3 W) than the DXP2800 does while reading (16.38 W).

It weakens the TS-264, which costs about $20.67/yr more than the DXP2800 to run, or about $103 over 5 years, on top of a higher price. For a Navidrome-only shopper, the ARM DH2300 is cheapest overall: $239.99 plus about $40 of power over 5 years, against $389.99 plus about $56 for the DXP2800. It can't run Plex's Sonic Analysis.

That is less than a 24-bit/96 kHz FLAC stream needs (measured at 3,129 kbps), so lossless hi-res playback away from home depends on port forwarding or a VPN, whichever NAS you buy.

pages.query: which nas is best for running nextcloud as my own cloud
pages.why_used: The rival pages that were cited (racksandwatts, esp32, the AIO readme) give only CPU names and RAM. None has a benchmark, so nothing shows that the DS925+'s 'AMD Ryzen', presented as the premium choice, is the slowest per core on the shortlist. This page adds PassMark single-thread and CPU Mark scores for all six candidates, plus a Docker Engine/API column that turns 'Docker support' into a comparable figure.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the Docker Engine version each NAS OS ships, or how that compares with the Docker API v1.44 that Nextcloud AIO uses by default. UGREEN UGOS Pro (29.6.2, API ≤1.55), ASUSTOR (29.6.2), QNAP Container Station (27.1.2, API 1.46) and TerraMaster TOS (27.2.1, API 1.47) all meet it. Synology DSM Container Manager (24.0.2, API 1.43), on the DS925+ and DS225+, is the only one below it. AIO's Docker socket proxy and AppAPI fail there unless you override the API version, which the AIO maintainers say they don't support or test.
angles.decides: This backs the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or DXP2800 as the pick for running Nextcloud AIO as shipped, and it weakens the DS925+, which ChatGPT called the 'best software experience' or 'best overall'. On DSM, AIO needs the DOCKER_API_VERSION override that the maintainers don't support, or the Docker Socket Proxy (needed by AppAPI/ExApps) turned off. Synology has kept Container Manager on Docker 24.0.2, which reached end of life in June 2024, through its August 2026 package update. QNAP and TerraMaster meet 1.44 but run older engines than UGREEN and ASUSTOR. Footnote for the table: the 'Docker support' tick every rival shows is not equal across brands.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out what it costs to keep each NAS running all day and night, which a Nextcloud server must do: at the US average home rate of 18.16¢/kWh (August 2026), the makers' own power figures come to about $60 a year for the Synology DS925+, $64 for the QNAP TS-464 and $27 for the Synology DS225+ with the drives awake, versus $20, $34 and $10 with the drives asleep.
angles.decides: This confirms the shortlist rather than changing it. The QNAP TS-464 costs the most to run in the makers' own figures: 40.5 W typical against 37.9 W for the DS925+ while drives are being accessed (about $4 more a year), and 21.6 W against 12.3 W with drives asleep (about $15 more a year). So its $639 price edge over the DS925+ ($829.99 at Micro Center in ChatGPT's answer) shrinks a little over 5 years. The DS225+ is by far the cheapest to run, about $27 a year, but tops out at 6 GB of RAM, short of the 16 GB ChatGPT recommends. Nextcloud's background jobs every 5 minutes tend to keep the hard drives from sleeping unless its data sits on SSD, so the drives-awake figure is the realistic one. That makes 'put the database on NVMe' a running-cost point as well as a speed point. For the DXP4800 Plus I could only source a reviewer's idle reading (KitGuru, 24.25 W, about $39 a year), which isn't comparable with the maker figures.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, as of November 2026, Synology's Container Manager still runs Docker Engine 24.0.2, which tops out at Docker API 1.43. That is below the v1.44 that Nextcloud AIO's own code calls by default, so on the DS925+ or DS225+ AIO only runs if you override the API version, a setup AIO's maintainers say they don't support. The UGREEN DXP models (29.6.2), Asustor (29.6.2), TerraMaster (27.2.1) and QNAP (27.1.2) all ship engines at or above 1.44.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's choice of the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or DXP2800 over the DS925+ for Nextcloud AIO. UGOS Pro's Docker 29.6.2 meets AIO's default API with nothing to configure. On the DS925+ (and DS225+) the shopper has to run AIO with DOCKER_API_VERSION overridden on an engine that went end-of-life in 2024, and also mount Synology's own socket path. Container Manager's GUI can't manage AIO, so it's run over SSH or a scheduled task, and AppAPI/External Apps errors have been reported. The DS925+ can still put its database on NVMe, but only with Synology-verified SSDs for an M.2 pool. QNAP, TerraMaster and Asustor all clear the API bar. In UGREEN's cheaper home line, the DS2300 should read DH2300: it has no official Docker, so it drops out for AIO, while the DH4300 Plus does officially support Docker.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Nextcloud All-in-One calls the Docker Engine API at a pinned v1.44 by default, while Synology's Container Manager is still built on Docker Engine 24.0.2 (newest build 24.0.2-1707, 2026-11-05), whose highest API is 1.43. On the DS925+ and DS225+, AIO therefore needs an SSH install with a DOCKER_API_VERSION override that Nextcloud says it does not support. UGREEN's UGOS Pro ships Engine 29.6.2, which needs no override.
angles.decides: It confirms UGREEN (DXP2800 / DXP4800 Plus) as the pick for Nextcloud AIO and pushes the Synology DS925+ down. DS925+ owners can't use AIO's default, supported setup from the Container Manager GUI. They need SSH or Task Scheduler as root, a custom socket path and DOCKER_API_VERSION=1.43, which the AIO readme says is not supported or tested by the maintainers. One DSM owner on Container Manager 24.0.2 reported the AIO mastercontainer warning that 'only v1.44 is officially supported' and AppAPI failing in a loop. QNAP (Engine 27.1.2) and TerraMaster (27.2.1) are above API 1.44, so the default works there. Shoppers who stay on Synology should be told to plan for the override, or to use the community nextcloud/docker image with Compose, which doesn't drive the Docker API.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that PassMark rates the DS925+'s Ryzen V1500B at 1,136 single-thread, about the same as the DS225+'s J4125 (1,151), below the TS-464's N5095 (1,492) and the DXP2800's N100 (1,879), and about a third of the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium Gold 8505 (3,197).
angles.decides: Our page wouldn't be making its own speed claim: PassMark's database ranks the V1500B last of the five for single-thread work. That speed decides how quickly each web request completes, which matters for an app like Nextcloud. The figures back the DXP4800 Plus as the pick when performance matters (2.8× the DS925+ single-thread, 2.0× its multi-thread at 8,997 vs 4,513). The DXP2800 ($ cheaper, N100) still beats the DS925+ per core (1,879 vs 1,136), and igor'sLAB measured it at only 14.5 W during transfers. So the DS925+ comes down to DSM software and ECC memory, not speed. Measured power doesn't penalise the faster UGREEN much: KitGuru measured the DXP4800 Plus idling at 24.25 W, and NAS Compares measured the DS925+ at about 28 W.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the plan works without extra setup only if Paperless-ngx runs on the NAS itself. On the NAS, the scanner pushes over SMB to a folder the NAS stores locally, so Linux inotify sees each new file. Put Paperless on a Pi or mini PC with its consume folder on an NFS or SMB share from the NAS, and the project says new files are not picked up under the default settings and the container's chown can fail with 'Operation not permitted'.

It also clears a v3 risk: v3's NumPy needs x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2) or the classifier crashes with SIGILL, and Intel lists SSE4.2 for both the J4125 (DS225+, DS224+) and the N5105 (AS5402T), so those budget Celerons are safe.

pages.query: best nas for photographers with 10 tb of raw files who edit in lightroom
pages.why_used: Fstoppers and Camera Lookout, the two rival pages cited for this question, repeat Synology's 522/565 MB/s headline and give 2.5GbE's raw ceiling. Neither works out what one editing computer actually gets. This page does that from the makers' test notes and MightyGadget's hard-drive test: 500–600 MB/s from the DXP4800 Plus over 10GbE against 295 MB/s on one 2.5GbE link, about 2× rather than 4×. It also gives QNAP's own measured drop to 275 MB/s with small files.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the makers' MB/s headlines into what one editing computer actually gets: Synology's 522 MB/s for the DS925+ is more than one 2.5GbE link can carry (312.5 MB/s raw), so one Mac gets about 295 MB/s, the figure QNAP measured on a single 2.5GbE link. A 10GbE box with four hard drives in RAID 5 gives one client 500–600 MB/s in MightyGadget's test. That is about 2× faster, not the 4× the port speeds suggest, and QNAP's own chart shows a single 10GbE link falling to 275 MB/s when the files are 1 MB each.
angles.decides: This supports the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus ($619.99 at UGREEN's store on 2026-11-08) as the pick for one photographer editing on one computer. For large transfers such as imports, exports and preview builds, its built-in 10GbE port with four HDDs in RAID 5 gives one client about 500–600 MB/s, roughly twice what a DS925+ can give one client (about 295 MB/s, with no PCIe slot to upgrade). The DS925+'s 522/565 MB/s needs both ports and several clients, which a single editor will not see. The QNAP TS-464 can reach 10GbE speeds, but only by using its one PCIe slot (Gen 3 x2) for the card. The footnote: 10GbE helps with batch work, not opening one RAW file at a time. With 1 MB files, QNAP's own single 10GbE link read 274.94 MB/s, about the same as one 2.5GbE link with large files. So a shopper who edits from local copies and only archives to the NAS can stay on 2.5GbE.

The only 4-bay candidate with built-in 10GbE costs about $8.50 a year more to run than the DS925+, which cannot add 10GbE at all. That is about $42 over five years, so power is not a reason to choose the Synology. The QNAP TS-464 costs the most to run of the four, because its disk-standby draw of 21.6 W is the highest. It also still needs a 10GbE card to match the UGREEN. A second derived point is worth stating: Synology's headline 565 MB/s write for the DS925+ is more than one 2.5GbE port can carry (312.5 MB/s raw). So a single editing computer on one cable stays at or below 312.5 MB/s, which means at least 8.9 h to load 10 TB. Camera Lookout quotes the 565 MB/s figure without saying this.

If the TS-464 gets a QXG-10G1T card, the NAS needs QTS 5.2.9 or later, and the card sits in a PCIe Gen 3 x2 slot.

Adobe sells the other app, Lightroom, as 'the cloud-based service' to 'create, edit, organize, store, and share your photos across any device', and both its $11.99/mo Lightroom plan and its $19.99/mo Photography plan include 1 TB, a tenth of a 10 TB RAW library. The whole plan (originals on the NAS, catalog and previews on a local SSD, 2.5GbE or 10GbE link) depends on the shopper using Lightroom Classic. The page should say so in the first lines. For someone on the cloud-based Lightroom app, the library lives in Adobe's cloud under a 1 TB plan, so a NAS can only be a backup or export target. In that case the 10GbE premium (DXP4800 Plus or GT over the DS925+ or TS-464) buys little, and the bigger question is Adobe storage. For Classic users the picks stand. pages.query: best nas to run pi-hole or adguard home plus a wireguard vpn for the house
pages.why_used: None of the cited pages (Synology's Container Manager page, UGREEN's DXP2800 page, the racksandwatts guides) says that DSM 7.3 runs Linux 4.4.302+ while WireGuard entered the kernel in 5.6. That means the 'run WireGuard in a container on the DS225+' route fails on stock DSM. This page sets each NAS OS's WireGuard route and kernel next to the deciding specs, and the pick rests on UGOS Pro's 6.18 kernel.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers' low idle figures are drive-hibernation numbers taken under different setups (UGREEN: one Seagate 2 TB drive; QNAP: all bays filled; Synology: setup not stated), or that UGREEN says Docker containers and always-active databases keep the drives from hibernating. So for a 24/7 DNS and VPN box the figures that compare are the drives-active ones: DXP2800 16.38 W, DS225+ 16.98 W, TS-264 29.086 W.
angles.decides: This backs the DXP2800 as the NAS pick, and it adds a cost against the QNAP TS-264, the only maker-confirmed native WireGuard server among the candidates. With containers running, the drive-asleep figures (5.24 / 6.08 / 18.288 W) don't apply, because UGREEN itself says Docker containers and always-active databases block hibernation. The like-for-like figures are 16.38 W (DXP2800), 16.98 W (DS225+) and 29.086 W (TS-264). That works out to about 143 kWh, 149 kWh and 255 kWh a year. So the TS-264's built-in WireGuard costs about 111 kWh a year more than a DXP2800 running WireGuard in a container. The DS225+ has nearly the same power draw as the DXP2800, but its makers' page lists no M.2 slot, so containers can't be moved off the hard drives to let them sleep. Its VPN Server also has no WireGuard. Both points favour the DXP2800 or TS-264 for anyone who wants the drives to sleep. Also normalised: native WireGuard on the stock OS. QNAP QVPN: yes (QNAP's own page). Synology DSM VPN Server: no (OpenVPN, L2TP/IPsec, PPTP only). UGREEN UGOS Pro: OpenVPN and WireGuard according to VPN Tracker only; no UGREEN page found.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the yearly electricity cost of leaving each candidate on 24/7 as the house DNS and VPN box, worked out from each maker's rated idle draw at the 2026 US average residential rate (EIA, 18.19 ¢/kWh year to date). The range runs from about $5 a year for a Raspberry Pi 5 to $10 for a Synology DS225+ with its disks asleep, $20 for an Asustor AS5402T and $29 for a QNAP TS-264 with its drives in standby.
angles.decides: Running 24/7 is the whole job here, so yearly power cost is the real gap between candidates. With disks asleep, the DS225+ (6.08 W, about $9.69 a year) and DXP2800 (about 7 W, about $11 a year) cost about the same to run. The QNAP TS-264 (18.288 W in disk standby, about $29 a year; 29.086 W operating, about $46) costs roughly 3× as much. Over 5 years that is about $146 to $232 for the QNAP against about $48 for the DS225+, which cancels a large part of the QNAP's main advantage, its native WireGuard server. A Pi 5 at about 3 W costs about $5 a year. That supports ChatGPT's advice to use a separate small box if the shopper doesn't need storage. One caution that is my own inference, not something a source said: the DS225+ has no NVMe storage pool (racksandwatts spec list), so Pi-hole or AdGuard containers would sit on the hard drives. Constant query logging could then stop the disks from sleeping, which moves it toward its 16.98 W access figure (about $27 a year). The DXP2800 can keep containers on NVMe.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which NAS operating systems have a maker-documented WireGuard server. Only QNAP and Asustor document one. QNAP's QVPN Service 3.0 offers it on x86 models only, and the TS-264 is x86. Asustor's VPN Server 1.1.0.r327 adds it, and Asustor's own App Central AdGuard Home package covers the Nimbustor 2 Gen2's AS54 series, so that NAS can run DNS filtering and WireGuard without Docker. Synology DSM 7.3 and TerraMaster TOS 6 list only OpenVPN, L2TP/IPsec and PPTP, and UGREEN has no maker document for its WireGuard server.
angles.decides: This changes the pick for a shopper who wants both services as maker-supported apps, with no Docker, macvlan or port-53 workarounds. The Asustor Nimbustor 2 Gen2 (AS5402T, AS54 series) is the only candidate where the maker's own App Central lists both a WireGuard VPN Server and AdGuard Home for its series. The QNAP TS-264 has a documented WireGuard server, but DNS filtering still goes through Container Station. Our current page says the AS54 series is not on Asustor's VPN Server list. That is wrong: the list I read on 2026-11-08 includes AS54. On the Synology DS225+ and TerraMaster F2-425 Plus, WireGuard needs a container or a community package. The UGREEN DXP2800's built-in WireGuard is backed only by VPN Tracker, a VPN software vendor. The DXP2800 can stay the best-hardware pick, but not the 'it's built in' pick.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Synology DSM runs Linux 4.4.302+, while WireGuard entered the mainline kernel only in Linux 5.6, so the 'WireGuard in a container' route ChatGPT suggested for the DS225+ (wg-easy or linuxserver/wireguard, both of which rely on the host's kernel module) has no module to use on stock DSM.
angles.decides: This moves the DS225+ out of 'best overall' for this plan. Pi-hole or AdGuard Home in Container Manager is fine. A WireGuard server, though, needs either an unofficial third-party kernel module (gpopesc build, tested only on a DS920+, 'at your own risk' class), Synology's native OpenVPN instead, or a userspace tool such as Tailscale. Gluetun is a userspace VPN client, so it does not provide a home VPN server. The UGREEN DXP2800 is confirmed as the pick: UGOS Pro 1.19.1 moved to kernel 6.18, well past 5.6, so wg-easy can use in-kernel WireGuard. TerraMaster says TOS 6 is built on Linux 6.1 LTS, which is past 5.6, but one TOS 6 beta owner reported the system actually ran 5.15.59 with WireGuard not working. QNAP (QVPN) and GL.iNet ship WireGuard as a built-in server and avoid the question.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured idle power for any of the candidates. ComputerBase measured the UGREEN DXP2800 at 18.6 W idle with two HDDs and 7.3 W with the HDDs in standby, and the same lab measured the J4125 Synology DS224+ at 18.6 W idle and 3.5 W in standby. PC-WELT measured the QNAP TS-264-8G at 26.5 W idle. ServeTheHome measured the GL.iNet Flint 2 at 5.6 W idle, and CNX Software measured it at 834–889 Mbps as a WireGuard server. For an always-on DNS + VPN box that is a 3–5× gap in power draw.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's own caveat that a router or Pi beats a NAS if the shopper needs only DNS + VPN, and it puts numbers on it. In ServeTheHome's test the Flint 2 idles at 5.6 W, about 49 kWh a year (5.6 W × 8,760 h). CNX Software measured it at 834–889 Mbps in WireGuard server mode. Jeff Geerling measured a Pi 5 8GB at 3.2 W, about 28 kWh a year. A DXP2800 whose HDDs keep spinning idles at 18.6 W in ComputerBase's test, about 163 kWh a year. For a shopper who also wants storage, the DXP2800 remains the NAS pick: ComputerBase measured it level with the Synology DS224+ at 18.6 W idle, and PC-WELT measured the QNAP TS-264 at 26.5 W idle, so it doesn't cost more to run. One condition goes with that pick: put the AdGuard/Pi-hole and WireGuard container data on the NVMe slot, not the HDD volume. Otherwise the HDDs can't reach the 7.3 W standby state.

pages.query: best nas to run proxmox or several virtual machines in a home lab
pages.why_used: The pages these answers relied on (Proxmox's requirements, QNAP's spec sheet, homelabpicks, computingforgeeks) give spec-sheet wattage at most. None of them measured wall power for the NAS and mini-PC hosts they recommended, and the one measured figure in reach (Notebookcheck's DXP6800 Pro review) was never cited. This page puts Notebookcheck's 11.8–15.9 W N5 Pro idle beside the DXP6800 Pro, DXP4800 Plus and MS-01 figures, and that comparison decides which box to run around the clock. It also adds the ZFS RAM arithmetic and the passthrough layouts owners reported.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Minisforum N5 Pro's three M.2 slots share four PCIe 4.0 lanes, split x1/x1/x2 (ServeTheHome), with the OS on one of the x1 slots, or that its 'x16' slot is wired x4. So the mirrored NVMe VM pool every ChatGPT answer recommends would run on an x2 and an x1 link, about 2 GB/s each way at most, while the QNAP TVS-h674's two M.2 slots are each Gen4 x4.
angles.decides: This confirms the N5 Pro as the CPU and RAM pick (12C/24T, 96 GB ECC) but changes how to build it: put the VM pool on an NVMe card in the x4 slot, or accept roughly 2 GB/s per drive. A shopper whose priority is fast mirrored NVMe VM storage with a free x16-length slot should look at the QNAP TVS-h674 (2× M.2 Gen4 x4, plus Gen4 x16 and x4 slots), at a much higher price. It also turns 'three NVMe slots' into one boot slot plus two narrow data slots, which matters for the 'two NVMe drives, mirrored' layout in all three ChatGPT answers.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works Proxmox's own memory rule (2 GB for the host plus 1 GB per TB of used ZFS storage) through for these 64 GB-ceiling NAS boxes. Done, it leaves 42 GB for guests with 20 TB of used ZFS data and 22 GB with 40 TB, so a full 6-bay pool takes about a third of the RAM before any VM starts.
angles.decides: This tempers the all-in-one pick. On any 64 GB-ceiling box (DXP4800 Plus, DXP6800 Pro, TVS-h674), filling the bays with a big ZFS pool cuts guest RAM to 22–42 GB, so 'several VMs plus TrueNAS-style ZFS' fits only with a modest pool or with VMs kept small. Per thread, the DXP6800 Pro is the cheapest UGREEN at $91.67, versus $103.33 for the DXP4800 Plus. For many VMs on top of a large pool, it points toward a box with a higher RAM ceiling. Intel lists 96 GB for the DXP4800 Pro's i3-1315U, but UGREEN's own ceiling for that box isn't sourced.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that UGREEN NASync boxes have a BIOS watchdog that keeps rebooting a non-UGOS OS such as Proxmox, TrueNAS or Unraid until it is turned off in the BIOS (Ctrl+F12 at the UGREEN logo), or that UGREEN's policy leaves the hardware warranty unchanged when you install a third-party system.
angles.decides: This confirms the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or DXP6800 Pro as the all-in-one Proxmox pick. Bare-metal Proxmox works once the watchdog is off, and per UGREEN's policy as the Debian wiki quotes it, the hardware warranty is unchanged. By contrast, homelabpicks says TerraMaster voids the warranty when you install another OS, and QNAP's TVS-h674 page lists only QTS and QuTS hero and says to use only QNAP memory. Where Proxmox is the main goal, this tips the choice toward UGREEN over TerraMaster.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro, ChatGPT's 'favorite all-in-one', splits its six bays across two SATA controllers (Intel Alder Lake-P AHCI at 00:17.0 plus an ASMedia ASM1164), while the DXP4800 Plus puts all four bays on a single ASM1164, so a TrueNAS VM under Proxmox gets every bay with one passthrough on the 4800 Plus but needs two on the 6800 Pro.
angles.decides: If the shopper's plan is Proxmox bare-metal with a TrueNAS VM that owns the drives, the DXP4800 Plus is the clean fit: one ASM1164 holds all 4 bays, and an owner passed it from the Proxmox GUI. On the DXP6800 Pro (and the DXP8800 Plus) one controller passthrough covers only some of the bays. You either pass both controllers, fall back to per-disk passthrough (an owner saw TrueNAS SCALE refuse a RAIDZ because the vDisks lacked unique serials), or let Proxmox run ZFS itself. On any UGREEN, the BIOS watchdog has to be turned off first or the box reboots about every 3 minutes without UGOS.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Notebookcheck measured the Minisforum N5 Pro (Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370, 12C/24T) idling at 11.8–15.9 W. That is below the drive-less UGREEN DXP6800 Pro (up to 22.4 W, Notebookcheck), the Minisforum MS-01 (25–29 W, ServeTheHome) and the MS-A2 (25 W, ServeTheHome), so the strongest VM box in the lineup also measured lowest at idle.
angles.decides: For a box running Proxmox around the clock, idle draw is the running cost. The N5 Pro has the most CPU of the candidates (Notebookcheck: Cinebench R23 multi 21,474) and still measured the lowest drive-less idle, so the extra cores cost nothing at idle. That backs the N5 Pro over the DXP6800 Pro for a VM-heavy all-in-one. pages.why_used: The cited Synology spec and KB pages say only that immutable snapshots exist 'on supported Synology models'. This page shows which NAS keeps a snapshot of the Veeam/Macrium SMB share that the share login saved on every PC can't delete: Synology's immutable snapshots, QNAP's that work only on QuTS hero, and the locks on Asustor, TerraMaster and UGREEN that only stop automatic cleanup.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the word 'immutable' or 'lock' means different things across NAS brands. On the Synology DS225+, an immutable snapshot can't be deleted by anyone until its protection period ends. On the QNAP TS-264 the same protection exists only after a switch from QTS to QuTS hero h6, and then deleting a protected folder needs a Secure Deletion USB key. On Asustor, TerraMaster and UGREEN, a 'locked' snapshot is only skipped by automatic cleanup and can still be deleted by hand. A third-party UGREEN API client found that a locked snapshot 'is deleted just the same' through the API. This matters because Veeam Agent and Macrium write to an SMB share whose credentials sit on every PC.
angles.decides: This confirms the Synology DS225+ as the pick when the backup target is an SMB share written by Veeam Agent Free or Macrium. Its product page says it supports immutable snapshots, so a ransomware-hit PC holding the share password can't delete the snapshot behind the backup files. The QNAP TS-264 can match this, but only after a switch from its default QTS to QuTS hero h6.0.2 (TS-264 is on the applicable-models list). The cells for the Asustor AS5402T, TerraMaster F2-425 Plus and UGREEN DXP2800/DH2300 should read 'lock (stops automatic cleanup, can still be deleted)', not anything that suggests immutability. A cheap 2-bay is fine if a second offline copy covers ransomware. If the NAS snapshot is meant to be the ransomware layer, that rules out every candidate except Synology Plus and QuTS-hero QNAP.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Veeam Agent for Windows cannot wake a PC that uses Modern Standby for a scheduled backup and does not start scheduled backups while the PC is in Modern Standby, and that Veeam Free allows only one backup job. They also don't state that the NAS makers' own image agents need BitLocker turned off before backup (QNAP HDP PC Agent) or decrypted (Synology ABB on DSM 7.3), while Veeam only needs the volume unlocked.
angles.decides: This confirms that a basic SMB NAS is enough when the PCs run Veeam Agent Free. Veeam supports a network shared folder target, a daily schedule and unlocked BitLocker volumes. The Modern Standby limit applies whichever NAS you buy, so the page should tell shoppers to leave the PCs awake or plugged in at the backup time, or to use the backup-on-lock or log-off triggers. It weakens the argument that 'Synology Active Backup for Business may eliminate your need for Veeam or Macrium', and the same goes for QNAP's HDP PC Agent. On BitLocker-encrypted PCs, both makers tell you to decrypt or turn BitLocker off first, and both say BitLocker has to be turned back on after a full restore. So for encrypted PCs, Veeam to a share on any Btrfs NAS (DS225+, DXP2800, TS-264) is the cleaner route than the NAS maker's agent. If shoppers buy a DS225+ or DS425+, they can fit their own hard drives on DSM 7.3. M.2 pools and cache still need drives from Synology's list.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that Windows 11 24H2 Pro requires SMB signing and blocks guest access to shares. Because of that, the Veeam Agent (or Macrium) target has to be a NAS share that allows signing, opened with a named NAS user account. If you skip credentials, Veeam connects as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Also, Veeam's scheduled nightly job won't start on a PC that is sleeping in Modern Standby.
angles.decides: It confirms the plan rather than changing which NAS to buy. Every candidate runs a Samba-based SMB server, so each can work, as long as you create a NAS user per PC (or one backup user), give it Full Control of the share, enter those credentials in the Veeam or Macrium job and in the recovery media, and leave guest access off. What really decides whether 'nightly' happens is the PCs, not the NAS: on a laptop or desktop that sleeps in Modern Standby, Veeam won't start the scheduled job, so set 'Backup once powered on' or keep the PCs awake. With Veeam Free, each PC gets exactly one backup job, has no synthetic fulls, and keeps 7 days of restore points by default. That favours a NAS with Btrfs snapshots underneath for longer history, which points to the DS225+/DS425+, DXP2800, F2-425 Plus or AS5402T over the ext4-only DS223j.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how fast these NAS boxes actually take a Windows image. Blackvoid timed Synology Active Backup for Business making the first full backup of a Windows 11 PC to a DS225+: 60.3 GB in just under 12 minutes (85 MB/s), stored as just over 40 GB after deduplication.
