pages.query: which nas has thunderbolt 4 so a mac can connect directly to it
pages.why_used: The cited QNAP and UGREEN pages give only rated figures: QNAP's 20 Gbps networking cap, and UGREEN's '40Gbps link' plus speed ranges it says are not its own test results. None of them gives a speed that a named reviewer measured over the Thunderbolt cable. This page puts the StorageReview, Liliputing, MacSources, Club386, Samsung Magazine and QNAP Labs measurements side by side, and they show the cable only beats Ethernet when the NAS is full of flash.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the two makers' Thunderbolt numbers on one scale. UGREEN advertises a '40Gbps link' and QNAP prints '20 Gbps Thunderbolt networking', but Liliputing found Windows reporting the UGREEN DXP480T Plus Thunderbolt network link at 20/20 Gbps, the same ceiling QNAP states. Measured on a Mac, every published figure is for a QNAP: 2,252 MB/s on the TS-h966TX (QNAP's lab) and 1,929 MB/s on the TBS-h574TX (StorageReview). No named reviewer has published a Mac-over-Thunderbolt number for any UGREEN.
angles.decides: It removes '40 Gbps' as a reason to pick UGREEN: both brands deliver one 20 Gbps-class IP link per cable, so the real difference is price and storage, not link speed. For a shopper who needs Mac numbers they can check, QNAP is the only brand with published Mac-over-Thunderbolt figures: TS-h966TX 2,252 MB/s write (QNAP's lab, MacBook Pro M4 Pro) and TBS-h574TX 1,929 MB/s write (StorageReview, M1 Max). The UGREEN DXP480T Plus at $849.99 is still the value pick. Its only published Thunderbolt figure is 1.51 GB/s from an Intel NUC, so on a Mac it should be described as unmeasured.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much faster the Thunderbolt link is than the NAS's own 10GbE port: on the same box, Thunderbolt reads were 1.39× faster on the DXP480T Plus, 2.13× on the TBS-h574TX and 1.70× on the TS-h966TX. UGREEN's own HDD figure (4-drive RAID 5 at 600–700 MB/s) is below the 1.09 GB/s Liliputing measured over 10GbE, so on hard drives the Thunderbolt cable mainly saves you a switch or a Mac 10GbE adapter and should not add speed.
angles.decides: It splits the pick by storage type. With all-flash storage, Thunderbolt is worth paying for: 1.4–2.1× the box's own 10GbE port. The TS-h966TX ($1,299, 9 bays, 2,004 MB/s read to an M4 Pro Mac in QNAP Labs) and the DXP480T Plus ($849.99, 1.51 GB/s in a copy test) give the most measured Thunderbolt speed per dollar. With hard drives, the DXP6800 Pro ($183/bay) and DXP8800 Plus ($171/bay) already have 2× 10GbE, so Thunderbolt there only saves cabling. The QNAP TVS-h674T ($417/bay) and TVS-h874T ($386/bay) are the exception: their built-in LAN is only 2× 2.5GbE (590 MB/s measured), so Thunderbolt is their only fast link without buying a card. That weakens ChatGPT's repeated 'safest pick' call for the TVS-h674T on value.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that QNAP's TS-h966TX page limits its direct-connect validation to 'Intel® and AMD®-powered USB4 / Thunderbolt™ 4 systems' without naming Apple silicon. On the same page, QNAP's own benchmark client was a MacBook Pro M4 Pro on macOS 26.0. The TVS-h674T and TBS-h574TX pages, by contrast, name M1/M2 Macs and set a macOS 13.5 minimum.
angles.decides: This keeps the TVS-h674T/h874T and TBS-h574TX as the QNAPs whose maker pages explicitly support Apple silicon Macs with a stated macOS minimum. The cheapest QNAP, the $1,299 TS-h966TX, gets a caveat: its formal validation names only Intel/AMD hosts, even though QNAP lab-tested it with an M4 Pro Mac (2,252 MB/s write, 2,004 MB/s read). For UGREEN, the firmware requirement (UGOS 1.2.0.2121+) is already in rival pages, so it is not new. TerraMaster has a maker how-to for Thunderbolt direct connect, but I could not open the F6-425 Pro's own spec page, so it stays an unconfirmed option.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how TerraMaster's Thunderbolt/USB4 NAS ports connect to a computer. TerraMaster's own help page says you use a separate IP link: in TOS you assign an IP address to an interface named 'TBLAN', the computer needs a Thunderbolt 3/4/5 or full-featured USB4 port and a certified Thunderbolt cable, and the Thunderbolt IP 'may change' after either device restarts.
angles.decides: Every NAS here works the same way: the Mac and NAS are both hosts, so the Mac gets an SMB share over a private IP link on the Thunderbolt cable and never sees a disk. A NAS qualifies only if its OS creates that network interface. QNAP (20 Gbps cap), UGREEN (DXP480T Plus, DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus on UGOS 1.2.0.2121 or later) and, per its help page, TerraMaster's TOS all do. Asustor's USB4 does not (our page's existing KB citation). So TerraMaster moves from 'unverified' to 'the maker says yes, but no review has measured it'. NASCompares' 16 Jul 2026 F6-425 Pro article lists the USB4 behaviour as still needing proper review testing. The pick stays: QNAP or UGREEN are the proven options, and the F6-425 Pro can only appear as a cheaper, maker-documented but unmeasured option.
products: UGREEN NASync DXP480T Plus / DXP6800 Pro / DXP8800 Plus

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a reviewer-measured Thunderbolt transfer speed for any QNAP model. StorageReview measured the TBS-h574TX at 1,929 MB/s write and about 1,850 MB/s read from an M1 Max MacBook Pro, and said that saturated the 20 Gbps link. Club386 measured the TVS-h874T at 1.3 GB/s copying a 20 GB file from a PC. Set next to MacSources' 396/369 MB/s for an HDD-filled DXP6800 Pro on an M4 MacBook Pro, these numbers show the 20 Gbps Thunderbolt link only pays off with flash storage.
angles.decides: This confirms the TBS-h574TX as the pick for someone who wants the direct Thunderbolt link to be fast. It is the only candidate with a named reviewer's measurement on a Mac that reaches the 20 Gbps (about 2.5 GB/s raw) ceiling: 1,929 MB/s. The all-flash DXP480T Plus came close at 1.42–1.51 GB/s (Liliputing, measured on a PC). The HDD-bay DXP6800 Pro, which ChatGPT kept recommending for capacity, measured only 396 MB/s write and 369 MB/s read on an M4 MacBook Pro with four HDDs in RAID 10 (MacSources). That is slower than its own 10GbE port, which Notebookcheck measured at 9.5 Gbit/s, about 1.19 GB/s. So for HDD arrays, Thunderbolt is a no-switch convenience, not a speed upgrade. Plain 10GbE does as well unless the pool is NVMe.

The TVS-h674T page gives no measured Thunderbolt speed at all.

Both are rated at the same 20 Gbps, and the TS-h966TX has the only QNAP-measured Mac result. The TVS-h674T only makes sense for the Core i5, 32 GB of RAM and 6 SATA bays. For the lowest price, the UGREEN DXP480T Plus at $849.99 is the cheapest officially supported model, but it holds NVMe drives only. The DXP6800 Pro at $1,099.99 is the cheapest supported model with hard-drive bays, though UGREEN publishes only reference speed ranges for it, not a measurement. The Jabra Evolve2 85 adds a dedicated USB adapter, and its MS version is Teams-certified. So the Jabra is the pick for PC and Teams calls, and the Sony and soundcore suit a phone plus a laptop over Bluetooth.

Microsoft says only LE Audio headsets, on Windows 11 24H2 with an updated Bluetooth driver, keep stereo playback while the mic is in use. The Jabra Evolve2 85 (supplied Bluetooth USB adapter) and the Sony WH-1000XM6 (LC3 and LE connections, per SoundGuys) have a route around the Bluetooth hands-free mode. The Sony route only works on a Windows 11 24H2 PC with LE Audio hardware and an updated driver. The soundcore Space 2 Pro lists only AAC, SBC and LDAC, so on a PC it falls back to HFP mono whenever the mic is on. Bose's page says USB-C carries playback but does not say the mic works over USB, so the Bose falls back to HFP on Bluetooth calls unless its USB mic is confirmed. The page should add a 'calls on a PC' column (LE Audio / USB mic / dongle / none), not just mic counts.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "best solar and wind generator". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What's the best solar and wind generator?
pages.why_used: The cited maker pages and the DOE guide list the L3600 and L6000 as '2,400 W solar, 150 W wind', which reads like the two add up. None of them says what the L3600 manual says: there is one shared Solar/Wind port, and the maker states the L3600 'is not designed to charge simultaneously with solar panels and wind turbine'. None says that the MyGrid 10K is the one unit with its own wind port. This page puts the shared-port fact, a refill time for each port and today's maker prices side by side.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the wind input on Nature's Generator units is a 'shared port' with solar. On the L6000 the solar side is two inputs of 12–60 Vdc / 1,200 W each, so the '2,400 W solar + 150 W wind' that ChatGPT added up is probably not available at the same time; connecting the turbine likely leaves one 1,200 W solar input. That 150 W is also only reached at a 27 mph wind.
angles.decides: It confirms the L3600 stays the pick among power stations with a wind port. pages.query: best triple-screen laptop extender for a 16-inch laptop with 19201200 panels
pages.why_used: The cited roundups and answers repeat the warning that base M1/M2 Macs support only one external display, and they offer driver-based extenders as the fix. None of them says that every Apple-silicon 16-inch MacBook Pro drives at least two external displays natively. None says that the USB-graphics drivers behind 'driver required' units block protected video on every screen. This page adds Apple's display counts per chip, FOPO's own driver and Mac statements, and Plugable's HDCP documentation.

angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro: 3 external displays; M5 Max: 4), the driver-free dual-16-inch extenders work with both screens extended and no driver. These are the FOPO S11 at $399.99 and the INVZI MagHub Dual Lite. That removes the Mac reason our page gives for picking the driver-based S788. The S788 is still the choice only for a buyer who wants three added screens, which makes four displays in total, not a triple-screen setup. For a laptop + 2 'triple' setup, the pick shifts toward the S11 or Dual Lite. The footnote for the table is: 'Triple' in product names is not a fixed count. FOPO S11 means laptop + 2 screens. FOPO S788 'Triple' means 3 added screens, so 4 displays. INVZI MagHub 'Quad Max' means 3 added screens.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that every 16-inch Apple-silicon MacBook Pro natively drives at least two external displays, so base-chip workarounds don't apply to a 16-inch Mac, or that the USB-graphics drivers behind 'driver required' extenders (DisplayLink, Silicon Motion InstantView) block HDCP-protected video such as Netflix and Prime Video on every screen of the Mac, including the built-in one, while they are connected.
angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro, the Mac caveat that pushed ChatGPT toward driver-based extenders doesn't apply. The 2021 M1 Pro already drives two external displays natively, and the current M5 Pro drives three. So a driver-free two-screen extender is the pick, as long as each screen gets its own native video output: the INVZI MagHub Dual Lite (USB-C plus mini-HDMI per its Best Buy listing title) or the FOPO S11. Driver-based units (FOPO S788, MagHub Trio 'Driver Required') add a third screen. On a Mac they cost you protected streaming on all screens, and on macOS 15 and later the Screen Recording permission they need may have to be renewed periodically. Only someone who needs three external screens, or has a laptop without two video-capable outputs, should take that trade.

None adds that Xebec's own store says the adapter is 'required for all Mac users' because Apple does not support MST, or that the Trio 3 Pro runs natively on an M4/M5 Air only over two USB-C cables, which fill both Thunderbolt ports. This page puts those facts together, with today's maker prices.

ChatGPT's six answers all say that M4/M5 Airs run two extended screens natively and that only M1/M2/M3 Airs need Xebec's adapter.

The cost is that it uses both Thunderbolt ports, so the Air charges through MagSafe and has no data port left (Mobile Pixels' driver is the one-cable fallback). The Xebec still needs the $59 adapter and a driver on any Mac. That makes Xebec's '13-inch fit' advantage cost the adapter on every Air, not only older ones, and it backs the Trio 3 Pro as the pick for a 15-inch M4/M5 Air. A 13-inch Air (30.41 cm wide) is narrower than UPERFECT's 32.5 cm minimum lid width, and the Trio 3 Pro (1.9 kg) weighs 154% of a 13-inch Air (1.23 kg).

It also runs through DisplayLink, which Macworld says caps at 60 Hz and blocks protected content on every screen. The Trio 3 Pro uses the Air's native two-display support over its two Thunderbolt ports with no driver, though that fills both of the Air's USB-C ports and leaves only MagSafe for charging. For M1, M2 and M3 Airs, every candidate needs software or a dock: the Trio needs Mobile Pixels' driver, the Xebec needs its Mac Adapter, and Kefeya says a docking station is required. So the pick should be split by chip, and the Xebec's 'Mac adapter needed' warning must not be limited to older Airs.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that macOS does not support DisplayPort MST for extended displays, so one native USB-C video cable can only carry one extended screen to a Mac. On an M4 or M5 MacBook Air, a driver-free triple extender therefore needs both Thunderbolt ports, one per screen, with MagSafe left for charging. The Xebec Tri-Screen 3 runs on a single cable, so it stays tied to the $59 DisplayLink adapter and its driver even on an M5 Air. That makes it a weaker buy for new Airs and moves it to the 'M1–M3 or must-be-one-cable' slot. On M1, M2 and M3 Airs every candidate needs a driver either way, so the finding doesn't change the pick there.

This page gives the measured output for each candidate, from OutdoorGearLab, Notebookcheck, StorageReview, The Solar Lab and The Technology Man (850–950 Wh, and 37.5 min at a 1,479 W load). angles.decides: This backs the current pick: the 1,800–2,000 W continuous units (AC180, Elite 100 V2, DELTA 3, C1000 Gen 2) run a 1,500 W heater at full power without using any lifting mode. A unit that only reaches 1,500 W through Lifting, X-Boost or surge (for example the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2: 600 W rated, '1,500W Lifting Power') would run the heater at lowered voltage and noticeably less heat, so it is out. They also weaken the 'at its limit; not recommended' cell our page gives the Jackery 1000 v2: The Solar Lab held 1,479 W for 37.5 min and 1,500–1,560 W for 10 min without a trip. For value, the BLUETTI AC180 at $499 is the cheapest candidate per minute of heat that I could price: about $13 per minute against about $16 for the EcoFlow DELTA 3. There is also a caution for the C1000 Gen 2: The Technology Man's UK unit overheated after 26 min on a 2 kW heater, so it can't be assumed to run safely right at the inverter limit.

pages.query: can a nas host a minecraft server for friends and which one is best
pages.why_used: The two cited rivals (racksandwatts.com and esp32.co.uk) give CPU names, and in esp32's case mixed clock claims. Neither gives a single-thread benchmark or says that the DXP4800 Plus's 4.4 GHz applies to only one of its five cores, and neither mentions Minecraft. This page ranks each NAS on PassMark single-thread rating (3,197 vs 1,879 / 1,492 / 1,151 / 1,136). It shows Intel's 1 P-core + 4 E-core split, and it ties both to the single-threaded server tick using PaperMC's own wording.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus's advertised 4.4 GHz applies to only one of its five cores (1 P-core at 4.4 GHz; the four E-cores top out at 3.3 GHz), or that this one core gives it a PassMark single-thread rating of 3,197, against 1,879 for the DXP2800's N100, 2,032 for the 8-core i3-N305 and 1,136 for the DS925+'s V1500B. Single-thread speed is the figure that matters for Paper's single-threaded tick.
angles.decides: It confirms the DXP4800 Plus as the pick on a number rather than a clock claim. Its one P-core scores 1.70× the N100 (3,197 / 1,879), 2.81× the DS925+ (3,197 / 1,136) and 1.57× the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro's i3-N305 (3,197 / 2,032). The F4-424 Pro's 8 cores look stronger on a spec sheet, and its multithread score is in fact slightly higher (9,337 vs 8,997), but Paper ticks the world on one thread, so the 8505 wins for Minecraft. The DS925+ costs about the same ($639.99 list vs $619.99) and has the slowest single thread in the table except the DS225+'s J4125. The F2-425 Plus's N150 scores the same as the N100 (1,889 vs 1,879, 0.5% apart), so its '3.6 GHz' buys nothing over the DXP2800's '3.4 GHz'.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium Gold 8505 scores 3,197 in PassMark single-thread. That is 2.8× the Synology DS925+'s Ryzen V1500B (1,136) and 2.1× the QNAP TS-464's Celeron N5095 (1,492), and single-thread speed is the figure Minecraft's tick loop depends on.
angles.decides: It confirms the DXP4800 Plus as the pick and pushes the Synology DS925+ down. The DS925+ costs about as much as the DXP4800 Plus, but its CPU has the lowest single-thread score of the four, below even the cheaper DXP2800's N100 (1,879 vs 1,136, 1.65×). The QNAP TS-464 also falls behind the $389.99 DXP2800 on this measure. Per dollar the two UGREENs are close: the DXP4800 Plus gives 5.2 single-thread points per dollar and the DXP2800 gives 4.8. So the DXP4800 Plus wins on raw tick speed without costing more per point.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Mojang's Bedrock Dedicated Server is built only for x86-64 (Windows 10 1703+ or Ubuntu 22.04+ on x86-64). On an ARM box such as the Raspberry Pi 5 or UGREEN's RK3588 DH line, the usual Docker image runs it only under box64 x86 emulation, while the Java server image runs natively on arm64. A Bedrock server also needs UDP 19132 open, not TCP 25565.
angles.decides: This confirms that the pick should be an x86 NAS: the DXP2800 or DXP4800 Plus (Intel), or the DS925+ (AMD). It rules out the cheaper ARM boxes (UGREEN DH4300 Plus at $399.99, Pi 5) when friends play Bedrock, because there the Mojang server runs only under box64 emulation; a Java server with Geyser is the arm64-native route. It also caps the DS225+ at 6 GB total RAM, using one approved Synology 4 GB module (D4NS01-4G), so it can't hold a 6–10 GB modded heap. The DS925+ takes up to 2×16 GB of Synology ECC modules (D4ES03-16G).

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that since Bedrock 26.50 (September 2026) the Bedrock Dedicated Server uses Mojang's WebRTC-based NetherNet transport by default, and that since 26.60 (27 October 2026) Bedrock clients no longer connect over RakNet. The old 'forward UDP 19132' setup therefore stops working: you now need TCP 19132 for signaling plus a range of UDP ports with one port per player (or TCP+UDP on 19132 for Geyser). playit.gg also says Bedrock Dedicated Server 'can't connect to playit by itself', so it needs a WaterdogPE proxy.
angles.decides: This doesn't change which NAS wins, because the transport works the same on any x86 Docker NAS (DXP2800, DXP4800 Plus, TS-464, DS925+). It does decide whether the shopper's plan works if any friend plays Bedrock (phone, Windows, console via Geyser). Two setups now work. (1) A Java server (itzg/minecraft-server, TCP 25565) plus Geyser build 1237 or later with transport set to nethernet, and 19132 open on both TCP and UDP. On Docker, Geyser also needs -DgeyserAdvertiseAddresses, because GeyserMC says it is for servers 'in containers or behind a NAT'. (2) Bedrock Dedicated Server with TCP 19132, a UDP range of at least max-players ports (default 10) and the public IP set in SERVER_UDP_PORTS. On playit.gg, that means adding WaterdogPE with online-mode=false. Either way the page should keep the 'Java server + Geyser on an x86 NAS' route as the main recommendation and correct the Bedrock port row.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that PassMark's measured single-thread rating, the figure that sets Minecraft Java tick speed, is 3,197 for the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium Gold 8505, compared with 1,879 for the DXP2800's N100, 1,492 for the TS-464's Celeron N5095 and 1,136 for the DS925+'s Ryzen V1500B (as of 8 Nov 2026).
angles.decides: This confirms the DXP4800 Plus as the pick for a Minecraft server for friends. Its single-thread rating is 1.70× the N100's (3,197 / 1,879), 2.14× the TS-464's N5095 (3,197 / 1,492) and 2.81× the DS925+'s V1500B (3,197 / 1,136). It also tops the i3-N305 in the F4-424 Pro (2,032). The $639.99 DS925+ and the $639 TS-464 that ChatGPT showed both rate below the $390-class N100 DXP2800 on the metric Minecraft depends on. The DS925+'s V1500B is level with the DS225+'s J4125 (1,151), so the 4-bay Synology is no better a game host than the 2-bay one. Measured idle power is similar across the 4-bay units (24–30 W, see the findings), so running one 24/7 doesn't change the pick.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got pairs each NAS's price today with its single-thread score. On 2026-11-08 the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus costs $619.99 at UGREEN's store and scores 3,197 on PassMark single-thread. The QNAP TS-464 costs $599–$639 on Amazon and scores 1,492 (Celeron N5095). The Synology DS925+ costs $819.99 on Amazon and scores 1,136 (Ryzen V1500B). Single-thread speed is what a Minecraft Java server depends on.

pages.query: cheapest nas to use as a remote hyper backup target for a synology at a relatives house
pages.why_used: The cited Synology pages give Hyper Backup's destination rules, and the rival answer gives two purchase prices. None of them gives a power draw, a yearly running cost or a payback time against cloud storage for a box left on all year at someone else's house. This page prices each candidate's waiting-state draw at the EIA August 2026 rate and works out how many months each box takes to beat Backblaze B2. On that basis the cheapest box to buy, the DS124, is also the cheapest to run.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, in a form the shopper can compare, that a non-Synology box used as an rsync destination still gets Hyper Backup's multi-version .hbk backups. Storage Alchemist lists 'another Synology NAS or server via rsync' among multiple-version destinations. Switching from a Synology running Vault to a cheaper non-Synology target loses entire-system and LUN backup (Synology's spec), not version history.
angles.decides: This settles what the cheaper box gives up. A UGREEN DH2300 or TerraMaster on rsync keeps versioned .hbk backups that Hyper Backup Explorer can restore. A DS124 or DS223j running Vault is needed only if the shopper wants entire-system or LUN backup, or Vault's task monitoring. Our current page says the UGREEN row is a 'single-version copy: no .hbk, no version history'. On this evidence that is wrong and should be corrected, or at least sourced. On power, Synology's official 'Access' figures and NASCompares' measured idle cannot be compared directly. Both Synology boxes publish hibernation figures (DS124 3.44 W, DS223j 4 W) that matter for a backup target that sits idle most of the day, and no source I opened measured DH2300 hibernation.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the yearly electricity cost of leaving the target running at a relative's house, or how many months the box takes to pay for itself against cloud backup. Worked out from spec-sheet or reviewer wattage and the August 2026 EIA residential rate (18.16¢/kWh), the cheapest box to buy is also the cheapest to run: a DS124 costs about $5.47 a year with its drive asleep and pays back its $159.99 price against Backblaze B2 in about 6 months at 4 TB. A UGREEN DH2300 costs about $15.91 a year at its measured idle and takes about 9 months.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's DS124 pick on total cost as well as sticker price. It is the cheapest to buy and to run: about $176 over 3 years for the box plus power, against about $189 for the TerraMaster F2-212, $229 for the DS223j and $288 for the UGREEN DH2300, all with drive asleep except the DH2300. At 4 TB stored, every NAS box pays itself back against B2 within a year, so cloud only wins for very small backups (around 2 TB-years or less for the DS124). This favors the Synology Vault pick over the UGREEN rows in our current page on cost as well as features.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which Synology model generations can still run Hyper Backup Vault as a target: Vault 4.2.x (current 4.2.2-4262, 2026-07-07) needs DSM 7.3 or later. The DS223j, DS118 and DS120j reach DSM 7.4, but a used DS216j stops at DSM 7.1, so it can't run Vault 4.2.x.
angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's 'used Synology' route but adds a cut-off. A used DS118 or DS120j (maximum DSM 7.4) can run the current Vault 4.2.2. Avoid used models capped at DSM 7.1 (for example the DS216j), which can't run Vault 4.2.x because it needs DSM 7.3. The new DS223j also reaches DSM 7.4, so it qualifies. For non-Synology targets (UGREEN DH2300 / DXP2800, QNAP): Synology's spec lists rsync servers for folder and package backup but not for entire-system backup. Hetzner's rsync guide recommends client-side encryption and offers a retention setting. Both of those exist only in multi-version tasks, which suggests multi-version .hbk to an rsync target works. QNAP's own documentation shows only single-version. Our page's statement that a UGREEN target is single-version only with no .hbk is therefore weakly sourced and should be softened to 'single-version is the documented path; multi-version .hbk over rsync is not documented by the NAS maker'.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Hyper Backup on DSM 7 has a multi-version rsync task, separate from 'rsync copy (single-version)'. That task writes the same versioned, client-side-encryptable .hbk backup to any rsync/SSH server that a Synology running Hyper Backup Vault would hold, and the .hbk can be restored without any Synology using Hyper Backup Explorer or the open-source hbkit.
angles.decides: If it holds, the cheapest box with a working rsync/SSH server gives the same versions, Smart Recycle and AES-256 client-side encryption as a DS124 or DS223j running Vault. That makes non-Synology targets real contenders on price, including the UGREEN DH2300, a cheap TerraMaster or a Pi with a USB disk. The current page's 'single-version, no .hbk' cells for the UGREEN rows should change to 'multi-version .hbk via rsync (SSH)'. A Synology target is still required in two cases: entire-system backup (Synology lists only a remote Synology NAS or C2), and Vault's view of the vaults a NAS hosts plus its concurrent-task limit.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured power draw for any candidate. PC-WELT measured the Synology DS223j at 16.4 W idle, 3.1 W with the drives asleep and 22.3 W under load. NASCompares measured the UGREEN DH2300 at 9.5 W idle with two 4 TB IronWolf drives. That matters for a box left running all year at a relative's house.
angles.decides: The finding confirms that a Synology J or value model with drive hibernation suits an always-on remote target, and it adds a running cost no rival gives. PC-WELT's 3.1 W sleep figure for the DS223j is about a third of the DH2300's 9.5 W idle (NASCompares). If the DS223j's drives sleep about 23 hours a day between nightly runs, it uses roughly 34 kWh a year, against about 83 kWh for a DH2300 that never spins down. The DH2300's lower idle draw (9.5 W vs 16.4 W) only wins if the Synology's drives never sleep. It does not change the case for the DS223j or DS124 as the Hyper Backup Vault pick, which rests on features, not power.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the cheapest new Synology target, the DS124 at $159.99 on Amazon today, costs less than every non-Synology NAS on the shortlist (UGREEN DH2300 $239.99, TerraMaster F2-425 $269.99, UGREEN DXP2800 $389.99), even though Synology's spec says those rsync-type targets can't take Hyper Backup's entire-system backups. It also doesn't state that the DS124 costs the same as about 23 TB-months of Backblaze B2 at $6.95 per TB a month.
angles.decides: This confirms the DS124 as the cheapest new pick and removes the reason to send buyers to a third-party NAS. Each non-Synology box listed here costs more today, and Synology's spec limits rsync servers to folder and package backup. Our own UGREEN DH2300 and DXP2800 rows should be framed as 'only if you also want a general home NAS', not as cheaper backup targets. For a small data set (about 1–2 TB), B2 at $6.95/TB/month undercuts the DS124 box for roughly 1–2 years before you even buy a drive.

None compares what each brand charges per added Wh, and none shows that adding EcoFlow's pack later costs $88 more than EcoFlow's 2 kWh DELTA 3 Max. None notes that the EcoFlow and OUPES bundles cost more than buying the two items separately.

EcoFlow's 5 kWh needs the 4,096 Wh DELTA Pro 3 extra battery on an adapter cable.
angles.decides: It supports ChatGPT's EcoFlow DELTA 3 pick for a shopper who wants to go from 1 kWh to 2 kWh: it has the smallest step (1,024 Wh) and the same 80% end point as DJI and Anker. The '~5 kWh' in ChatGPT's table is misleading for an add-one-battery buyer, because one DELTA 3 pack stops at 2,048 Wh. For a bigger single jump, the DJI Power 1000 V2 reaches 3,072 Wh with one pack at 4,000 cycles to 80%. DJI's US product URLs redirected to a 404 page on 2026-11-08, so that route needs a US availability check before anyone recommends it.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the AC180's add-on pack feeds the station only through its 500 W (12–60 V) solar/DC input in Power Bank Mode. Under any load above 500 W, the AC180's own 1,152 Wh battery still drains, at the load minus 500 W.
angles.decides: The AC180 belongs with the 'can't truly expand' models, not alongside the DELTA 3 / 3 Plus, Jackery 1000 Plus / HomePower 1000 Plus v2, DJI Power 1000 V2 and OUPES Mega 1. Its pack is an external charger capped at 500 W, not a battery on the station's internal bus, and it needs a separate P090D cable. Our page's AC180 row ('max 4,224 Wh', B300) should say this. The B300 is also sold out at $1,399 today. The pick stays a model with a dedicated extra-battery port, such as the EcoFlow DELTA 3 / 3 Plus.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured usable figure for any candidate. Side by side, OutdoorGearLab measured 870 Wh (85%) from the EcoFlow DELTA 3, 880 Wh (86%) from the DJI Power 1000 V2 and 950 Wh (82%) from the BLUETTI AC180, and StorageReview measured 910 Wh (88.9%) from the DELTA 3 Plus.

The AC180's 950 Wh beats them on the base unit, but its add-on storage goes through the DC input rather than a battery port. pages.query: which kvm switch holds 4k 144 hz between a macbook pro and a gaming pc on one monitor
pages.why_used: The cited TESmart and Level1Techs pages only tell Mac buyers to 'confirm the external-display limits of the exact Mac model', or to use a USB-C-to-DisplayPort cable. None of them gives Apple's limits for each port. This page now does, from Apple's own documents: on M2 Pro to M4 Max MacBook Pros, 4K 144 Hz is rated only on the HDMI port and Thunderbolt only to 6K 60 Hz. The M1 Pro/Max HDMI port is limited to 4K 60 Hz, and only the M5 Pro/Max and M6 are rated for 4K 144 Hz on any port. That splits buyers between the HDMI route and the USB-C-to-DP route those pages recommend, and it corrects our old top row, which put the Mac on the monitor's USB-C.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Apple rates the M2 Pro to M4 Max MacBook Pros for 4K above 60 Hz only on their HDMI port, with Thunderbolt listed at 6K 60 Hz. The same results also don't state that every DP 1.4 '4K144' claim needs DSC because 4K144 at 8-bit RGB carries 28.67 Gb/s of active pixels against DP 1.4's 25.92 Gb/s payload. Together these favour an HDMI 2.1 KVM over the USB-C-to-DisplayPort route ChatGPT and Level1Techs suggest.
angles.decides: The pick now depends on which Mac the shopper has. With an M2 Pro, M3 Pro or M4 Pro/Max MacBook Pro, the only port Apple rates for 4K above 60 Hz is HDMI. So an HDMI 2.1 KVM whose maker lists a 4K high-refresh mode is the sourced path: the TESmart HDK202-M24 lists 'Dual 4K@144Hz/160Hz (DSC 1.2a)', and the HKS201-M24 lists 4K240 (DSC). A DP 1.4 KVM fed by USB-C-to-DP (Level1Techs, TESmart DKS202-M24) has no Apple 4K144 rating on those Macs and needs DSC at 4K144 in any case. With a 2021 M1 Pro/Max, an HDMI KVM caps the Mac at 4K60. M5 Pro/Max is rated for 4K144 over Thunderbolt or HDMI, so either KVM type is possible. The current page's 'use the monitor's KVM' advice still holds, because a direct HDMI cable avoids the middle device, and Apple says to 'Connect displays directly to your Mac for best results'.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the arithmetic: uncompressed 4K at 144 Hz and 8-bit colour needs 31.35 Gb/s, which is 121% of the 25.92 Gb/s a DisplayPort 1.4 (HBR3) KVM can carry (151% at 10-bit). 4K at 120 Hz and 8-bit fills 99.6% of that link. So every DP 1.4 KVM's '4K144' claim depends on DSC, while an HDMI 2.1 48G link carries 4K144 at 10-bit uncompressed at 93% of its 42.0 Gb/s.
angles.decides: On a DP 1.4 KVM (Level1Techs, TESmart DKS202-M24, StarTech D86A2, UGREEN 25962), 4K144 only works if DSC works end to end, Mac included. That is the very part ChatGPT kept telling the shopper to 'verify'. The finding favours connecting a MacBook Pro (M2 Pro/Max or later) from its own HDMI port, with no adapter, to an HDMI 2.1 48G KVM. That link has the headroom for 4K144 without compression. One catch: TESmart's HKS201-M24 page lists 4K144/165 as running 'through DSC' and makes no Mac claim, so no switch is proven to carry 4K144 uncompressed. This supports the current page's lead pick (use the monitor's built-in KVM, a direct link with no DSC middleman). It does not overturn it.

Apple also says adapters aren't supported at those HDMI rates, so the Mac's own HDMI port has to go straight into the switch.
angles.decides: The Mac's chip decides the switch type. With an M2 Pro/Max (2023) or later, base M4/M5/M6, or M3/M4/M5 Pro/Max, the Mac's built-in HDMI port can feed an HDMI 2.1 KVM such as the TESmart HKS201-M24 at 4K 144 Hz alongside the PC. It must be a direct HDMI cable, not a USB-C-to-HDMI adapter. With an M1 Pro/Max or base M3 MacBook Pro, the HDMI side stops at 4K 60 Hz or 4K 120 Hz. Those Macs need the USB-C DP Alt Mode route into a DisplayPort KVM, using a DP Alt Mode USB-C-to-DP cable (Cable Matters says its switch 'is not natively compatible with computers with a USB-C port'). On that route, 4K 144 Hz depends on DSC working end to end (Cable Matters FAQ; L1Techs FAQ: 'Without DSC, no'), and Level1Techs officially rates its switch only to 4K 120 Hz. This keeps our page's verdict of using the monitor's built-in KVM for M1 Pro and base M3 owners, and it allows an HDMI 2.1 KVM for M2 Pro and later.

On top of that, Level1Techs' own spec is 4K 120 Hz, with 144 Hz only through DSC. This also corrects our current top row. It puts the Mac on the monitor's USB-C (DP Alt Mode), which Apple documents only to 6K 60 Hz on these chips, so the Mac should go on the monitor's HDMI 2.1 input instead. For an M1 Pro/Max (2021), Apple documents no 4K 144 Hz output at all, so no switch fixes it. For the M5 Pro/Max and M6, Apple lists 4K 144 Hz or more on any port, including Thunderbolt, so DP and USB-C paths are documented too.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "what is the lightest 1000 wh lifepo4 power station for car camping". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What is the lightest 1000 wh lifepo4 power station for car camping?
pages.why_used: Every cited rival and our own earlier page passed over the Jackery HomePower 1000 v2 (23.4 lb) because they said it had no solar input. Jackery's own help-center spec sheet lists 400 W of solar on two DC8020 ports, an 8 A car-socket input (about 11 h) and charging down to 14°F, against 32°F for the Explorer 1000 v2 and the Anker C1000 Gen 2. No result states any of that, so the lightest unit really is a car-camping unit, and this page now says so with the maker's figures.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that Jackery's HomePower 1000 v2 (23.4 lb) does charge from solar: it has two 200 W DC ports, 400 W in total, which is the same layout as the Explorer 1000 v2. Several results do agree it is the lighter unit, but ChatGPT's "no solar" caveat is wrong. None of them puts each maker's solar figure on the same footing either: the Explorer's 400 W needs two panels on two ports at 200 W each, and the Anker C1000 Gen 2 takes only 8.2 A below 29 V, so its 600 W needs a high-voltage panel array.
angles.decides: This changes the pick. If the HomePower 1000 v2 has 400 W of solar on two 200 W DC ports, it is the lightest solar-capable 1 kWh LiFePO4 unit at 23.4 lb, 0.4 lb under the Explorer 1000 v2's 23.8 lb. The Explorer's lead in Wh per lb rests on its 1,070 Wh rating. Jackery's own blog listing shows it at 1,024 Wh, which works out to 43.0 Wh/lb against the HomePower's 43.8. Normalising solar also changes the runner-up advice. With one panel of about 20 V Vmp, the Explorer can take up to 200 W, while the Anker C1000 Gen 2 is held to about 164 W by its 8.2 A limit. The Anker's 600 W only arrives at 29–60 V, which in practice means several panels in series. Weight to the HomePower, but this needs a check on Jackery's own US page before it goes live.

pages.why_used: The cited Schumacher and Advance Auto pages and the top roundups put a plug-in combo's 100–200 A engine start next to a pack's 1,000 A or more peak. None of them says these are different kinds of rating. This page explains the plug-in figure: it is a capped current from the wall, limited to 7 seconds per crank and under 3 seconds on a hard crank, with a 180 s cool-down after repeated cranks, and it needs a battery installed in the car. It then compares that with the pack combos that jump-start without an outlet.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Schumacher's plug-in 'engine start' amps are not the same kind of rating as a lithium pack's 'peak amps'. The SC1281/SC1309 rate is a capped current fed from the wall. It flows for up to 7 seconds per crank, and if the starter draws more than that rate the crank can last less than 3 seconds. Repeated cranks then trigger a 3-minute cool-down. A pack's '1,000 A peak' is a brief maximum, so 100 A vs 1,000 A is not a 10× difference in starting power.
angles.decides: This confirms that the plug-in Schumacher combos (SC1281 at 100 A, SC1309 at 200 A) suit a shopper who has an outlet and time. The charger gives a capped, timed boost with a 2-minute wait before cranking, and on a hard-to-turn engine the crank can drop below 3 seconds. A shopper who needs a strong start away from an outlet should not choose by comparing the 100 A or 200 A figure with a pack's peak amps. They should choose a lithium pack or a pack-plus-charger unit such as the Battery Tender CNS 4120. The page should footnote the amp column as 'charger engine-start rate (AC, capped, 7-second crank) vs pack peak (instantaneous)'.

angles.decides: This confirms rather than overturns ChatGPT's picks. Every plug-in combo it showed charges at 6 A, so all of them refill a battery equally slowly, about 10 h for a large truck battery. They differ only in engine-start amps and price, so the shopper should choose on cranking amps (100 A for cars, 150–200 A for trucks) rather than expect any of them to charge faster. If faster recharging matters, a 10 A unit cuts the 1000 CCA case to 7 h, but the manual-timer wheeled models (SC1446, SC1667) need the 135-minute timer reset about 4 times to get there. A shopper who wants a hands-off overnight recharge should pick an automatic 6 A unit (SC1281L or SC1309) over a timer-wheeled one.

pages.why_used: The cited OREI support pages rate one kit at 115 ft and another at 394 ft, and call both '4K60 4:4:4, 18 Gbps'. None says that HDBaseT before 3.0 carries 10.2 Gbps and needs compression for that signal, or that HDBaseT 3.0 is rated to only 328 ft uncompressed. This page puts every kit's 4K60 reach on the same basis and adds AV Access's 131 ft rating as an outside reference for an 18 Gbps HDBaseT link.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that an HDBaseT link is limited to 10.2 Gbps, so a 4K60 4:4:4 signal (an 18 Gbps feed) has to be compressed to cross it. OREI still calls its UHD14-EXB400-K 'uncompressed' at 394 ft for 4K60 4:4:4. AV Access rates its own 18 Gbps HDBaseT extender at only 131 ft for that same signal.
angles.decides: ChatGPT's 'best for long distances' pick (OREI UHD14-EXB400-K, 394 ft at 4K60) is the figure that conflicts with the 10.2 Gbps HDBaseT limit and with AV Access's 131 ft rating for 4K60 4:4:4. It is also listed as 'Unavailable' on orei.com today. For full 4K60 4:4:4/HDR, the safe way to compare is each maker's own 4K60 distance figure: about 115 ft (OREI UHD12-EX115-K), 131 ft (AV Access over Cat6a/7) and 196 ft (J-Tech, chroma not stated). A run longer than that should be treated as 1080p, or as possibly compressed 4K, until the maker says otherwise. The finding supports the OREI 1x2 for runs under 115 ft and makes the long-distance pick doubtful.

pages.why_used: The cited rivals each print half of the picture. Charge-Test gives XTAR's measured energy and Light And Matter gives EBL's, but neither sets measured energy next to the label. So nobody shows that the 38% label lead the XTAR 4150 has over the EBL 3000 shrinks to 0.5–4.5% when measured, that the EBL beats its own label while the XTARs reach 82–86% of theirs, or that the label that looks biggest (PUJIMAX 4,255 mWh) measured the least. The page also adds Gough Lui's mAh × voltage check, which explains the gap, and his cycle-wear test, which Charge-Test says it did not do.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that once you swap printed ratings for measured energy, the 38% capacity lead the XTAR 4150 mWh AA has over the EBL 3000 mWh AA on the label shrinks to roughly 0.5–4.5%: XTAR measured 3,420 mWh (82% of its rating) and EBL measured 3,273–3,404 mWh (109–113% of its rating).
angles.decides: ChatGPT called the XTAR 4150 'best overall' for 'high capacity' and the EBL 3000 mWh 'budget'. On measured energy the two are close: within about 5%, or 6–11% if you use XTAR's own 0.25 A figure (3,605 mWh). So the pick between them should rest on price per pack, charger fit and high-current behaviour, not on the mWh printed on the label. The XTAR CLR 4300 is still the measured capacity leader at 3,703 mWh. Its lead shrinks at high drain: about 2,300–2,440 mAh at 2 A against 2,676 mAh at 1 A. Caveat: the XTAR and EBL figures come from different test rigs (charge-test averaged 0.1/0.4/1 A; Light And Matter used an XTAR VX4 V2 with no current stated). This is directional, not a head-to-head test.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states cost per measured watt-hour. At the maker stores on 2026-11-10, the XTAR CLR 4300 costs $1.82 per measured Wh as a 4-pack ($26.99 ÷ 4 × 3.703 Wh) and $1.69 as an 8-pack, while the EBL 3000mWh that ChatGPT called the 'budget option' costs $2.31–2.40 per measured Wh at EBL's own store.
angles.decides: This confirms the XTAR CLR 4300 as the pick on value as well as capacity, and it challenges ChatGPT's 'budget' label for the EBL: at the maker stores the EBL costs about 30% more per measured Wh than the CLR 4300 (4-pack against 4-pack: $2.36 vs $1.82). There is one catch for first-time buyers. XTAR says the CLR series needs a compatible charger (the VX4 V1 cannot charge it), and the L4 Pro + 4 × CLR 4300 bundle at $39.99 works out to $2.70 per Wh for the first purchase.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that XTAR's 1.5 V AA cells have their own charge-management chip and take 4.75–5.5 V only from a charger that supports XTAR's 1.5 V Li-ion protocol. That means a NiMH charger won't do it, and XTAR's own store says its VX4 V1 charger cannot charge the CLR 4300 that ChatGPT made its top pick.
angles.decides: This confirms the XTAR CLR 4300 as the pick only if it's bought with a charger XTAR lists as compatible: the L4 Pro, MX4, L4 or L8, or a VX4 V2 but not a V1. The cheapest sure route is XTAR's USA L4 Pro + 4× CLR 4300 bundle at $39.99, against $26.99 for the batteries alone. Someone who already owns a NiMH charger, such as the Tenergy TN480U that Dealectric lists, can't charge these cells with it. The same mechanism explains each candidate's low-battery behaviour: the EBL holds 1.5 V and then cuts off, the XTAR 4150 steps down to 1.1 V, and the CLR 4300 declines linearly to about 1.0 V. In devices that judge charge by voltage, only the stepped and sloped designs give a warning before the device dies.
products: XTAR VX4 V1 charger vs XTAR 1.5V AA CLR 4300

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how fast a 1.5V lithium AA actually wears out: Gough Lui ran the XTAR 4150mWh AA through 100 lab cycles and measured a loss of 0.85–0.89 mWh per cycle, which projects to 80% of its energy at about 843 cycles against XTAR's 1,200-cycle rating, with only about 63% of the charging energy coming back out.
angles.decides: It backs XTAR 4150mWh as the best value pick, and that is the cell Dealectric already lists (xtar-1-5v-aa-4150mwh-8-pack). It is the only candidate with a published cycle-wear measurement, and the projection of about 770–840 cycles to 80% is honest life data, about 30–35% short of the 1,200-cycle claim. The CLR 4300 still leads on energy per charge: Charge-Test measured 3,703 vs 3,420 mWh, and 3,719 vs 3,297 mWh at 1 A. But nobody has measured its cycle life, so a durability-minded shopper has a measured reason to choose the 4150 at $24.99. Gough Lui's I-V testing also suggests keeping loads below 1.25 A, which matters for flashes and other high-drain devices.

pages.why_used: The cited guides say only that 'some sets' share one USB receiver, or confirm it for the Logitech MX pair alone. None says which mechanical combos use one dongle and which need two (Redragon's own HORUS combo needs two). None says that sharing works only between a maker's listed models, with at most two devices on Logitech's keyboard receiver. And none quotes Logitech and Razer advising separate receivers for full performance and polling above 1 kHz. This page counts the USB ports each combo uses, from the makers' own text, and explains the trade-off.

angles.name: Normalise

On the S168 the headline says 12,800 DPI but the top on-board step is 8,000; the S136 says 7,200 and its top step is 7,200. Redragon says the S136, S144 and BS8773 share one 2.4 GHz dongle, but the S168 description never says so.
angles.decides: This mostly confirms the pick rather than changing it. At $59.99 both the S136 (K628 + M693) and the S168 (K673 PRO + M693) are tri-mode 75% mechanical combos. Only the S136 page says one shared dongle serves both, and its 7,200 DPI headline is a real on-board step. The S168's 12,800 DPI needs Redragon's software, since its buttons stop at 8,000. For a shopper who wants a single USB receiver and specs that hold without software, the S136 is the cleaner $60 pick. The $36.99 BS8773 also uses one shared dongle, but it has low-profile switches (Redragon cuts the height by 30%) and its mouse tops out at 2,400 DPI, so it suits office use more than gaming. In the premium tier, Keychron is the only maker here that states one dongle controls both devices and a 1,000 Hz mouse polling rate (K2 HE + M3, $179.99). But it rates the mouse battery only in Bluetooth mode (95 h), so that figure is not comparable with the keyboard's unqualified 110 h.

A gamer should plan on two USB ports, or accept the shared-dongle trade-off.

That figure is what shows the 6.5 kW SGM-6510M (4.6 h) and Renogy's 400 W kit (9 h) can't refill in one day, while the $4,949 SGR-8K10E refills in 2.8 h. pages.why_used: The cited rival pages give inverter output only in VA or W. I opened Solar Waypoint, PluginSolarCheck, Solar United Neighbors and APsystems' pages, and none of them converts those ratings to amps on the house circuit. None checks the totals against the EZ1-LV's dedicated 10 A circuit condition or works out how much current breaker masking can let through. None points out that APsystems' own claim of '2 units on a standard 15A circuit' (15 A) is more than that condition allows. This page adds the current figures from the makers and retailers, the arithmetic, Hoymiles' plug and shutdown timings, and the CEC efficiencies.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the VA ratings into amps on the house circuit: APsystems EZ1-LV 900 VA = 7.5 A and Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV 360–500 VA = 3.0–4.17 A, so one EZ1 uses 75% of the 10 A dedicated circuit that rivals cite as its install condition, and the two-unit '1,800 W on a standard 15A circuit' setup on APsystems' own consumer page adds 15 A, the full rating of a 15 A circuit.
angles.decides: This confirms the EZ1-LV as the two-panel pick, but only as a single unit: one unit at 7.5 A fits a 10 A dedicated circuit, while two units add 15 A. For a shopper who can't add a dedicated circuit, the HiFlow Pro LV adds only 3.0–4.17 A per unit. That makes it the low-load choice for one panel, which ChatGPT's 'budget' label doesn't explain.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives each inverter's yearly output in kWh or its price per yearly kWh. In NREL PVWatts v8 for Kansas City, a 900 VA APsystems EZ1-LV with matched panels makes about 1,288 kWh a year at a 20° tilt and about 865 kWh hung flat (vertical) on a balcony. That works out to $0.25 to $0.38 of inverter price per yearly kWh. A 360 VA Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV makes about 515 kWh (20° tilt) or 346 kWh (vertical), which is $0.31 to $0.46 per yearly kWh.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's pick of the EZ1-LV. It gives 2.5× the yearly energy of a 360 VA HiFlow Pro LV (1,288 vs 515 kWh) at a lower inverter cost per yearly kWh ($0.25 vs $0.31). At the US average rate that is about $234 vs $94 a year. It also matters for balcony buyers: hanging the panels vertically cuts yearly output by about a third. From November to January, though, a vertical array makes more than one at 20° (December: 98.4 vs 80.6 kWh per kW), so railing mounts lose mostly in summer. Caveats: the APsystems page carries a 5-unit order limit, and two rival pages say the EZ1-LV is sold out. I could not source the EcoFlow STREAM's AC rating, so it is left out of the comparison.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which solar panels each plug-in microinverter can take: the APsystems EZ1-LV accepts 18 A per input across two inputs (25 A short-circuit) with a 27–45 V tracking range and recommended 315–660+ Wp modules, while each Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV takes one module at 14–16 A and 64 V max, so a large modern panel above 14 A fits the EZ1-LV but is current-limited on the smaller HiFlow models.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's EZ1-LV pick for a two-panel build. It is the only candidate with two 18 A inputs and a published 315–660+ Wp module range, so one unit can run two current large-format panels. The HiFlow Pro LV is one panel per unit, and the model has to match the panel: the 360/391/420 models allow 14 A, the 450 allows 15 A and the 500 allows 16 A. A shopper pairing a high-current panel with the $149 HMS-360 would lose output. Panels must stay under the 60–64 V input ceiling. That rules out series-wiring two panels into one input, and it rules out high-voltage rooftop strings.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the breaker-masking current. A plug-in inverter's output goes onto the branch wiring without passing through the breaker, so one APsystems EZ1-LV (7.5 A nominal) on a shared 15 A circuit can let part of that wiring carry up to 22.5 A without tripping. APsystems' own consumer page still advertises two EZ1s, 1,800 W or 15 A, 'on a standard 15A circuit', while the CSA UL 3700 conditions reported by Solar Waypoint and Plugin Solar Check allow only a dedicated 10 A circuit. The Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV adds only 3.0 A (360 VA model) and drops its plug to 34 V or less within 1 second of unplugging.
angles.decides: Confirms the EZ1-LV for one unit on its own dedicated circuit: 7.5 A fits a 10 A circuit. It rules out ChatGPT's implied path of stacking two EZ1s for 1,800 W on an ordinary shared 15 A outlet, because 15 A of backfeed exceeds the certificate's 10 A dedicated-circuit condition. For a shopper who must use a shared outlet, the Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV is the safer pick: it adds 3.0 to about 4.2 A per unit, plugs into a GFCI outlet, and its plug goes dead within 1 s. Either way, the deciding question is which circuit the outlet is on, not the inverter's VA rating.

No cited page says the cheaper non-EPO Gen II only alerts and does not disconnect, or that both take the same RSM30W surge module. pages.why_used: The cited roundups (Tech Advisor, and the 'up to 12 days' vs 'around one day' cards) give only whole-watch battery claims. None puts the makers' own GPS-workout hours on one footing, notes that the Venu 4 falls to 9 h (45 mm) / 6 h (41 mm) with all satellites plus music, or shows that Amazfit's under-$300 watches rate 33-64 h of GPS against Garmin's 20 h and Apple's 10 h. Angle A had the highest standout (3), and every figure in it now has a source.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the makers' own continuous-GPS workout hours side by side: Apple Watch Series 12 up to 10 h, Apple Watch SE 3 up to 7 h, Fitbit Versa 4 up to 12 h, Garmin Venu 4 up to 15 h (41 mm) / 20 h (45 mm) in GPS-only mode but only 6 h / 9 h with all satellites plus music, while Samsung and Google publish no GPS-hours figure at all for the Galaxy Watch8 and Pixel Watch 4.
angles.decides: It confirms Garmin Venu 4 as the pick for long GPS sessions only in the 45 mm size and only in GPS-only mode (20 h); the 41 mm in all-satellite + multi-band + music mode (6 h) is shorter than an Apple Watch Series 12 outdoor run (10 h) and a Fitbit Versa 4 (12 h). For a shopper doing sub-2-hour workouts, the 10-day vs 1-day gap is about charging habit, not whether a workout gets tracked, so the Apple Watch Series 12 at $399 and the Versa 4 are fully competitive. Galaxy Watch8 and Pixel Watch 4 cannot be placed on this scale from maker data.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many days a fitness smartwatch lasts when you actually run with GPS for an hour every day: Garmin Venu 4 45 mm works out to about 7.7 days per charge at that duty cycle (6.2 days for the 41 mm), against 1.0 day for Apple Watch Series 12 and 0.75 day for Apple Watch SE 3, computed from the makers' own smartwatch-mode and GPS-mode ratings.
angles.decides: Confirms Garmin Venu 4 as the fitness pick but changes the advice inside it: a daily GPS runner should buy the 45 mm (7.7 days between charges, 20 one-hour GPS runs per charge) over the 41 mm (6.2 days, 15 runs). It also shows the Apple watches are strictly charge-every-night devices under a daily-workout cycle: Series 12 covers 10 one-hour GPS workouts per charge, SE 3 only 7, so on a run-every-day schedule Apple's 'all-day' claim is exactly one day with no slack. Samsung Galaxy Watch8 cannot be placed on this scale because Samsung publishes no GPS-mode hours.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the makers' phone floors: Apple Watch Series 12 / SE 3 require an iPhone 11 or later on iOS 27, Galaxy Watch8 requires Android 12 with 1.5 GB RAM and cannot pair to an iPhone at all, Pixel Watch 4 requires Android 11 with no iPhone support, and Samsung's ECG/blood-pressure features require a Galaxy phone, a user aged 22+, and a cuff recalibration every 28 days.
angles.decides: Confirms ChatGPT's split (Apple for iPhone, Samsung/Pixel for Android, Garmin/Fitbit for either) but adds the hard exclusions: a shopper on an iPhone X/XS or older, or on iOS 26, cannot pair the Apple Watch Series 12 or SE 3 that ChatGPT recommended; an iPhone owner cannot use the Galaxy Watch8 or Pixel Watch 4 at all; an Android phone below Android 12 (Samsung) or Android 11 (Google) is excluded; and a non-Samsung Android owner buying the Galaxy Watch8 loses ECG, blood pressure and sleep coaching, which moves them toward the Pixel Watch 4 or Garmin Venu 4. Garmin's ECG is region-limited and 22+ only, so the Venu 4's 'works with both phones' advantage does not extend to ECG everywhere.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the pairing mechanism in the makers' own words: Samsung's compatibility table lists iOS as 'Not supported' for the Galaxy Watch8 series (Android 12.0 or higher, 1.5 GB RAM), Apple requires iPhone 11 or later on iOS 27 for Series 12 / SE 3, and Garmin's manual says text replies are 'available only for compatible Android phones' because the phone, not the watch, sends the SMS, so a Garmin Venu 4 on an iPhone shows texts but cannot answer them.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the maker's solar panel stops charging the battery below 32°F (0°C). Kiwibit says its panel "will not charge the battery below 0°C", and Birdfy puts the solar-charging range at 32–104°F. Both feeders still run below freezing, Birdfy to 14°F and Kiwibit to −4°F, so through a freezing spell the battery only drains and is not refilled, however sunny it is.
angles.decides: This settles whether 'solar powered' works year-round. In a yard that stays below 32°F for days, a solar feeder from any of these makers runs on its battery alone. It still works, but you have to charge it indoors by hand. So in cold climates battery size matters more than panel wattage. My own reasoning, which no source states: Birdfy's 9,000 mAh feeders (Feeder 2 series, Feeder Metal 2 4K) should outlast the 5,000 mAh Soliom BF08 and Bird Buddy's 3,800–3,900 mAh units on a cold, non-charging stretch. pages.why_used: The cited Newport FAQ and Minn Kota pages say only that the Newport's meter misreads lithium. None quotes Newport's own store line that the Smart Battery Box is 'not compatible with lithium batteries'. None says that the lithium-rated LiTime box's only breaker is 16 A, or that its 8.66 in interior is too short for 9.38–9.45 in tall Group 31 batteries. angles.decides: The 'breaker' line on these boxes means different things. On Newport and Minn Kota it is a 60 A breaker on the motor circuit. So LiTime ($84.99 today) is not a breaker-equipped alternative to Newport ($69.99): it still needs an inline motor breaker sized to the motor. For the lead-acid shopper, Newport stays the pick, though most Newport motors under 62 lb also need Newport's recommended 50 A or 40 A breaker. For a LiFePO4 shopper, Newport's store listing rules its box out. pages.why_used: None of the cited guides gives the built-in preamp's actual line-output voltage for any deck. One of them says outright that no output is stated for any pick. Angle A puts maker figures on five decks: AT-LP70X 252 mV, AT-LP120XUSB 240 mV, Sony PS-LX3BT 180 mV and the Fluance RT81 and RT81+ at 140 mV each. That shows the AT-LP70X is about 5 dB hotter into powered speakers, and that the RT81+ upgrade adds no line level. Angle C's Sony finding goes in as a supporting detail. None of the site's products is a turntable, and Amazon blocked the ASIN lookup, so the pick (Audio-Technica AT-LP70X) is a product we don't list and its link goes to the maker's page.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the built-in preamp's line-out voltage. Audio-Technica rates the AT-LP70X at 252 mV (240 mV for the AT-LP120XUSB) at 1 kHz, 5 cm/sec. Fluance rates both the RT81 and the RT81+ at 140 mV (−17 dBV) with no test condition. That is about 5 dB less signal into the same powered speakers, from a preamp with about 4–5 dB less implied gain (32 dB and 31 dB, against A-T's stated 36 dB).
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's pick of the AT-LP70X for a shopper who will plug straight into powered speakers. Its line out is about 1.8× the voltage of the RT81 and RT81+ (20·log10(252/140) ≈ 5.1 dB). All of them sit below the −10 dBV (316 mV) consumer line reference, and the Fluance pair sits furthest below it. The Fluance therefore needs more volume from the speakers or amp to play as loud. The RT81+'s stronger cartridge (4.0 mV against 3.5 mV) does not raise its stated line output, which stays at 140 mV. As a result, upgrading from the RT81 to the RT81+ gives no extra level at the LINE output, going by Fluance's own figures.

angles.decides: This mostly confirms the picks and adds one real limit. At the 25.6 V nominal voltage, a 100 A BMS (LiTime, Redodo) caps a single battery at about 2,560 W. That's below a 3,000 W inverter even before inverter losses. Epoch's 120 A continuous gives about 3,072 W. That still falls short once you allow about 10% inverter loss (a 3,000 W load then draws about 130 A), but Epoch's 200 A for 60 seconds covers motor starts and compressor kicks. Epoch is the premium pick for high-draw or cold-weather installs, and a single LiTime or Redodo fits loads up to about 2,000 W unless you add a second battery in parallel. On cycle life, Epoch's 3,500+ looks lower than LiTime's 4,000+ at 100% depth of discharge. Neither states end-of-life capacity, and Epoch's page puts its test conditions in a datasheet I couldn't read, so the headline numbers shouldn't decide between them.

pages.why_used: The guide ChatGPT cited (extruly) blames fused print-in-place joints on first-layer squish but never names the setting. This page reads each maker's stock slicer profile: Bambu A1 mini 0 mm, A1 0.075 mm, QIDI and Flashforge 0.15 mm. For fidget toys the slower, quieter mode costs little. extruly already advises dropping outer walls to 150 mm/s for clean print-in-place joints, which is well below the 500 mm/s headline. So the speed spec should not decide between the A1 mini and the A1. Build size (180 vs 256 mm) and the AMS lite colour option decide it. Any print-in-place piece longer than 180 mm has to go diagonally on the mini, and the length plus width must stay at or under 254.6 mm. It also shows that the Brio 520 and the Moderna 720/730 share one test record: 0.76 kWh/day, 0.74 gal/h of cold water at 42°F and 46 cups/h of hot water at 167°F. pages.query: fitness tracker with blood pressure monitor
pages.why_used: The cited pages (FDA safety notice, Samsung's US launch release, Hilo's comparison blog, Android Authority, Cardilog, Wareable and TechRadar on the Watch D3) never put the candidates on one accuracy yardstick. None states that the Watch D2 passed ISO 81060-2 while the Watch D3 being recommended has not been validated and was measured outside the 5 mmHg mean bound. None says the validated Omron HeartGuide code is discontinued while the BP8000-M still sold carries an unvalidated code.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on a single accuracy yardstick (passing the ISO 81060-2 clinical validation) only the Huawei Watch D2 among the cards passes for the general population, while the newer Watch D3 it recommended has not been validated yet (Fnac measured it 7/6 mmHg below an Omron cuff), and the 'FDA-cleared' Omron HeartGuide is discontinued and has a second model code (HEM-6411T-ZM) with no published validation.
angles.decides: It moves the cuff pick from the Watch D3 to the Watch D2. The D2 is the only cuff watch on offer with a pass under ISO 81060-2 (85-subject primary study plus stress and ambulatory studies). The D3 has no validation yet, and a named reviewer measured it outside the 5 mmHg mean-error bound. It also takes the Omron HeartGuide out of the 'medical-focused' slot: Medaval lists it as discontinued, and the clearance (K182481) covers the HEM-6410T-ZM, so the HEM-6411T-ZM code is not a validated buy. Samsung, Hilo Core and Apple stay as trend or notification tools. Samsung and Hilo call their products wellness features, and neither publishes a validation result for its estimates.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many blood pressure readings each device gets per charge. From the makers' battery test conditions: Huawei Watch D2 and D3 get about 36 cuff readings per charge at 6 a day for 6 days, and up to 96 when 24-hour ABPM (ambulatory blood pressure monitoring) is on at 15-minute intervals, though then the battery lasts only 1 day. Omron HeartGuide gets about 16 cuff readings per charge at 8 a day for 2 days. Hilo Core gets up to 210–525 optical estimates, and none of those are cuff readings.
angles.decides: This confirms the Huawei Watch D2/D3 as the pick for someone who wants many real cuff readings and still a weeklong battery: about 36 cuff readings per charge, against about 16 for the Omron HeartGuide, which also has to be charged about every 2 days. It also exposes a catch the answers miss. A full 24-hour ABPM session runs the Huawei battery down to about 1 day, and Expert Reviews' Jonathan Bray saw about 3 days when testing 'multiple times per day'. Hilo Core gives far more readings per charge, but they are optical estimates checked against a cuff, not cuff readings. The figure helps choose a watch but does not overturn the medical caveat.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Huawei's own compatibility table for the Watch D2 marks cuff blood-pressure measurement and 24-hour ambulatory BP (ABPM) as supported on iPhone (iOS 13.0+), the same as on Android, and that both airbag strap sizes come in the box: M for 130–160 mm wrists, L for 161–210 mm. For comparison, Samsung's BP needs a Galaxy phone, and Apple's hypertension notifications show no readings and leave out Apple Watch SE.
angles.decides: ChatGPT ended by asking 'Which phone do you use?', and this finding answers that. For iPhone users who want real mmHg readings, the Huawei Watch D2/D3 is the only cuff watch here whose maker lists BP and 24-hour BP as working on iOS. It is still an import with no FDA clearance and no US warranty. Apple Watch gives only hypertension alerts, on Series 9+/Ultra 2+ and not SE, so Dealectric's listed Apple Watch SE 3 gets no BP feature at all. Galaxy Watch BP works only with a Galaxy phone, and only on a watch and phone bought in the US. Dealectric's listed Galaxy Watch 8 qualifies under that rule. Android users on non-Samsung phones get Huawei Health from AppGallery, not Google Play. Hilo Core needs iOS 16+ or Android 14+.
products: Samsung Galaxy Watch (Watch4 and later, incl. Watch8/Watch9)

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Huawei Watch D2's cuff is an inflating airbag that only works when the watch is held level with the heart on a wrist 130–210 mm around, using whichever of the two included straps fits (M 130–160 mm, L 161–210 mm), and that Huawei itself warns that arrhythmia, a heart rate below 40 or above 180 bpm, or severe arteriosclerosis can make readings fail or come out wrong.
angles.decides: This confirms that the cuff watch is the only kind in ChatGPT's picks that actually measures blood pressure rather than estimating it. It also adds conditions that ChatGPT left out. A shopper whose wrist is outside 130–210 mm, or who has atrial fibrillation or frequent premature beats, should not count on the D2's cuff and should use an upper-arm cuff instead. Turning on the D2's 24-hour monitoring cuts battery life to about 1 day. On the Samsung side, the feature needs a Galaxy phone on Android 12 or later and a separately bought upper-arm cuff every 28 days. Samsung also says its Health Monitor app works only on devices bought in a country where the service is offered.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that in the5krunner's four-person seated test against an Omron upper-arm cuff, the Huawei Watch D3 read low on 18 of 20 systolic readings and 16 of 20 diastolic readings. The per-person average gaps reached -14/-8 mmHg (139/90 on the cuff, 125/82 on the watch) and -13/-17 mmHg (115/76 on the cuff, 102/59 on the watch). Notebookcheck's three-reading test found the D3's mean systolic reading only 0.5% below an Omron RS4 wrist monitor's, but its diastolic reading about 11% higher.
angles.decides: ChatGPT's second chat ranks the Huawei Watch D3 'Best for actual blood pressure measurements'. Named measurements partly support this: on systolic, Notebookcheck measured the D3's mean 0.5% below an Omron RS4. They also qualify it: the5krunner found the D3 read low on most readings across four people, with two people reading 13–17 mmHg low on one number. Only the Omron HeartGuide (HEM-6410T-ZM) has a published ISO 81060-2 validation with numbers: -0.9 ± 7.6 / -1.1 ± 6.1 mmHg (Kuwabara et al., 2019). For a shopper who wants readings they can act on, this favors the HeartGuide, or at least checking any cuff watch against an upper-arm cuff. The cuffless options are a different case. Notebookcheck's single pair for the Hilo Band was 5/8 mmHg high, and a 2026 Digital Health study found smartwatch errors grew to 3.4/5.1 mmHg once blood pressure moved 10 mmHg from the calibration point. Both point to using these bands for trends, not for spot readings.

The cheapest one that also gives a full fitness watch is a Galaxy Watch8 40mm ($299.99 at samsung.com) plus the separate arm cuff Samsung requires for calibration (Omron Bronze BP5150, $46.99 MSRP), $346.98 in total and Galaxy phone only. The others: Hilo Core costs $239.98 in year one and $389.97 over two years. The Huawei Watch D2 is a $409 import. The D3 is sold only as a $659 China-version import. The Watch9 adds $130 for no BP difference, since Samsung lists Watch4 and later. A real cuff on the wrist (Huawei D2) costs about $62 more as an unofficial import with no US approval. Hilo is cheaper in year one but costs more by year two, and its band does no fitness tracking. iPhone users get no BP numbers at any price. The Omron HeartGuide should not be recommended because Omron US no longer lists it.

pages.why_used: The rival pages only list single EcoFlow bundles. They never total what a full 60 kWh build costs, never give a cost per Wh, and never compare EcoFlow against Anker with the needed home panel counted. This page adds up both builds part by part at today's store prices: 61.44 kWh for $26,691 bare, $29,691 with Smart Home Panel 3, or $29,092 for the E10 with Power Dock. It also shows why neither build reaches 60 kW.

On that basis the highest is EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X at 36 kW with 3 inverters, followed by Anker SOLIX E10 at 22.8 kW rated, EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra at 21.6 kW and BLUETTI EP900 at 18 kW from 2 units (7.6 kW off-grid on 2×B500). The only true 60 kW unit, the Sol-Ark 60K, outputs 277/480 V three-phase only.
angles.decides: This confirms the DELTA Pro Ultra X as the pick for anyone who reads '60000w' as power for a US home. Three paralleled inverters give 36 kW, which is the highest of any 120/240 V option here. That is still only 60% of 60 kW, and the page should say so plainly. If the shopper really needs 60 kW, they need a commercial 277/480 V three-phase system such as the Sol-Ark 60K, which a normal split-phase house can't use without a three-phase service. If they mean 60 kWh, one DPU X inverter with 10 batteries holds 61.44 kWh. Today the cheapest way to build that from EcoFlow's US store is the $7,899 bundle plus 8 Smart Extra Batteries at $2,349 each, for $26,691. ChatGPT showed card prices of $18,798 and $12,699, and both sit far below that figure.

This page gives Netflix's own rule: phones can cast Netflix only to Chromecast 3rd gen or older, a Nest Hub, or select Vizio and Compal TVs, and only on Standard or Premium plans. It then sorts each Wi-Fi mini projector by whether Netflix actually plays on it.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that both makers' '2.5 hours' battery claims are Eco Mode figures. Outside Eco mode, Expert Reviews measured 1 h 52 min of streaming on the XGIMI MoGo 4 and reported 60 to 80 minutes on the Nebula Capsule 3 at full brightness. Only the MoGo 4 lasts through a typical film on battery without dimming.
angles.decides: This settles the travel and outdoor pick ChatGPT made. It called the Capsule 3 'best for travel' because it has a battery, but at full brightness its 60 to 80 minutes won't cover most films. The MoGo 4 ($479 at XGIMI US) ran 1 h 52 min outside Eco mode. It also switches itself into Eco mode whenever it starts unplugged, so the 2.5 h is real only on the dim setting. The $519 MoGo 4 + PowerBase Stand bundle is the battery option. The Capsule 3 suits buyers who mainly want a small, light (0.85 kg vs 1.31 kg) projector for dark rooms.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the cost per hour of battery playback: the $519 XGIMI MoGo 4 + PowerBase Stand bundle plays 5 h of video, which works out to $103.80 per battery hour and two 2-hour movies per charge. The $479 MoGo 4 alone plays 2.5 h, or $191.60 per battery hour, so $40 more doubles the runtime.
angles.decides: If the shopper wants a battery projector for outdoor or travel movie nights, the derived figures point to the MoGo 4 + PowerBase bundle rather than the bare MoGo 4. The bundle fits two films per charge at $1.15 per ISO lumen, and the bare MoGo 4's 2.5 h barely covers one film. The MoGo 2 Pro (New) has the cheapest lumen ($0.83 per ISO lumen at $359), but none of the pages I opened shows a built-in battery for it, and the original MoGo 2 Pro is rated at 65 W from the wall. ChatGPT's 'best value' card should therefore be treated as plug-in only until XGIMI confirms otherwise.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the power-bank minimum for the two battery picks: the MoGo 4 needs a third-party bank or adapter of at least 65 W (20 V/3.25 A), and the Capsule 3 needs at least 45 W PD 2.0 at 5–20 V. The Capsule 3's USB-C port only charges and does not carry video.
angles.decides: This confirms the Capsule 3 over the MoGo 4 for a shopper who wants to run the projector from a power bank. The Capsule 3 works from a 45 W PD bank, while the MoGo 4 needs a bank that delivers at least 65 W at 20 V. It also shapes the iPhone advice. On the Capsule 3, Nebula says DRM content cannot be mirrored over AirPlay, and the USB-C port can't take video, so Netflix should come from the built-in licensed app or over HDMI. On the MoGo 4, XGIMI's iOS mirroring route is MagiCast plus Cast Screen on the same Wi-Fi, not native AirPlay. It also rules out Dealectric's Aurzen ZIP for this question, even though Dealectric lists it. ZIP has no Google TV or Netflix app, and Aurzen says Netflix, Hulu and Disney+ cannot be mirrored or cast to it. So it fails the 'Wi-Fi for streaming' need without the separate CastPlay accessory, which Aurzen lists at $129.99.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states Netflix's own rule: casting Netflix from a phone or tablet only works to a 3rd-gen-or-older Chromecast, a Google Nest Hub, or select cast-enabled Vizio and Compal TVs, and casting or mirroring needs a Standard or Premium plan. So a Wi-Fi mini projector without a licensed Netflix app built in, such as the Aurzen ZIP, cannot show Netflix wirelessly at all.
angles.decides: It confirms that the Google TV and licensed-Netflix picks (XGIMI MoGo 4, MoGo 2 Pro, Aurzen EAZZE D1 and D1 air) are the safe answer for a shopper who wants Netflix. It also rules out mirroring-only Wi-Fi mini projectors like the Aurzen ZIP for Netflix, Hulu and Disney+ unless an extra dongle is bought. On a Wi-Fi projector, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth alone are not enough; the licensed app is the feature that decides it.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, in ProjectorCentral's lab, the XGIMI MoGo 4 drops from 400–404 ISO lumens in Performance mode to 151–154 in the ECO mode its 2.5-hour battery claim depends on, so the battery-runtime advantage and the 'brighter than Capsule 3' claim come from different power modes.
angles.decides: The finding confirms the MoGo 4 as the brighter pick when it's plugged in. ProjectorCentral measured about 400 lumens against 201 that Projector Reviews measured for the Capsule 3 in Bright mode, and 125–145 in its other modes. On battery the gap narrows: the MoGo 4 measured 151–154 lumens in ECO, which is the mode its 2.5-hour claim depends on. The Capsule 3 loses about 40% on battery (Projector Reviews), which by my arithmetic leaves roughly 75–120 lumens. Expert Reviews puts its runtime at 60–80 minutes at full brightness. The MoGo 2 Pro ($359 in ChatGPT's answer) measured 463 ANSI lumens on mains (Projector Reviews), above the MoGo 4's 400. That makes it the better value for brightness indoors. It is a 2023 test, with no measured lag. For gaming, the MoGo 4 measured 22.1 ms in Game Mode.
