pages.why_used: The cited rival pages (3dtoolchangers.com/printers, 3dprinteray.com/toolchanger-printers) give only maker swap-time claims and prices. None has a named tester's results on the same model. This page has them: CNC Kitchen's 4-colour cube took under 4 h on the U1 and Prusa XL and about 7 h on the Bambu H2C, and a colour change took about 40 s on the H2C against 10–15 s on a toolchanger. It also has Notebookcheck's Creator 5 Pro waste and prep-time figures and today's prices: U1 $699, Creator 5 Pro $849. The pick, the Snapmaker U1, is not a product we list. Snapmaker isn't in our programs and amzcheck found no U1 on Amazon. Our QIDI and Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro printers have a single nozzle and win no segment of this question, so the page adds no product of ours.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the U1's 5-second swap and the INDX's 12-second swap are measured differently. Prusa's ~12 s runs from the last extrusion on one tool to the first extrusion on the next, while Snapmaker's 5 s is an undefined 'typical' lab result. A hands-on reviewer timed the U1 at 10–12 s per colour change, which is about the same as the INDX, not 2.4× faster.
angles.decides: It removes the U1's apparent speed edge over the INDX. Measured the same way, both swap in about 10–12 s, so the $749-vs-$1,999 choice comes down to enclosure and chamber heat (INDX up to 55 °C, U1 only an optional unheated Top Cover), waste per swap (INDX 0.013 g claimed with no prime tower, U1 about 0.049 g measured from its prime tower), and the INDX's smaller Y travel. Swap speed doesn't separate them. This confirms the U1 as the value pick but not as a faster one.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much tool-change time and waste a full job adds. Per 1,000 tool changes, the Prusa CORE One+ INDX spends about 3.3 h swapping (12 s each) and wastes about 13 g of filament (0.013 g each). The Snapmaker U1 spends about 1.4 h (5 s each). So on a print with many colour changes, the INDX's low-waste nozzle swap adds about 1.9 h per 1,000 changes.
angles.decides: For dense multicolour work (thousands of changes per plate), this favours the U1 or Creator 5 Pro on time, since a full toolhead swaps in about 5 s. The INDX makes sense when the buyer cares more about nozzle or material variety and near-zero waste (13 g per 1,000 changes) than about speed. Its 8-tool configuration also brings the price per tool close to the budget machines: $281 assembled, $244 as a kit.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that tool changing can be added to a Prusa printer someone already owns only with the kit made for that model: the INDX kit for CORE One/+ is $693.52 for 4 tools, the separate kit for CORE One L/L+ is $763.80, the CORE One+ kit does not fit the L, and both ship after February 2027; also, an original XL with a Dwarf board marked 07 or lower needs new Dwarf boards before the $230.56 XL+ upgrade.
angles.decides: This does not change the pick for a buyer with no printer. ChatGPT's list stands: Snapmaker U1 is the cheapest true toolhead changer, and the XL+ is the large-format choice. It does change the answer for anyone who already owns a Prusa. A CORE One/+ owner can get INDX for $693.52 instead of $1,999 for an assembled printer, but delivery is after February 2027. A CORE One L owner must buy the L kit. An original XL owner should get the $230.56 XL+ upgrade, after checking the Dwarf board number, rather than buy a new XL+ at $3,899 or more. The original XL can't use the new 50 °C enclosure, so anyone buying a used original XL is stuck with the older enclosure until they upgrade.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that full-toolhead changers still waste filament at every swap: the Snapmaker U1 keeps all four heads preheated and builds a prime/wiping tower at each colour change, and Prusa says the XL's parked heads must drop to an idle temperature or they ooze, then prime 15–35 mm³ into a wipe tower. Prusa's CORE One+ INDX tools have no heaters of their own, and Prusa says they need 'No waste/prime tower', using 13 mg per change.
angles.decides: If the shopper bought a tool changer to stop wasting filament, this favours the Prusa CORE One+ INDX ($1,999 for 4 tools, $2,249 for 8, assembled). Its parked tools are unheated and need no prime tower. The Snapmaker U1 and Prusa XL+ still print a wipe/prime tower and need idle-temperature settings. The U1 also holds at most four spools per job. Whole-head changers still make sense for a different reason: each head has its own extruder and hotend. A low waste figure is not the reason to pick them.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that in CNC Kitchen's same-model test, a 4-colour cube took 7 hours on the Bambu Lab H2C in Purge Saving mode. The two full toolchangers, the Snapmaker U1 and the Prusa XL, each printed it in under 4 hours. The H2C took about 40 s per colour change including purge, against 10–15 s on a toolchanger.
angles.decides: This backs the full-toolchanger pick over the H2C, which ChatGPT listed 'from around $2,199' as an alternative. One reviewer, on the same model, measured the $749 Snapmaker U1 and the Prusa XL at about twice the H2C's multicolour speed. Notebookcheck adds a caution for the Creator 5 Pro: it needed 28 minutes of preparation before a 4-filament print, and its factory settings made 36 g of waste on a 16 g Benchy until the reviewer tuned it down to 8 g. On waste, CNC Kitchen found the U1's prime tower 'a bit' larger than the XL's, so the U1's edge is price and speed, not the lowest waste.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Snapmaker's US store now sells the U1 for $699 (it was $999), with a complete spare toolhead at $64.99. That is $50 less than the $749 ChatGPT and 3dprinteray quoted. It makes the U1 the same price as the open-frame Flashforge Creator 5 ($699) and $150 below the enclosed Creator 5 Pro ($849, not the $949 ChatGPT showed).
angles.decides: This confirms the U1 as the value pick and makes the lead wider. At $699 it costs the same as the Creator 5 but has a larger build volume (270 mm vs 256 mm cube). A full spare toolhead with its hotend costs $64.99. On the INDX, adding 4 passive tools costs about $62.50 each, but the printer is $1,999 assembled. The Creator 5 Pro at $849 is now the $150 step-up for anyone who needs an enclosed chamber heated to 65 °C. The Prusa CORE One+ INDX ($1,699 kit / $1,999 assembled for 4 tools) only makes sense if you need 8 tools or Prusa's ecosystem. Its changes take about 12 s against the U1's 5 s, and its build volume is smaller at 248 × 205 × 270 mm. Dealectric lists no toolchanger printer. Our QIDI Q2/Plus5/Max4 and Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro are single-nozzle and don't answer this question.

None of them shows that Rev-A-Shelf's kidney ratings (25/50/64/84 lb for 18/24/28/32 in) all come from one area rating, so dropping from 28 to 24 in costs 22% of the capacity. None prices the units per rated pound, and none separates a bare bearing's rating from a shelf's rating. The pick, Rev-A-Shelf Lazy Daisy LD-2472, is not a product Dealectric lists, and none of our listed products wins any part of this question. angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Rev-A-Shelf's per-shelf ratings for its kidney lazy susans (25 / 50 / 64 / 84 lb for 18 / 24 / 28 / 32 in) all work out to one rating of 20 lb per square foot. That means a shelf's capacity grows with the square of its diameter: dropping one size from 28 in to 24 in loses about 22% of capacity, and an 18 in shelf holds 30% of what a 32 in shelf holds.

The 400 lb Everbilt bearing figure is for the bare plate. It tells you nothing about how much a finished shelf will hold.

pages.why_used: The two cited TP-Link FAQs (947 and 83) explain how to set up schedules and Auto-Off. Neither says what happens when the internet or power goes out. TP-Link's own FAQ 2463 does: schedules, timers and Away Mode run on the plug with the internet down, there is a 32-rule cap per plug, the timers stop after a power cut until the plug goes back online to reset its clock, the priority order is Timer > Schedule > Away, and Tapo's Away Mode can run past midnight while Kasa's can't. The product pages add the 1/6 HP motor limit behind the '15 A' rating, against 1/2 HP on the EP40. Angle A is the only one that is fully sourced from the maker for every row, and it changes the pick for outdoor/motor loads and for cabins with no internet.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that TP-Link's Kasa and Tapo plugs keep running their schedules and timers when the internet is down but stop running them after a power cut until they get back online to reset their clocks, or that the plugs' '15 A' rating covers only 1/6 HP for motors.
angles.decides: This confirms Kasa or Tapo for the usual lamp-or-fan schedule: the schedules are stored on the plug and run with the internet down. It changes the pick in two cases. (1) If the timer must recover by itself after a power cut while the internet is also out, as in a cabin, a holiday house or an aquarium during a storm, these plugs stop running schedules until they're back online. That points to the plain programmable timer ChatGPT offered as its 'No Wi-Fi required' option. (2) For a motor load such as a pump, dehumidifier or compressor, the '15 A' headline drops to a 1/6 HP motor rating on both the EP10 and the P125M. Within TP-Link, Tapo beats Kasa for overnight away/vacation lighting, because Tapo Away Mode can run past midnight and Kasa's can't. For 'shut off X minutes after every turn-on', the P125M has a built-in Auto-Off setting on every Tapo plug. On the EP10, TP-Link's own FAQs only show it done as a Smart Action, and automations need the internet.
products: general (Kasa EP10, EP40, Tapo P125M and other listed plugs)

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a Kasa/Tapo plug stores its schedules on the plug and keeps running them with the internet down, but after a power cut it stops running them until it gets back online and resyncs its clock. TP-Link staff (Wayne-TP) said so on TP-Link's community forum: 'if the smart plug experiences a power cut, the schedule will not continue until the smart plug reconnects to the internet to synchronize device time.'
angles.decides: This confirms Kasa/Tapo Wi-Fi plugs as the pick for an ordinary indoor timer on reliable home Wi-Fi with internet. Schedules live on the plug, so a router or ISP outage does not stop them. There are up to 32 schedules per Tapo plug, and Auto-Off runs on every Tapo plug and on Kasa EP40M, KP125M and EP25 V2. But if the plug will run where power cuts are common, or with no internet (a garage on a hotspot, a cabin, a router-reboot plug), a power cut stops the schedule until the plug gets back online. For that case the page should point the shopper to the 'No Wi-Fi required' outlet timer that ChatGPT only mentioned in passing. Or, as TP-Link staff suggest, set the plug's power-on Default State and add repeat OFF schedules. The Minoston Z-Wave plugs Dealectric lists are not a standalone timer pick: they need a Z-Wave hub to set up and run schedules.

pages.why_used: Both of ChatGPT's searches ended in 'solar panel compatibility', and its answer told shoppers to 'choose a panel explicitly compatible with your exact model' without naming any. The cited rivals (SafeWise, Bob Vila, HomeGearLab, RottenWiFi) give no panel model numbers or generation exclusions, apart from HomeGearLab's one Blink line and its mention of USB-C for Ring. This page adds a maker-sourced fit chart (Reolink, eufy, Ring, Arlo VMA by camera model number, Blink), each maker's exclusions, Reolink's 0 °C charging floor and its 9 m extension limit.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the makers' sunlight claims into one comparable figure. eufy's '2 hours of sun' for the SoloCam S340 rests on a harvest of 800–1,200 mAh a day against 100–200 mAh of use, so it carries a 4–12× margin. Reolink's '20 minutes with the 3 W panel' (Argus PT Ultra) works out to only about 1 Wh at the panel's rated output, and Tapo's '50 minutes' (C465) is measured at lab standard sun of 1,000 W/m² with up to 100 events a day. The gap between 2 hours and 20 minutes comes from how each maker builds its claim, not from a 6× difference in panels. Also, every maker's charging floor is 32°F, even where the camera is rated to run at -4°F.
angles.decides: This backs the S340 and Argus 4 Pro picks. It removes a false tie-breaker: a shopper shouldn't choose the Argus PT Ultra over the S340 because '20 minutes' sounds better than '2 hours'. The claims are built on different margins and conditions. On the same 300 s/day basis that both makers use, the S340 (10,000 mAh, 3 months) lasts longer on battery alone than the Argus 4 Pro (5,000 mAh, about 2 months), and that reserve is what matters when the panel can't charge. For buyers where winters freeze, the 32°F floor from eufy, Reolink and TP-Link means no panel size will charge a frozen camera. Battery reserve and a sunny, south-facing mount matter more than panel watts.
products: Reolink Argus 4 Pro + Solar Panel 2 (6 W)

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how long a drained kit takes to refill from its own panel, or how many days the battery can carry the camera with no sun. Worked out from the makers' own figures: a fully drained eufyCam S3 Pro needs about 16–52 days of optimal sun to refill (13,000 mAh at a net 250–800 mAh per day). A drained Reolink Argus PT Ultra needs about 22 days of eufy-style 'claimed minimum' sun (21.6 Wh at 1 Wh per day from 20 minutes on its 3 W panel). So the battery reserve (about 60–130 days) is what gets these cameras through winter, not the panel's wattage.
angles.decides: This backs the eufyCam S3 Pro kit for shady or northern sites: its own figures give at least 2.25× surplus on a sunny day (450 ÷ 200) and 65–130 days on battery alone. It counts against the Reolink Argus 4 Pro for those sites. Its maker claims only about 2 months per charge at 300 s of recording a day, about half the 4 months Reolink claims for the 21.6 Wh Eco Ultra and PT Ultra. For the shopper who 'just needs a panel', it shows that a bigger panel shortens refills but does not add reserve days. Reserve is the battery's job.
products: Reolink Argus 4 Pro + Solar Panel 2 (6 W)

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a maker-sourced chart of which solar panel fits which camera generation. For example: Arlo's Pro (6th Gen) VMC4070 and Ultra (3rd Gen) VMC5050 are listed only for the VMA7600 Universal panel, not the magnetic VMA5600. The VMA3600 is for 1st-gen Essential only and the VMA6600 is for 2nd-gen Essential only. Ring's USB-C panel excludes the 1st-gen Stick Up Cam. Blink's Solar Panel Mount works only with Outdoor (3rd Gen) and not with Outdoor 4, XT or XT2. Reolink's 3/6/12 W panels fit every Reolink battery camera except the original Argus and Keen, and charge only from 0 to 45 °C.
angles.decides: This mostly settles the second branch ChatGPT offered, 'just a solar panel for my existing camera'. The right panel is set by brand and generation, not by watts, and buying the wrong Arlo or Blink generation means a connector or mount that doesn't fit. It confirms Reolink's 6 W Solar Panel 2 (USB-C) as the right add-on for the Argus 4 Pro and Argus Eco Ultra that ChatGPT showed. For the eufy S340 and S3 Pro, it points to eufy's own 3 W panel ($29.99, sold as certified for both) rather than a third-party panel, because eufy warns non-certified panels may damage the battery. Ring Outdoor Cam/Spotlight owners can buy the $59.99 USB-C panel unless they own a 1st-gen Stick Up Cam.
products: Arlo VMA6600 Essential Solar Panel (2nd Gen)

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, from the maker's own pages, that the cameras it recommended stop taking solar charge at 0 °C (32 °F) even though they are rated to keep running far colder: eufy SoloCam S340 charges at 0–40 °C but operates down to −20 °C, and Reolink's Solar Panel 2 charges at 0–45 °C while the Argus 4 Pro operates down to −10 °C. It also isn't stated that Reolink's Solar Panel 2S, which has a built-in 5,900 mAh battery, keeps the camera powered from 0 °C down to −20 °C.
angles.decides: For shoppers where winter days stay below freezing, the 6 W Solar Panel 2 bundled with the Argus 4 Pro and Argus Eco Ultra, and the S340's built-in panel, put no charge into the camera on sub-freezing days. The camera runs down its own battery until a day above 0 °C. That doesn't change the pick for mild climates, where the Argus 4 Pro or S340 is fine. For cold climates it changes which panel to buy: for a Reolink camera, choose the Solar Panel 2S, whose internal battery recharges down to −10 °C and powers the camera from 0 °C to −20 °C. The Argus 4 Pro itself is rated only to −10 °C (14 °F), so the camera, not the panel, is the cold limit there. Reolink also lists the original Argus, Keen and Doorbell (Battery) as unsupported by its panels. eufy has no equivalent in what I read, so S340 owners in cold areas get no solar charge below freezing.

pages.why_used: The cited guides give each split-phase inverter a single 240 V total and never say how much one 120 V leg can carry. This page adds EG4's own manual limit of up to 8 kW of L1/L2 imbalance for the 18kPV, and the 6000XP's 3,000 W ceiling per leg (25 A × 120 V, SolarTech). That limit is the catch behind the usual 'budget off-grid' pick.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the headline split-phase rating you can draw on one 120 V leg. EG4's 6000XP manual caps output current at 25 A, which works out to about 3,000 W on a single 120 V leg, half its 6 kW label. EG4's 18kPV manual says that unit can take up to 8 kW of imbalance between L1 and L2.
angles.decides: This matters most for ChatGPT's 'best budget off-grid' pick. If a cabin or shop runs mostly 120 V loads, the EG4 6000XP behaves like a 3 kW inverter per leg, not 6 kW, so the shopper may need two units or a different inverter. The EG4 18kPV handles up to 8 kW of imbalance, which supports keeping it as the value pick for whole-home backup where loads are rarely balanced. I couldn't open a source for the Sol-Ark 15K's per-leg rating, so the comparison table has to footnote it as missing rather than fill it in.
products: Sun Gold Power 6000W 48V Split Phase Inverter Charger

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the yearly energy the inverter burns just by being switched on (idle W × 8,760 h): about 788 kWh/yr for the Sol-Ark 15K, 613 kWh/yr for the EG4 18kPV, 438 kWh/yr for the EG4 6000XP and 70 kWh/yr for the Schneider XW Pro 6848. None works the 18kPV's daily idle draw (1.68 kWh) out as about 12% of a 14.3 kWh battery.
angles.decides: It backs the EG4 18kPV as the value pick for whole-home hybrid use: about $333–$408 per battery-only kW against the Sol-Ark 15K's $471–$479, and it idles 20 W lower (613 vs 788 kWh/yr). For off-grid cabins the EG4 6000XP is cheapest per kW ($250). The Schneider XW Pro costs the most per kW ($544) but wastes about 1/9 the 18kPV's idle energy, about 1/11 the Sol-Ark 15K's and about 1/6 the 6000XP's. That matters on a small battery with little winter sun. Dealectric's own Sun Gold Power 6000W unit is cheap at $203/kW but has no MPPT, so it needs a separate solar charge controller, and every variant showed as sold out on 2026-11-10.
products: Sun Gold Power 6000W 48V Split Phase Inverter Charger

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EG4's own warranties for the 18kPV (10-year) and the 6000XP (5-year) exclude 'damages incurred from voltage or current spikes due to open-loop lithium battery communications'. So the battery has to talk closed-loop with the inverter or the inverter's warranty doesn't cover that damage, and EG4's product pages only promise closed-loop with EG4 48V batteries.
angles.decides: ChatGPT's 'best overall value' pick, the EG4 18kPV, still stands. But the page should say it suits buyers who use EG4 batteries, or another closed-loop battery on EG4's list, because pairing it with an open-loop battery leaves spike damage outside the 10-year warranty. A buyer who wants to mix battery brands should look at the Sol-Ark, whose warranty rule is similar but tied to its own approved list. The finding also separates the two EG4 cards: the 6000XP has half the warranty term (5 years against 10). And a whole-home build through EG4's GridBOSS is limited to three inverters, even though the 18kPV parallels up to 10 on its own.
products: Sun Gold Power 6000W 48V Split Phase Inverter Charger

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the EG4 6000XP, its 'best value' and 'budget off-grid' pick, can deliver only about 3,000 W on each 120 V leg and does not shift load between legs. Its 6,000 W rating is a 240 V total, so a house with 4,000 W of 120 V loads on one leg overloads the inverter even though the total is under 6,000 W.
angles.decides: The finding qualifies the 6000XP pick. The shopper typed 'split phase', which suggests a house panel full of 120 V circuits. On the 6000XP, any single leg above about 3,000 W trips the inverter, so the shopper has to balance circuits between L1 and L2 or choose another unit. Choose a bigger hybrid like the 18kPV or Sol-Ark 15K, with higher per-leg headroom, or a low-frequency transformer unit like the Sun Gold Power 6000W LF or Schneider XW Pro. The page should tell shoppers to add up the 120 V loads on each leg before buying, not to compare only the headline wattage.

The Solar Lab measured the Sol-Ark 15K at 97 W in standby and the EG4 18kPV at 60–70 W idling on battery, about 0.65–0.89 kWh a day more for the Sol-Ark. SunForgeLab measured the EG4 6000XP at 55–65 W idle and 94.2% battery-to-AC efficiency.

For the budget pick, SunForgeLab's 6000XP data shows a real-world cost: 55–65 W idle (1.3–1.6 kWh/day) and 90.8% efficiency below 500 W.

pages.why_used: The cited pages say only that base M1 and M2 MacBooks support one external display. None of them gives Apple's lid-open limit for the M3, the MacBook Neo limit, or the M4 Air as the first base Air that runs two displays. None says what each extender needs on each chip: free software for the Trio 3 Pro, a $59 DisplayLink adapter that Xebec requires on every Mac because macOS lacks MST, or the FOPO driver.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a triple extender only works with the laptop lid open, and with the lid open a base M1/M2/M3 MacBook natively extends to just one of the two added screens. Apple says the M3 Air drives a second external display only with the lid closed. On those Macs the Trio 3 Pro needs Mobile Pixels' free software for the second screen, and the Xebec Tri-Screen 3 needs Xebec's DisplayLink-based Mac Adapter, while M4/M5 Airs drive both screens natively.
angles.decides: This confirms the Trio 3 Pro as the pick for Windows laptops and M4/M5 or Pro/Max MacBooks. For a base M1/M2/M3 MacBook, every 'single USB-C' claim needs a footnote: the Trio needs Mobile Pixels' free software (which Macworld only describes as 'rather like DisplayLink') and the Xebec needs its separately sold Mac Adapter, which uses DisplayLink. Xebec's own help pages warn that DisplayLink screens can show black video in protected streaming apps. ChatGPT's 'MacBook?' follow-up should send these owners to the chip-and-lid row of the table, not to a ranking. Separately, the Trio's 300-nit figure assumes a power adapter plugged into one of its USB-C ports. That adapter is also the source of the 65W pass-through, so a 'one-cable' desk setup really uses two cables.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much screen area each extender adds per pound or per dollar. UPERFECT BE14BF's two 14" 16:10 panels add 176 sq in at 3.39 lb, which is 52 sq in/lb and $2.21 per added sq in. Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro adds 179 sq in at about 4.19 lb (42.7 sq in/lb). Xebec Tri-Screen 3's 13.3" 16:9 panels add only 151 sq in at 3.7 lb (40.9 sq in/lb).
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's 'best value' pick (UPERFECT BE14BF): it adds about the same area as the Trio 3 Pro (176 vs 179 sq in) and is about 0.8 lb lighter. It weakens the case for the Xebec Tri-Screen 3 as the 'travel' pick, because it adds the least area per pound of the three and needs a separate Mac adapter for MacBooks. It does not separate the Trio 3 Pro from the UPERFECT on sharpness: both are about 187–189 ppi.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, according to Apple's own spec pages, the base M3 MacBook Air and the base 14-inch M3 MacBook Pro natively drive only one external display while the lid is open (a second one needs the lid closed, which defeats a laptop-plus-two-screens triple setup), that the MacBook Neo is limited to one external display even with the lid closed, and that the M4 MacBook Air is the first base Air that natively drives two external displays alongside its open built-in screen.
angles.decides: The pick changes for Mac owners. On a base M1, M2 or M3 MacBook, or a MacBook Neo, a 'driver-free, no-adapter' triple extender extends to only one side screen with the lid open. The shopper needs DisplayLink-type software (Trio 3 Pro: free software plus a power adapter for a single cable, per Macworld) or Xebec's Tri-Screen 3 Mac Adapter, which Xebec says every Mac user needs. On M4/M5 and Pro/Max Macs, the Trio 3 Pro works natively over two USB-C cables, which keeps it as the best overall pick. For Xebec, the separate adapter has to be added to the $699 price for any Mac.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that macOS on every Mac, including M-series Pro/Max/M4, lacks DisplayPort Multi-Stream Transport (MST). So a 'single-cable' triple extender like the Xebec Tri-Screen 3 can't drive two separate screens from one USB-C cable on a Mac without Xebec's DisplayLink-based Mac Adapter and driver. Meanwhile the Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro gets around this by using two USB-C cables, one per screen, not the 'single USB-C connection' ChatGPT described.
angles.decides: For a Mac buyer, this changes the pick. Xebec's single-cable design only works on a Mac with the extra $59 DisplayLink adapter and driver, a cost and a dependency ChatGPT left out of its $699 'best premium travel' pick. The Trio 3 Pro's two-cable design is native on any Mac with two DP-capable USB-C ports: M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max and M4/M5, per Macworld. Base M1/M2 Macs (Apple: 'One external display') still need Mobile Pixels' driver software whichever extender they use. For Windows buyers whose USB-C ports support DP Alt Mode, the single-cable design works as advertised, so the Trio 3 Pro stays the overall pick.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states any lab-measured figure for a triple extender. The closest numbers come from other models: Notebookcheck measured each side screen of the Monduo 16 Pro Duo at about 402–430 cd/m² center and about 15 W, or about 30 W for both, and PCWorld weighed a KYY triple extender at about 6.5 lb against a 1.6 kg claim. A page should tell shoppers to plan on a wall adapter, and to treat 300 nits and the listed weight as claims.

ChatGPT's own answer says such a battery needs a matching charger, but no result names or prices one. The arithmetic for a 100 Ah lithium trolling battery run down to 20% (80 Ah to put back) is about 8 h at 10 A per bank, 13.3 h on 6 A banks (MK 318 PCL) and 16 h on the 5 A banks of the NOCO GEN5X3. NOCO's GEN-series manual also limits each GEN5X3 bank to batteries of up to 120 Ah, against 230 Ah per bank for the GENPRO10X series.

The GEN5X3 (5 A/bank, about 16 h) and MK 318 PCL (6 A/bank, about 13.3 h) won't refill a 20%-SoC battery overnight. 10 A per bank (NOCO GENPRO10X3 or Minn Kota MK 330 PCL, about 8 h) is the minimum for an overnight refill. For back-to-back fishing days, 15 A per bank (MK 345 PCL, about 5.3 h) is the pick, but Minn Kota sizes a generator for it at 700 W against 450 W for the MK 330 PCL. On lithium voltage, the GENPRO10X3 (14.6 V) and Minn Kota PCL (14.5 V max) are effectively the same, so voltage does not separate them.

That charger needs about 16.7 h to refill a flat 100 Ah lithium battery, so it is not an overnight charger for a shopper who fishes days back to back. 10 A per bank (MK 330 PCL, GENPRO10X3) gives about 10 h, a long night. 15 A per bank (MK 345 PCL) gives about 6.7 h, the only onboard Minn Kota PCL tier that fits a short night. With separate 12V batteries (one per bank), multi-bank 12V onboard chargers stay the picks: NOCO GENPRO10X3 Lithium mode 14.6V and Minn Kota PCL max 14.5V. Both sit inside Redodo's 14.4V ±0.2V 12V LiFePO4 window. With one single 24V or 36V LiFePO4 pack, every charger ChatGPT listed is excluded. The shopper needs a single-output charger matched to the pack's voltage, such as Redodo 29.2V 20A / 43.8V 25A or Dakota 28.8V / 43.2V, and should use the battery maker's own charger because Redodo (2×/3×14.6V) and Dakota (2×/3×14.4V) use different setpoints.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Minn Kota's PCL applies no temperature compensation in lithium mode, while a typical LiFePO4 trolling battery's own BMS refuses charge below 32°F (Redodo: resumes only above 41°F). So in cold weather the battery, not the charger, decides whether an onboard charger left plugged in overnight puts any charge back.
angles.decides: For any of the multi-bank chargers ChatGPT named, the fact confirms the 'one bank per 12 V battery, chemistry set per bank' plan. It adds one condition that decides whether charging works at all: an angler charging lithium in late fall, winter or early spring needs a battery whose BMS has a low-temperature charge cutoff, or self-heating. No charger setting replaces that. The PCL's temperature compensation does not apply to lithium, and Minn Kota publishes no cold limit. A practical pairing is a PCL or GENPRO bank on a Redodo low-temp-cutoff battery, or the Redodo self-heating model for below-freezing launches. Expect no charge until the battery warms above 41°F. The PCL's 14.5 V maximum sits 0.1 V under Redodo's recommended 14.6 V charger. Minn Kota itself tells buyers to check that against the battery maker's spec.

pages.why_used: The rival pages give Synology's 'more than 2 GB' VM rule and Home Assistant's 2 GB VM minimum separately. None of them subtracts the HAOS VM from each NAS's shipped RAM. This page does: 6 GB left on the DXP2800, TS-264 and DXP4800 Plus, 2 GB on the DS925+, and none on a stock DS225+, which cannot start a VM at all.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts these together: a stock Synology DS225+ ships with exactly 2 GB, Synology's VMM rule says VMs run only on a NAS with more than 2 GB, and Home Assistant says an HAOS VM needs at least 2 GB. So the DS225+ cannot run an HAOS VM until a RAM module is added, even though its spec sheet lists '2 recommended VM instances'. On a 2 GB DS220+, VMM offered the auto-generated VM only 272 MB.
angles.decides: It rules out a stock DS225+ for an HAOS VM, so 'DS225+ / DS925+' on our page should become 'DS925+, or a DS225+ only with an added 4 GB module'. The DS925+ (4 GB ECC, 8 recommended VM instances) and the QNAP TS-264 (8 GB, where Virtualization Station needs at least 4 GB and QNAP advises giving VMs at most 50% of memory, leaving about 4 GB for HAOS) both clear the 2 GB HAOS minimum out of the box. On USB, all three main makers pass through a single device rather than a whole port or controller, so USB support doesn't separate them. On QNAP the only USB-speed caveat is guest-OS USB 3 support, which HAOS's Linux kernel meets, and the TS-264 also has USB 2.0 ports. UGREEN's DH2300 and DH4300 Plus cannot run VMs at all, so only the DXP models qualify.
products: Synology DS220+ (2 GB sibling, used as evidence for DS225+ behaviour)
Synology (VMM) with Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how much RAM each NAS has left once Home Assistant's own 2 GB VM minimum is taken out. The DS925+ keeps 2 GB for DSM, while the QNAP TS-264-8G and UGREEN DXP2800 each keep 6 GB.
angles.decides: This takes the Synology DS225+ out of the 'buy and run' group: it needs a RAM module before VMM will start any VM. It also shows the DS925+ (4 GB ECC) leaves only 2 GB for DSM next to a 2 GB HAOS VM, so an upgrade is realistically required there too. The 8 GB QNAP TS-264 and UGREEN DXP2800 run HAOS out of the box with 6 GB to spare. So on headroom the pick goes to TS-264 or DXP2800; Zigbee passthrough reliability is still the separate deciding factor. The power figures add that any NAS host draws roughly 10× more always-on energy than a Home Assistant Green (about 140–255 kWh a year against 14.9 kWh). That matters only if the NAS would not otherwise be running 24/7.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Synology DS225+ ships with 2 GB of RAM while Virtual Machine Manager runs VMs only on NAS units with more than 2 GB, so a stock DS225+ can't run a Home Assistant OS VM until the D4NS01-4G module is added.

A buyer of the Home Assistant ZBT-2 stick who plans to use Synology VMM should be told to flash the stick on a desktop first.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the mechanism that decides whether a passed-through Zigbee stick keeps working. The KVM/libvirt layer gives a USB device a device number at connect time, and only the physical port number stays the same (libvirt's own words). When a stick resets or re-enumerates, the VM keeps waiting for the old number. Sticks also differ: a ConBee II (CDC-ACM, /dev/ttyACM) failed on a UGREEN VM where a Sonoff ZBDongle-E, which uses a WCH CH34x-family serial bridge, worked straight away. The Home Assistant ZBT-2 disappears from Synology VMM during its mandatory first firmware flash.
angles.decides: The finding moves the deciding factor from NAS brand to stick. All three NAS VM apps can pass a USB device through. Whether it survives a reboot, replug or firmware flash depends on how the hypervisor rebinds it and on the stick's USB-serial bridge. For the pick: on UGREEN, Synology or QNAP, use a stick that has been reported working under VM passthrough (Sonoff ZBDongle-E on UGREEN). Avoid the ConBee II. If buying a ZBT-2, flash its firmware on another computer before passing it through. Expect to restart the VM, not just HAOS, after the stick drops. This supports ChatGPT's network-coordinator fallback (SMLIGHT SLZB-06), which avoids USB re-enumeration entirely, and makes it stronger.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts measured always-on power draw side by side for the NAS candidates. PCWorld measured its pick, the QNAP TS-264, at 26.5 W idle. ComputerBase measured the UGREEN DXP2800 and Synology DS224+ at 18.6 W idle each. raspberry.tips measured that a running HAOS VM adds only about 1–2 W on a DXP2800.
angles.decides: This doesn't decide whether USB Zigbee passthrough works. It does work as a tiebreak on running cost for a box that's on 24/7. ChatGPT's top pick, the QNAP TS-264, drew 26.5 W idle in PCWorld's test, against 18.6 W for the DXP2800 and DS224+ in ComputerBase's test. That gap is about 69 kWh a year: 7.9 W × 8,760 h. The DS925+ (28 W, NASCompares) and the DXP4800 Plus (24.25 W, KitGuru) cost more to run than either 2-bay. The HA VM itself adds only about 1–2 W (raspberry.tips). The labs used different drives and setups, so these figures show the size of the gap, not exact differences.

pages.query: best 3 in 1 magsafe charging station that keeps the phone cool
pages.why_used: The rival pages we could read (Macworld's ESR and UGREEN reviews and its roundup) say heat makes an iPhone throttle 25W charging, but none says the stations cool by two different mechanisms (fan versus thermoelectric cooler plus fan), that each cools only while its fan is on, or that Anker's Sleep Mode turns cooling off. This page adds those, Apple's own thresholds, and the one named fan-on versus fan-off measurement (Android Authority, 82°F against 90°F on the Belkin).

angles.decides: It confirms ESR as the pick on price but removes cooling as the reason. Belkin's 12°F cannot be read as nearly double ESR's 6.5°F, because one is a maximum and the other a mean, and Belkin's footnote names no ambient temperature or baseline. Anker's $229.99 'best premium cooling' pick rests on the hardware (thermoelectric cooler plus fan, TÜV label) and not on any published temperature drop. angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that regenerative braking is a charge into the pack, so a LiFePO4 battery whose BMS blocks charging below 32°F also blocks regen current. For them, a pack with a 32°F charge cutoff and no heater cannot take regen current on a cold morning. That covers LiTime 48V 100Ah and Vatrer's standard 105Ah kits, which are ChatGPT's budget and value picks. The fix is a self-heating pack. pages.why_used: I could read one of the cited pages in full (StackandValue) and the start of a second (Dupple). Neither says what Windows does to a Bluetooth speaker that supports hands-free calling. TechRadar, Tom's Hardware, Tom's Guide and PC Gamer returned only their titles, and Wired blocked the fetch, so the angle agents could not rule them out. Microsoft's driver docs say that once any app opens the speaker's mic, playback switches to mono at 8 or 16 kHz, and on Windows 10 the stereo stream is thrown away. This page gives each candidate's Bluetooth profile or mic listing and its wired fallback, and picks the A2DP-only Creative Pebble Pro, which plays USB audio.

A PC user who wants full power is therefore on Bluetooth (SBC only) or AUX. On a PC's own USB-C port with USB audio they get 10 W RMS (Pebble Pro) or 15 W RMS (Pebble X Plus). The mains-powered Creative T60 gives 30 W RMS while taking USB-C audio.
angles.decides: It changes the pick for a shopper who wants wired USB audio from a PC, which is the setup both ChatGPT answers pushed for gaming and calls. In that setup the Pebble Pro ($66.49) gives 10 W RMS and the Pebble X Plus ($123.49) gives 15 W RMS. The T60 ($94.99, with its own 18 V 2 A adapter) gives 30 W RMS while playing USB-C audio. ChatGPT's 'best overall value' Pebble Pro is a third as loud as the T60 in the mode ChatGPT recommended, unless the shopper buys a 30 W PD brick and moves to Bluetooth SBC or AUX. The Pebble Pro is still the right pick for a small desk where 10 W RMS is enough. For more volume over USB, the T60 is the better buy, and it costs less than the X Plus.

A Pebble Pro or Pebble X Plus buyer who adds the 30 W PD adapter for full power still needs a second connection for sound: USB-C to the PC, Bluetooth, or AUX. The Pebble V3 must stay USB-powered even in Bluetooth mode. The Pebble Pro stays the value pick for a PC with a USB-C port, since Creative rates 10 W RMS from a 10 W USB-C port. The T60 and M60 have no such power-source caveat on the pages I read, and the T60 ships with its own 18 V 2 A AC adapter.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Windows switches a Bluetooth speaker that supports the Hands-Free Profile to mono playback at 8 kHz or 16 kHz as soon as any app opens that speaker's microphone input. Microsoft says this happens on Windows 11 and that Windows 10 discards the stereo stream outright. Microsoft also lists only SBC, AAC, aptX Classic and aptX Adaptive (aptX Adaptive only on select Qualcomm radios) as Windows A2DP codecs, so a mic-less, A2DP-only speaker such as the Creative Pebble Pro, or a wired USB-C connection, avoids the problem.
angles.decides: For a PC used for both media and calls, pick a speaker that is A2DP-only with no built-in mic, or one with a wired USB-C audio input. That confirms the Creative Pebble Pro (A2DP only, SBC, USB audio, no built-in mic) as the safe default. A single portable speaker with a hands-free mic, such as the Marshall Emberton III, is a poor PC choice when calls matter. The moment Teams or Discord opens its mic, Windows drops the speaker to mono 8 kHz or 16 kHz, and the Emberton III has no wired audio input to fall back on (its USB-C is listed only for charging). The Creative T60 lists HFP alongside A2DP, so Windows 11 creates a mic input for it. Over Bluetooth, keep the PC's default mic set to something else, or use the T60's USB-C audio. A further point for the Pebble Pro: the 30 W RMS figure needs a separate 30 W USB PD adapter, which is not included. Powered from a PC port it is 10 W RMS.

None notes that the portable Bose Flex (2nd Gen) has no wired input. This page gives the HT-S100F's measured 62 ms (ARC) and 70 ms (optical), which is 1.5–1.7 frames and inside the ITU's 125 ms limit. It also sets out a wired-input check for every candidate.

pages.why_used: Every page ChatGPT cited compares the Yamaha CD-S303, Onkyo C-7030 and Denon DCD-600NE on the makers' own 105 / 107 / 112 dB claims; none carries a bench measurement. This page adds Audio Science Review's and Hi-Fi News' lab figures, which put the Yamaha and Denon at the same 95 dB noise floor and give the output-level gap, so the choice falls to outputs and USB, where the Yamaha wins.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the three makers' noise, distortion and output figures on one line and says that the Yamaha CD-S303's Pure Direct mode switches off the optical and coaxial outputs that are its main hardware edge over the optical-only Denon DCD-600NE, nor that Denon's own manual (12 W, 4.3 kg) and US product page (13 W, 4.0 kg) disagree with each other.
angles.decides: On the makers' own numbers the Denon leads on S/N (112 dB) and dynamic range (101 dB) but has no coaxial output; the Onkyo is the only one with a headphone jack and is the cheapest; the Yamaha is the only one with USB playback but loses both digital outputs whenever Pure Direct is on. For a shopper feeding an external DAC the Yamaha's advantage is conditional, which confirms the Onkyo as the practical pick and the Denon as the analog-only pick.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a Denon DCD-600NE left powered but idle draws 12 W against 0.3 W in standby, that its 30-minute Auto Standby ships switched off, or that the Yamaha-vs-Denon running-cost gap works out to about 1.5 kWh a year at 2 h of play a day.
angles.decides: Running cost cannot separate the Yamaha CD-S303 and Denon DCD-600NE: 11 W vs 12 W playing and 0.2 W vs 0.3 W in standby is about 1.5 kWh a year apart at 2 h/day. What does matter is behaviour: the Denon ships with Auto Standby off, so a forgotten unit burns 12 W around the clock (about 105 kWh/yr) until the owner holds POWER 5 s to enable the 30-minute timer. Both put out 2.0 V RMS on RCA, so neither needs a different amp input gain; the FiiO DM13 line out is 2.5 V RMS, about 1.9 dB hotter, which matters if the shopper is weighing the portable FiiO against a full-width deck for the same stereo.

angles.decides: Confirms the Onkyo C-7030 only as the pick for a shopper who owns an Onkyo RI amp or receiver (one remote, auto input switch); for any other brand of stereo amp the RI jack is dead weight and the Onkyo should be connected only by RCA/optical/coaxial. The Denon DCD-600NE has no amplifier link jack and no coaxial output, so it suits an amp with an optical input or RCA only. Yamaha CD-S303 remains the pick for USB/FLAC playback (rival-stated), but maker confirmation of its USB limits was not reachable.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Denon DCD-600NE and Onkyo C-7030 both put out a fixed 2.0 V RMS analog line level (Onkyo rated into 600 Ω), so the stereo must offer a line-level CD/AUX/TAPE input and the player cannot drive volume itself, nor that the Denon caps data discs at 512 files/256 folders, 48–320 kbps MP3/WMA, refuses non-finalized CD-Rs and copy-protected WMA, and outputs digital on optical only.
angles.decides: For a stereo with a spare analog CD/AUX/TAPE input the mechanism does not separate the three: each delivers a fixed ~2.0 V RMS line level over RCA, so any of them works and the player has no volume control of its own (a PHONO input is the wrong place). The mechanism only decides the pick when the stereo's free input is digital: a coaxial-only input rules out the Denon DCD-600NE (optical only); any digital link needs Pure Direct off on the Yamaha CD-S303 or Mode 1 on the Denon, else silence. For shoppers with burned discs, the Denon manual says non-finalized CD-Rs and copy-protected WMA will not play and caps a data disc at 512 files and 320 kbps.

Two usable details: the Denon's 1.92 Vrms output is near the 2 V standard while the Yamaha's 1.74 Vrms sits 1.2 dB low (the Yamaha will sound quieter at the same volume setting), and the Yamaha was verified bit-perfect as a transport over optical, which matters for anyone feeding an external DAC. Dometic's own spec for the US CFX5 45 is 1.05 Ah/h at 32 °C (90 °F) outside and 4 °C (39 °F) inside. For summer car camping, size the station at about 300 Wh per day for a 45 L compressor cooler, not the 160–200 Wh/day the 75 °F lab numbers suggest. A weekend in the heat needs about 600 Wh, which rules out 245–300 Wh stations (RIVER 3, Tenergy T320, ALLPOWERS R600) for anything past one night. The 1,024 Wh class is the right pairing for a 3-day trip. ChatGPT's '500 Wh ≈ 1–2 days' holds in heat (500/302 = 1.7 days) but undersells mild weather (500/163 = 3.1 days).

pages.why_used: The cited rivals (firstlayerlab, 3dprintgearlab) list the P2S chamber only as 'passive' or 'no active heating listed' and give the Q2's 65 °C without its heater wattage. None of them places the P2S's 50 °C passive ceiling and CNC Kitchen's measured 50.3–54.1 °C next to the Q2's separate 280 W heater, and none shows that the $349 Q2C drops that heater for $100 less on the same frame. This page covers all three.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Bambu Lab P2S's own '50 °C chamber' figure is a passive limit with no heater: it comes from bed heat held in by an automatic air flap, and owners log about 37–52 °C depending on the aux-fan setting. The QIDI Q2's '65 °C' is a setpoint held by a dedicated 280 W chamber heater. The two figures look comparable but are not.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's split pick. For PLA and PETG, the P2S's passive chamber is enough. For ABS, ASA and nylon, the Q2 at the same $449 has a 280 W heater that holds 65 °C. The P2S's 50 °C is a best case that one owner logged at 37–42 °C with the right aux fan at 100% in heating mode. It also warns shoppers off the QIDI Q2C ($349): it has the same 270 × 270 × 256 mm build volume, but its US store blurb doesn't list chamber heating, while the Q2's blurb does.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the cost of a heated chamber in dollars per liter of build space. On QIDI's own US store, the QIDI Q2 costs $449 for 18.66 L ($24.06 per liter). The QIDI Q2C has the same 270 × 270 × 256 mm volume for $349 ($18.70 per liter), and its listing does not mention the Q2's 65 °C active chamber heating. On QIDI's own figures, the heated chamber costs $100. The Q2's 280 W heater can use up to 2.8 kWh over a 10-hour ABS print, on top of the printer's 350 W rating.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's split: the QIDI Q2 for ABS, ASA and nylon, where an actively heated chamber matters, and a cheaper passive printer otherwise. It also adds an option ChatGPT never mentioned. A shopper printing only PLA or PETG can buy the QIDI Q2C for $349, the same build volume as the Q2 for $100 less ($18.70 vs $24.06 per liter). The extra $100 for the Q2 only pays off for engineering filaments. Dealectric already lists the qidi-q2 (awin:qidi), so a Q2 vs Q2C section would point to a product we can link.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the add-on multicolor units for two of its recommended enclosed printers are tied to specific models: the QIDI Box comes in separate Plus4, Q2 and Max4 versions (different Box Hub and signal cable, $40.99 kit to move it to another printer), and Creality's K1-series CFS upgrade kit for the K1C works only with the integrated-nozzle hotend and keeps the top cover from closing fully, so the K1C stops being fully enclosed for ABS unless you print the height-extension part.
angles.decides: This backs the QIDI Q2 as the pick for a shopper who wants an enclosed printer for ABS/ASA now and multicolor later. QIDI's US Q2 page says it works with the QIDI Box, and QIDI says the Box can dry and print at the same time (up to 65 °C) and chain up to 4 units. Buy the Q2 version of the Box, or plan $40.99 for the upgrade kit if you move it to another printer. It counts against the Creality K1C for the same shopper. ChatGPT pitched it as 'enclosed', but adding Creality's CFS means an integrated-nozzle hotend, a top cover that no longer closes fully (Creality supplies height-extension files for ABS), and a smaller 220 × 215 × 250 mm print volume. The finding doesn't change the pick for a shopper printing PLA/PETG in one color.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the P2S's chamber ceiling. It has no chamber heater: its only heat is the bed, held in by a motorized airflow flap that switches to recirculation, which tops out at about 50 °C. The QIDI Q2 adds a separate 280 W PTC chamber heater (rated 350 W + 280 W) that holds up to 65 °C whatever the bed is doing.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's split. If the shopper mostly prints PLA, PETG or small ABS/ASA parts, the P2S works: its bed heat, held in by the flap, reaches about 50 °C, and in cooling mode it pulls in outside air so PLA can print with the door shut. If they print large ABS/ASA parts, PC or nylon, they need a heater that works independently of the bed, and among the cards shown only the QIDI Q2 has one (65 °C, 280 W PTC). The P1S, K1C and Adventurer 5M Pro all rely on bed heat alone. The Q2 heater pushes the rated draw to 630 W, which does not affect a standard 15 A US outlet. For a PLA-only buyer the Q2's heater is no advantage. QIDI's own blog lists heat creep among the risks of too much chamber heat.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured chamber temperature for any of these printers. CNC Kitchen's thermocouples read 50.3 °C and 54.1 °C inside the Bambu Lab P2S's passive chamber, with the bed at 100–110 °C. Clever Creations timed the Creality K1C's chamber at 30 minutes to rise from 25 °C to its 38 °C maximum.
angles.decides: The measurements back ChatGPT's split pick and make it more precise. The P2S's passive chamber was measured at about 50–54 °C, which is far warmer than the K1C's measured 38 °C maximum. That makes the P2S a fair choice for occasional ABS/ASA. It also weakens the K1C as a choice for ABS. The case for the QIDI Q2's 65 °C active heater rests only on QIDI's own claim, because I found no independent measurement of it. So the Q2 pick for engineering filaments stays plausible but is not measured.

At $677 the Q2 + Box costs $112 less than the X2D AMS Combo, and both have a 65 °C heated chamber. The Q2 alone is the same $449 that 3dprintgearlab gives for the P2S, but it adds active heating and about 11% more build volume (18.66 L vs 16.78 L). The P2S stays the pick only for mostly-PLA buyers who want Bambu's ecosystem. angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 100 Ws Godox V100 gives about 0.4 stop more light per pop than the 76 Ws V1Pro, yet both flashes deliver about the same total light per charge (V100 40,000 J vs V1Pro 38,000 J, from the same 7.2 V/2980 mAh ≈ 21.5 Wh battery). angles.decides: A dome diffuser costs light, so a flash with more power per pop helps. The V100 gives about 0.4 stop more per pop (log2(100/76) = 0.40) for $20 more, but it delivers 100 fewer full-power flashes per charge (400 vs 500), recycles slower (1.7 s vs 1.3 s) and weighs 616 g with its battery. For event shooting with a dome, the V1Pro stays the pick: more pops, faster recycle, lower cost per flash. The V100 is the pick only if the shopper bounces off high ceilings or uses the larger AK-R22 dome and needs the extra 0.4 stop.

The newer V1 mid is the current option for Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm and Olympus/OM bodies. Panasonic users should pick the V1-P. A TT685II or V860III owner needs the separate S-R1 adapter before any round dome will fit. ChatGPT asked 'What camera do you use?', and the camera brand is what decides which flash version to buy.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a flash only widens its zoom for a dome if it can detect the dome: Nikon's SB-5000 senses its own Diffusion Dome and sets the zoom head to 12, 14 or 17 mm on FX (8, 10 or 11 mm on DX). The Godox V1 manual says nothing about detecting accessories, and its zoom only goes down to 28 mm.
angles.decides: This confirms how the plan works more than it changes the pick. A dome only softens light by spreading it wide and bouncing it off nearby surfaces. Nikon's own manual pairs the dome with bounce flash ('can be further diffused during bounce flash photography') and says the flash zooms to its widest setting by itself when the dome is fitted. On a Godox V1 with an AK-R11, the flash doesn't do this, so the shopper should set the zoom to 28 mm with the ZOOM button and point the head up or to the side. If they leave auto zoom on, the flash follows the lens focal length and sends a narrower beam into the dome. For a shopper who wants it to just work, a system flash that ships with its own dome and senses it (the Nikon SB-5000 with its SW-15H) is the hands-off choice. A Godox V1 plus AK-R11 does the same job at much lower cost but needs that manual step.

pages.why_used: BatteryTrail tabulates 100 A continuous for five brands and ExploringOffGrid says a 100 A BMS is about 1,280 W, but neither names a Group 24 100Ah battery with a 150 A BMS, neither lists Vatrer or Redodo, and neither converts the amp rating into the inverter size one battery can carry. This page does all three with maker-page figures dated today.

angles.decides: Confirms ChatGPT's LiTime-for-value pick but on a different basis: once cycle counts are put on the same 100% DoD footing, LiTime and Battle Born claim the same order of life, so the premium is paying for ETL pack listing and a 10-year warranty, not longevity. It also flags that Redodo's '4000-15000 cycles' spans undeclared DoD tiers, and that the Dealectric-listed Vatrer Group 24 at $259.99 is the only sub-$300 pack here with a 150 A BMS (1,920 W continuous) and a UL 1973 claim, which matters for inverter loads.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BMS continuous-discharge rating is the hard cap on the inverter one battery can feed, and that Vatrer's Group 24 100Ah carries a 150A BMS (150 A × 12.8 V = 1,920 W) where LiTime and Redodo Group 24 batteries stop at 100 A (1,280 W) and Epoch's 105Ah at 105 A, so a 1,500 W inverter runs on one Vatrer but trips a single LiTime, Redodo or Epoch.
angles.decides: For a shopper who will run a 12 V inverter: 100 A BMS batteries (LiTime Group 24 Bluetooth, Redodo Group 24 Bluetooth) are limited to 1,280 W from a single unit and Redodo's own page excludes water pumps, electric jacks and mowers; the Vatrer 12V 100Ah Group 24 (150A BMS, $259.99, UL 1973) is the only Group 24 100Ah candidate confirmed on the maker's page to carry a 1,500 W inverter alone, and it is cheaper than the LiTime pick ChatGPT led with ($311.09). For shoppers without an inverter the 100 A batteries are fine and the finding confirms LiTime/Redodo as value picks. Every candidate stops charging at 32°F; only the Epoch Essential and the Vatrer/LiTime heated versions can charge below that, and Epoch's heater only works while a charger is connected.

It also says which switch and keycap family each board ties you to: Keychron's MX-style low-profile on the RGB hot-swap version only, Lofree's Kailh low-profile that isn't MX pin-compatible, and full-size switches on the Q1 Max.

With the lights on, the full-height Keychron Q1 Max is rated for only about 30 h, at its lowest RGB brightness (it claims up to 180 h unlit), and the low-profile NuPhy Air75 V2 is rated for 35–57 h (it claims up to 220 h unlit). pages.why_used: The work and call-headset lists that were cited rank mics and quote music battery hours. None of them explains that using the mic over standard Bluetooth on a computer switches a headset to mono hands-free audio, that the Sony WH-1000XM6's cable turns off Bluetooth so the headset can't take a call, or that Bose added USB-C PC calls only in firmware 8.2.20. This page makes the computer-call route the deciding test and gives the Jabra's 100 Hz–14.5 kHz call band against hands-free's 8 kHz ceiling.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers' call-time ratings are much lower than the music-playback numbers the rival pages quote: Jabra rates the Evolve3 85 at 55 h for music but only 21 h of talk time with ANC and busylight on, and Sony rates the WH-1000XM6 at 24 h of talk time with NC on, so on calls the Sony is rated to last longer than the Jabra, the reverse of what the 55 h vs 30 h headlines suggest.
angles.decides: For someone buying headphones mainly for calls, this backs ChatGPT's 'Sony WH-1000XM6 best overall' pick and undercuts the main reason to pay more for the Jabra Evolve3 85 as the 'work' choice. On the makers' own call ratings the Sony gets 24 h with NC on and the Jabra 21 h with ANC and busylight on. The Jabra's 55 h is a music figure, and talk time is 38% of it. The Sony's talk time is 80% of its 30 h music rating. Among the budget options, the Soundcore Space 2 Pro (which Dealectric lists) is the only Soundcore model whose US page states a talk time: 20 h, against 30 h of music with ANC on. The Space Q45 that ChatGPT showed states no talk time and is listed as out of stock on Soundcore's US store. Every rated talk time here is at least 20 h, so any of them covers a single workday of calls. The finding changes which one wins on longevity across several days of calls, not whether one makes it through a day.

The Jabra's case has to rest on its mic and office features, not battery life. Among the products Dealectric lists, the soundcore Space 2 Pro is the value call headset at about $10 per rated talk hour vs about $15.83 for the Sony.

Microsoft's own explanation is that A2DP stereo 'doesn't allow the microphone to be used' and that HFP 'plays back audio in mono with lower fidelity'. Avoiding that on a PC takes either an LE Audio headset paired with an LE Audio-capable Windows 11 24H2 PC and an updated driver, or a maker's dongle such as the Jabra Evolve3 85's Link 390, which Jabra rates at 100 Hz–14.5 kHz super-wideband in call mode.

Sony's own guide says the WH-1000XM6 has to be set to 'Headset (WH-1000XM6 Hands-Free)' (HFP/HSP) for both speaker and mic on a PC. On a Bluetooth Classic link that means mono, lower-fidelity playback during the call. Sony documents LE Audio pairing only for Android phones. The Jabra Evolve3 85 ships with its own Link 390 dongle and is rated 100 Hz–14.5 kHz SWB in speak mode, so it is the safer PC-call pick. Bose's QC Ultra 2nd Gen lists A2DP/HFP/AVRCP/BLE and no LE Audio, so its PC calls also go through hands-free mode. For phone-only use, all three work as ChatGPT described. Plugging in the XM6 cable doesn't avoid this: Sony says 'the Bluetooth function cannot be used' then, and calls are answered on the phone and spoken into the phone's mic.

pages.why_used: I opened the ranked guides: ProjectorVerdict (both pages), iTechGuides, Austin Gallery and Projector Reviews. None turns projector lumens, screen area and gain into a brightness figure, and none says how large a screen a 200–450-lumen portable projector can light. Wirecutter, read through a reader copy, gives only a percentage brightness loss for one budget screen. Esquire blocked the fetch, so I could not check it. This page uses Elite's foot-lambert formula and the SMPTE 16 fL target to give the lumens each screen needs and the screen size that suits each projector.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the screens' advertised diagonals into the picture you actually get for a 16:9 movie. By Elite Screens' own conversion, a square-format Tripod screen sold as 113 inches shows a 92-inch 16:9 picture (80 × 45 in). That is smaller than the 105-inch Yard Master 2, whose 16:9 surface is about 91.5 × 51.5 in, roughly 24% less picture area.
angles.decides: This backs the Yard Master 2 as the movie pick. Elite's 1:1 and 4:3 Tripod sizes are measured across a square or 4:3 surface, so a 16:9 movie fills about 80 × 45 in of a '100"' 4:3 or '113"' 1:1 Tripod, which works out to 92 inches. The Yard Master 2's 1.3-gain CineWhite UHD-B is also brighter than the Tripod's 1.1-gain MaxWhite 2. Anyone buying a Tripod for movies should choose a 16:9 Tripod model (60"–120"), not the 1:1 or 4:3 ones that ChatGPT's 'Best for presentations' card covers. The Aurzen 120" (1.1 gain, 16:9, $24.99) is the low-cost way to get a picture bigger than 100 inches, but stock pages don't say whether it includes a stand.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how bright the picture will be. The rule (from Elite Screens' own article) is foot-lamberts = projector ANSI lumens ÷ screen area in sq ft × gain, with SMPTE 196M's minimum of 12 fL and ideal of 16 fL in a dark room. By that math, a 200-ANSI-lumen portable projector like the Aurzen EAZZE D1G gives only about 5 fL on a 120-inch, 1.1-gain portable screen. That projector reaches 16 fL only at about 68 inches, and a 120-inch, 1.1-gain screen needs about 620 lumens to get there.
angles.decides: The finding sets the screen size and favours higher gain rather than naming one product. ChatGPT's default advice of 100–120 inches only works with a projector of about 400–620 ANSI lumens. A shopper with a 200–300-lumen portable projector should buy about 70–80 inches, or accept a dim picture. At the same size and lumens, the Yard Master 2's 1.3 gain gives 18% more brightness than the 1.1-gain Elite Tripod and Aurzen screens (1.3 ÷ 1.1). So it is the better pick of ChatGPT's choices when the projector is dim, as long as it is sized down.

Among Dealectric-listed units, the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus (6,000 W on a 120/240 V L14-30R, 3,200 W solar input) remains the pump pick, but Anker's page shows it sold out today. pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "what size power station and solar panel run an off-grid cabin for a weekend". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What size power station and solar panel run an off-grid cabin for a weekend?
pages.why_used: The cited cabin guides give sizing formulas, sun-hour ranges and a two-day storage figure, but none works out how many days a specific kit's panel needs to refill its battery or what the kit costs. This page does that for each priced kit. One 200 W panel needs 5.2 poor-sun days to refill a 2 kWh station, against 2.4–2.6 days with 400 W. Of the kits priced here, only the 3,168 Wh kit meets SolutionEnergy's 2.5–3 kWh two-day storage figure without any sun.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says how much power the stations use just by keeping the AC inverter on all weekend for the fridge. Normalised to a 44-hour Friday-evening-to-Sunday-afternoon weekend, the drain is about 420 Wh on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (9.5 W, The Solar Lab) and about 600 Wh on the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max (13.6 W, The Solar Lab). On the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus it is about 4.9 kWh (112 W, Zelpio), which is more than its 3,840 Wh battery, so the inverter alone empties it in about 34 hours.
angles.decides: This confirms the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 as the pick at about 2 kWh. Its idle draw is the lowest sourced here (9.5 W, about 420 Wh over the weekend). APH Networks also measured 2,028 Wh usable from it at a 987 W load, 97.8% of rated. The DELTA 2 Max has the same nominal capacity but loses about 180 Wh more to idle over the weekend. It also rules out ChatGPT's F3800 Plus suggestion for a fridge weekend. Zelpio measured 112 W with the inverter on and nothing plugged in. Anker's own firmware post claims only a 50% cut, which would still be about 56 W and about 2.5 kWh over 44 hours. The page should put idle watts × 44 h in the table as a line in the energy budget, with a footnote naming who measured each figure and the firmware caveat.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how many December days a kit's own panel needs to refill its battery. Using SolutionEnergy's figure of 2 kWh per kW of panels on a December day, the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit ($1,199) needs 5.2 sunny days to refill, so its panel cannot top it up within a weekend. The ALLPOWERS R2500 V2 + SP037 400 W kit ($948) needs 2.4 days, supplies about 3,330 Wh over a two-day December weekend and has the lowest cost per usable Wh of the kits checked ($0.55).
angles.decides: The panel bundled with a kit decides the pick more than the battery size does. A single 200 W panel on a 2 kWh station refills it only every 2.4 summer days or 5.2 December days, so for a weekend the battery has to carry nearly all the load. With 400 W, a kit adds about 1.6 kWh over a December weekend. That moves the pick to a 2 kWh-class station with 400 W of panels: the ALLPOWERS R2500 V2 + SP037 at $948 if it can be confirmed in stock, or the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 2× 200 W at $1,499. It moves away from the Elite 200 V2 + 350 W, which now costs $1,449 and ships from Dec 25, and from the Elite 200 V2 + 200 W. The AC180 + 200 W ($769) supplies about 1.8 kWh over a December weekend, which covers SolutionEnergy's 2 kWh weekend load on that page's numbers. It falls well short of ChatGPT's 2,270 Wh fridge example.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's 350 W panel has a 33 V open-circuit voltage. Two in series reach 66 V, over the Elite 200 V2's 12–60 V solar input, and two in parallel are held to the station's 20 A limit, which caps them below 660 W (20 A × 33 V). So the $2,148 Elite 200 V2 + 2×350 W bundle cannot put 700 W into the station. Two SP200L 200 W panels (24.6 V Voc each, 49.2 V in series) do fit under the 60 V limit.
angles.decides: This confirms the Elite 200 V2 + 2×200 W SP200L kit ($1,499 on 2026-11-13) as the 400 W pick, wired in series: 49.2 V Voc is under the 60 V ceiling. In parallel the two panels' 21.6 A short-circuit current is over the 20 A input limit. It argues against stepping up to the 2×350 W bundle ($2,148). Series wiring is ruled out by the 60 V limit, and in parallel the 20 A limit keeps the input under 660 W. So the extra $649 buys less than its 700 W nameplate. Separately, the single 350 W kit price on BLUETTI's store is now $1,449, not the $1,249 on our page.

pages.query: which portable power station can be a ups for a nas and send a usb shutdown signal
pages.why_used: The cited rivals cover NUT 2.8.3, the usbhid-ups driver and the RIVER 3 Plus low-battery bug, but none says EcoFlow's USB link cannot switch the station's AC off and back on after the NAS shuts down (NUT #2735: 'Shutdown does nothing', AC live 60+ s), so the NAS stays off after a short outage. None says EcoFlow's Power Manager lists only the RIVER 3 Plus, or that EcoFlow's Synology package needs port and device-name edits. This page puts those findings in the table and gives a separate pick for each segment, including a UPS that does restart the NAS (UGREEN US3000).

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that stock Synology DSM 7.3.2 does not see an EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus as a USB UPS (it shows "No USB UPS Connected"). It only works through EcoFlow's Power Manager NAS package, after hand-editing its port (3496 to 3493) and device name (nutdev1 to ups) and switching DSM to Synology UPS Server mode. Even then, several owners report that the NAS never shut down. So "NUT 2.8.3+ support" means support for anyone who runs current NUT, not for the NAS firmware people actually have.
angles.decides: It confirms that no portable power station is a plug-and-play USB UPS for a Synology or QNAP on stock firmware. The RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus only make sense if the NAS can run current NUT itself (2.8.3 or later, which on Debian means forky or sid, not Debian 12 or 13) or can poll a separate NUT server. For a Synology or QNAP owner who wants an automatic shutdown, the pick is a conventional USB HID UPS (APC BE600M1, CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD). The EcoFlow is then a long-runtime source that you shut down on a timer, not one that sends a low-battery signal.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the cost of adding NAS runtime while keeping the USB shutdown link. EcoFlow's DELTA 3 Series Smart Extra Battery adds 1,024 Wh for $388 ($0.38/Wh). The RIVER 3 Plus EB300 adds 286 Wh for $149 ($0.52/Wh), and the RIVER 3 Plus stops at 858 Wh. Measured DELTA 3 Plus output is 910 Wh per 1,024 Wh, so DELTA 3 Plus plus one extra battery gives about 57 h on a 32 W 2-bay NAS and about 31 h on a 59 W 4-bay NAS.
angles.decides: The USB shutdown requirement leaves only EcoFlow units with a data port: RIVER 3 Plus (USB-B), DELTA 3 Plus (USB-C) and DELTA 3 Ultra / Ultra Plus (USB-C UPS-HID). Among those, the pick depends on how many NAS hours you need. Up to a few hours: RIVER 3 Plus. Overnight or more: DELTA 3 Plus, adding the $388 extra battery if needed. That costs less per added Wh than stacking RIVER 3 Plus EB300s, and the RIVER 3 Plus tops out at 858 Wh. If you need 2 days or more on a 4-bay NAS, the DELTA 3 Ultra at $1,299 for 3,072 Wh ($0.42/Wh nominal) has the lowest cost per hour of any unit with a data port. This supports ChatGPT's RIVER 3 Plus / DELTA 3 Plus split and adds a price-based reason to choose the Ultra.
products: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus + DELTA 3 Series Smart Extra Battery
EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus + EB300 Smart Extra Battery

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EcoFlow's USB HID link cannot cut the station's AC output after the NAS shuts down. NUT's open issue #2735 for the RIVER 3 Plus (firmware V1.33.81.61, Oct 2026) says 'Shutdown does nothing' and that the AC output 'stays live for 60+ seconds', so the NAS stays off when mains power returns. Nor does any result state that EcoFlow's own Power Manager software lists only the RIVER 3 Plus as a supported device, which leaves the DELTA 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Ultra without it.
angles.decides: This confirms the RIVER 3 Plus as the only power station with a maker-documented NAS shutdown path: EcoFlow names it as the only device Power Manager supports, and the cable is in the box. It also limits what the RIVER 3 Plus can do. It can tell a NAS to shut down, but it cannot switch its AC off and back on, so the NAS will not restart by itself after an outage. DSM also needs manual config edits, and commenters on a DS920+ report it hanging instead of shutting down. Shoppers who need unattended recovery should get a conventional USB HID UPS (APC BE600M1 or CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD) or UGREEN's US3000 for NASync. The DELTA 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Ultra only work through generic NUT 2.8.3 or later, without EcoFlow software.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus give NUT no command to switch their AC output off and back on (no load.off, load.off.delay or shutdown.return), so after the NAS shuts itself down the station keeps its outlets live. If mains returns before the battery runs flat, the NAS never sees a power loss and stays off until someone presses its power button.
angles.decides: This confirms the RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus as the only stations here that can signal a shutdown, but it adds a limit to the pick. They can shut a NAS down cleanly, yet they cannot bring it back by themselves after a short outage, because the 'restart after power failure' setting only fires when the NAS really loses power. A NAS the shopper needs to reach remotely, such as one serving a VPN, will stay off. Two things avoid that: a conventional HID UPS (the APC class), which exposes load-off-with-delay commands, or a timer or Wake-on-LAN workaround. The table's 'What a NAS sees' column should add 'won't power the NAS back on after a short outage'.
products: APC Back-UPS ES (BE650G2, same family as BE600M1)

For the RIVER 3 Plus, the October 2026 owner report means our cell 'an open NUT bug never reports low battery' should change. In that report on Ubuntu, upsmon did start a low-battery shutdown, but NUT has no shutdown command for the unit and the AC output stayed on for 60+ seconds. A NAS set to power back on when AC returns may therefore not restart. Measured switchover adds nothing new: all the data-port EcoFlows test at 8 to 9 ms (StorageReview), and computingforgeeks already has most of those numbers.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which portable power station runs a resmed airsense 11 cpap for a week of camping". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which portable power station runs a resmed airsense 11 cpap for a week of camping?

angles.decides: This keeps the AC180 as the pick, but adds a condition. ChatGPT's 7–9 nights assume the AC180 runs the CPAP all night through the 12 V port with the humidifier off. Willitrunpower puts that draw at about 7 W, inside the AC180's DC ECO range of 5–10 W. If ECO is on with a 10 W threshold, the port can switch off 1–4 hours into the night. Using AC instead doesn't avoid this, because the AC ECO range is 15–30 W. So the page should tell AC180 buyers to turn ECO off in Setting mode, or set it to 5 W, and test a full night at home. The table footnote should list each station's low-load cutoff next to its capacity. Also, the ResMed converter draws up to 10 A at 12 V, which is exactly the AC180's 12 V/10 A port rating. That leaves no headroom if the humidifier and heated tube run on DC.

angles.decides: This only matters for shoppers who keep the humidifier on, which is the question ChatGPT ended its answer with. For them it reverses ChatGPT's 'AC180 won't last' verdict. The AC180 + 200 W kit gets through a humidified week if the site gets about 3 hours of strong sun a day, and offgridvolt saw a 200 W panel add 51% of the AC180 in one camping day, which is about 588 Wh against a need of 420–571 Wh. In short November days or shade, the Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit ($1,199) needs only about 1.4–2.3 sun-hours a day and starts with 4.3 humidified nights stored, so it is the safer pick there. With the humidifier off, nothing changes: the AC180 on the ResMed DC converter is still enough, as rivals already say.

Nor do they say the converter sells in the US for $95 with no prescription.

The converter switches off when its supply runs too low, so you should test a full night at home before the trip. The page should list the converter (ResMed ref 39231, $95, no prescription per cpapsupplies.com) as a required add-on to the AC180, about $594 in total at today's $499 BLUETTI price.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI AC180's ECO auto-off can't be set below 15 W on AC or 5 W on DC. ResMed's table, as Willrun reports it, puts a humidifier-off AirSense 11 at about 7 W, so with ECO on, the AC outlet will cut the CPAP within 1–4 hours, and the 12 V port will too if its threshold is set to 10 W.
angles.decides: The AC180 pick still holds, but this changes how the page should tell people to set it up. A humidifier-off AirSense 11 (about 7 W) on the AC180's AC outlet is under the lowest AC ECO threshold (15 W), so with ECO on, the outlet will switch off within the 1–4 hour window every night. Even with the humidifier on (about 19 W), it stays under the 30 W setting. On the 12 V car port through ResMed's Air11 DC/DC converter, 7 W only stays above the cutoff if the DC threshold is set to 5 W, not 10 W. The page should say to turn ECO off completely (hold AC and DC together to enter settings). If ECO stays on, use the 12 V port with the DC threshold at 5 W. This also backs up the DC route, since it's the only one that can stay on with ECO enabled.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured standby drain from a candidate's 12 V DC port. The Technology Man measured about 11 W with nothing plugged in on the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 (100% to 24% in 20 hours). That is more than the AirSense 11's own 7 W humidifier-off draw that Willitrunpower quotes, so the DC 'nights per charge' figures that rival pages work out from nameplate capacity are optimistic unless the port is switched off between nights.
angles.decides: It backs the AC180 as the one-charge pick, with a condition. Four named tests put its usable energy at 950–1,030 Wh. With the CPAP alone at 7 W × 8 h = 56 Wh a night, that covers 7 nights easily. If the DC port idles at an Elite-30-V2-like 11 W and stays on, a night costs (7 + 11) × 8 = 144 Wh, and 7 nights need about 1,008 Wh, which is right at the AC180's measured ceiling. Left on 24 hours a day, the port alone would eat about 264 Wh a day and the AC180 would not last the week. So the page should say: switch the 12 V port off in the morning (or use ECO mode), or step up to the Elite 200 V2. pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which power station can run a home oxygen concentrator in a power outage and for how long". No rival names the one station rated for a 0 ms path, and none shows that lab-timed switchovers land at 8–16 ms. This page pairs those facts with reviewer-measured watt-hours.

At 350 W, though, even the largest station on our page, the Elite 300 at 2,670 Wh measured, falls about 25 minutes short of 8 hours. For overnight cover the shopper needs an expandable unit plus a battery: AC200L + B300K, or DELTA 3 + extra batteries. The 1 kWh units (DELTA 3, C1000 Gen 2, Jackery 1000 v2) land within 0.1 h of each other, about 2.5 to 2.6 h, so capacity doesn't separate them; switchover and price have to.

angles.decides: Batteries are compared on Wh, but the deciding question is whether the concentrator stays on when the grid drops. Every station on our page publishes a 10–20 ms switchover, which is 0.6–1.2 cycles at 60 Hz. That is longer than the 0.5-cycle dropout the EverFlo manual documents, so in UPS mode the shopper should expect the concentrator to stop and sound its power-failure alarm (the alarm is per our page's citation of the EverFlo manual), not run through. Two ways around it: (a) put the concentrator on the left two AC outlets of a BLUETTI Apex 300, set to 240 V mode and fed from the grid through the 15 A AC input, which BLUETTI rates at 0 ms; or (b) plan for a restart plus backup tanks. The page should make the Apex 300 (0 ms outlets, 2,764.8 Wh, about 6.7 h at 350 W) the pick for anyone who needs no interruption. It should present the 10–20 ms stations as runtime-only choices.
