pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which portable power station keeps a 75-gallon tropical aquarium alive through a 24-hour outage". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which portable power station keeps a 75-gallon tropical aquarium alive through a 24-hour outage?
pages.why_used: The cited rivals guess a heater duty cycle (15–30%) or leave the heater out, and none turns a 75-gallon tank's cooling times into heater watts. This page works out the heater load from the tank's heat loss: about 52 W wrapped and 184 W with a glass lid in a 59 °F room. That shows insulation decides whether any station lasts 24 hours, and it gives measured runtimes for each station.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the Elite 300's measured AC-on idle draw (19 W, which is 456 Wh a day) or points out that its 94% efficiency was measured at a 1 kW load. A 75-gallon tank's 27 W filter and air pump load at night is a very different case, so the real 24-hour budget at 20% heater duty is about 2,544 Wh against the 2,819 Wh it measurably delivers.
angles.decides: It confirms the BLUETTI Elite 300 as the pick and leaves less room to spare. With 19 W measured idle instead of the 15 W assumed, the 20% heater-duty budget rises from 2,448 Wh to 2,544 Wh. That is about 90% of the 2,819 Wh The Technology Man measured it delivering. At 30% duty (3,264 Wh) it falls short. The Elite 200 V2's idle draw is lower (10 W per The Gadgeteer, or 240 Wh a day), but that does not make up its 940 Wh capacity deficit. The page should fold the measured idle draw into the duty-cycle table instead of a flat 15 W.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the 75-gallon tank's own heat loss into a heater load. AquariumToolbox's cooling times for a 75-gallon tank at 77 °F in a 59 °F room work out to about 52 W wrapped in a blanket (17% duty on a 300 W heater), 184 W with only a glass lid (61%) and 323 W open (more than a 300 W heater can supply). That makes a wrapped tank about a 2 kWh day: the Elite 300 lasts about 31 h, the Elite 200 V2 about 24 h and the DELTA 2 Max about 22 h. With only a lid, no candidate passes about 12 h.
angles.decides: The heater's duty cycle comes from how well the tank is insulated, not from the shopper's guess, so insulation decides the pick before capacity does. In a 59 °F room, a blanket-wrapped tank (≈69.5 W of equipment plus the station's own draw) is covered for 24 h by the BLUETTI Elite 300, with about 7 h to spare. The Elite 200 V2 ($899) just reaches 24 h, and the DELTA 2 Max falls short at about 22 h. A tank with only a lid needs about 5.2 kWh, which no single candidate holds; the Elite 300 lasts about 12 h. An open tank loses more heat than a 300 W heater can replace, so no battery holds temperature. In a 68 °F room with only a lid, the Elite 300 lasts about 21 h. This supports the Elite 300 pick, with the condition that the tank is wrapped. It also makes the Elite 200 V2 the cheaper pick when wrapped, at $0.47 per measured usable Wh against $0.45 for the Elite 300.

The B300K list names AC200L, AC200MAX, AC300 and AC500. The B500K list names Apex 300, AC300, AC500, AC200L and AC200MAX, and the store sells it as 'B500K for Apex 200 & Apex 300'. So the Elite 300 can't grow to cover the 30 % heater-duty case (about 3.2 kWh). The expandable BLUETTI Apex 200 (2,560 Wh, $1,099) takes B300K/B500K, and BLUETTI sells Apex 200 + B300K as a $2,199 bundle (5,324.8 Wh).

The Apex 200 + B300K bundle (5,324.8 Wh, about 4.5 kWh usable at 85 %) covers 30 % duty with room to spare and nearly covers 50 % duty (4.6 kWh). It costs $0.41/Wh against the Elite 300's $0.40/Wh. In a warm room at 15–20 % duty the Elite 300 still wins: the Apex 200 alone (about 2.2 kWh usable) has less energy than the Elite 300 for $100 less. The AC200L also takes B300K/B500K, but BLUETTI US shows it unavailable today.

Once the heater's thermostat stops calling for heat, the station's load is only the filter and air pump, about 27 W. Using the measured 19 W overhead instead makes it about 2,544 Wh (+4 W × 24 h = 96 Wh). The Elite 300's measured output of 2.67–2.82 kWh covers that, with only 130–275 Wh to spare. The 2 kWh stations measured 1.6–1.91 kWh, which falls short of even ChatGPT's own 15%-duty budget (about 2.1 kWh). Every 2 kWh unit ($879–$1,049) ends up about 700 Wh short. The next in-stock unit of 3 kWh or more, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra, costs $100 more, and the ALLPOWERS R4000 is sold out.

It argues against ChatGPT's other two answers, which led with 2,048 Wh units (DELTA 2 Max $1,049 at Home Depot, DELTA 3 Max $879 at Best Buy). pages.query: which power station runs a starlink mini and a macbook for a remote workday off grid and for how many days
pages.why_used: The cited pages size this setup from Starlink's 25–40 W rating, a MacBook figure that is assumed rather than measured, and a flat 85% efficiency factor, so they land at 450 Wh a day and about 1.9 days per kWh. None uses the Mini's measured 21 W (Wirelessmoves), the MacBook Air's measured 3.3 W (Notebookcheck) or a station's tested low-load efficiency (techreviewer.de, 80%). This page does, and gets 195 Wh a day and 4.2 workdays from a 1 kWh station. It also checks which ports really carry 20 V/5 A to both devices.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a power station's "2× USB-C" can mean very different things for this setup. Starlink says the Mini needs a 100 W (20 V/5 A) USB-C PD supply. A Jackery retailer page lists the Explorer 1000 v2's ports as 1 × 100 W + 1 × 30 W, so only one port can run the Mini and the MacBook gets 30 W at most from USB-C. The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 lists a 140 W (28 V/5 A) USB-C port and a separate small USB-C1 that shares 20 W with USB-A.
angles.decides: Among the 1 kWh picks ChatGPT showed (Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, Anker C1000), the Jackery can run the Mini or a MacBook Pro from USB-C, not both at full power. The second laptop has to use the inverter or the 12 V car port with an adapter, and the inverter's idle draw lowers runtime (kilohour assumes 10 W for AC versus 2 W for DC). On listed ports, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is the better 1 kWh pick for an all-USB-C workday. Days per charge barely change: OutdoorGearLab measured 910 Wh usable from the Jackery's 1,070 Wh, about the same as the 85% derate ChatGPT used. The footnote on cycle life also favours Anker and BLUETTI: the same '4,000 cycles' is claimed to 80% by Anker and BLUETTI but to 70% by Jackery.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, using measured inputs (Starlink Mini about 21 W average per Wirelessmoves, MacBook Air M4 about 3.3 W in Notebookcheck's 150-nit Wi-Fi test, and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 at about 80% usable at double-digit-watt loads per techreviewer.de), one 8-hour workday uses about 195 Wh and a 1,024 Wh station lasts about 4.2 workdays, not the 1.9 days ChatGPT gave.
angles.decides: The days are shorter than the rated figure suggests, because the station loses more at low loads. The light-day load is also about half what ChatGPT assumed. So a 1 kWh LiFePO4 station with two 20 V/5 A USB-C ports (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, $499, 25 lb) covers about 4 light workdays, or about 2 at the worst case (Mini at 40 W, MacBook at max brightness). That makes the 2 kWh, 40–52 lb class ChatGPT suggested for 'multi-day' unnecessary unless the dish runs 24 h (about 1.5 days per charge). A 200 W kit panel refills a light day in about 1 h at its nameplate output.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the Starlink Mini can run from a power station's 12 V car outlet through Starlink's own Mini Car Adapter (12–24 V in, 60 W out), which leaves the station's one full-power USB-C port free for the MacBook. Anker's US spec table for the SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 gives the 20V/5A, 140 W rating only to USB-C 2 and puts USB-C 1 in a 20 W total shared with USB-A, so on that station the Mini and the MacBook can't both run from USB-C.
angles.decides: This confirms the C1000 Gen 2 as a 1 kWh pick but changes how it gets wired. If USB-C 1 really is capped at 20 W, the MacBook takes the 140 W USB-C 2 and the Mini goes on the 12V/10A (120 W) car outlet through the Starlink Mini Car Adapter. That avoids the AC inverter, which is the efficiency point ChatGPT raised without saying how. Our current page cell 'C1000 Gen 2: 2× 140 W' disagrees with Anker's US spec table and needs fixing. Rule for every candidate: the station needs either two USB-C ports that each offer 20V/5A at the same time, or one such port plus a 12 V car outlet rated about 60 W or more for the Mini Car Adapter.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, ChatGPT's top pick, has only one USB-C port that can supply the Starlink Mini's required 100 W (20 V/5 A) contract. Anker's own spec table gives USB-C 2 140 W max, while USB-C1 shares 20 W max with USB-A. So ChatGPT's advice to run both the MacBook and the Mini from USB-C does not work on that station. One of them has to go on the 120 W 12 V car socket or on the AC inverter.
angles.decides: It doesn't remove the C1000 Gen 2, but it changes how the page tells you to wire it, and it favors stations with two 100 W USB-C ports for an all-DC setup. On the C1000 Gen 2, put the MacBook on USB-C 2 (up to 140 W) and the Mini on the 12 V/10 A (120 W) car socket through the Mini's 12–48 V DC barrel input. The other option is the Mini on USB-C 2 and the MacBook's charger on AC, which costs inverter losses and cuts the days. Our page's 'USB-C: 2× 140 W' cell for the C1000 Gen 2 contradicts Anker's spec table and must be fixed. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 and AC200L rows claim 2× 100 W USB-C. If that holds today, they run both devices on DC with no inverter. That favors them for multi-day trips, but this session didn't confirm it from the maker.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for the power station's own drain: The Technology Man measured the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 losing 20% of its charge in 12 hours with the AC inverter on and nothing plugged in (about 17 W). With only the DC side on, the charge stayed at 100%. Over an 8-hour workday that inverter drain adds about 136 Wh to a Starlink Mini plus MacBook Air load of about 320 Wh, and the measured draws (Mini about 21 W, MacBook Air M4 8.7 to 29.9 W) are well below the 450 Wh a day ChatGPT planned for.
angles.decides: The measurements support powering everything from DC and USB-C and switching the inverter off. Measured usable capacities in the 1 kWh class sit close together (Anker C1000 Gen 2: 850–907 Wh on AC and 844 Wh on DC; Jackery 1000 v2: 910 Wh; BLUETTI AC180: 950–983 Wh; EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: 910 Wh). The inverter idle drain (about 14–17 W) changes the result more than which station you buy. On DC, 844 Wh ÷ about 320 Wh a day is about 2.6 workdays for the Anker C1000 Gen 2. Running through the inverter adds about 136 Wh a day, so roughly 850 ÷ 456 is about 1.9 days, which happens to be ChatGPT's own figure. That favours a station with two 100 W+ USB-C ports, such as the Anker C1000 Gen 2 (2× 140 W, per our page) or the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (2× 100 W), so the Mini and the MacBook both avoid the inverter. The AC180 has only one 100 W USB-C port (per our page), so the second device would have to go through AC or 12 V. For multiple days, StorageReview measured 1.91 kWh out of the Elite 200 V2, about 6 workdays at 320 Wh by the same arithmetic.

At the makers' own US stores on 2026-11-08, a 2,048 Wh EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max cost $879 and a 1,152 Wh BLUETTI AC180 cost $499, against ChatGPT's 2 kWh pick, the DELTA 2 Max, at $1,029. ChatGPT showed the Jackery 1500 v2 at $999 (B&H), but jackery.com had it at $849, and the Jackery 2000 v2 was sold out with pre-orders shipping Nov 16.

ChatGPT's picks cost more per workday: DELTA 2 Max about $266, Jackery 1500 v2 about $293, Jackery 2000 v2 about $259 (and out of stock). For a 2-day trip, the AC180 ($499, about 2.2 days) beats the Anker C1000 Gen 2 that ChatGPT showed at $549.99. For 3–4 days, the DELTA 3 Max at $879 beats the DELTA 2 Max at $1,029 for the same 2,048 Wh at the same store. pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which portable power station recharges a 700 wh e-bike twice on a camping weekend". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which portable power station recharges a 700 wh e-bike twice on a camping weekend?
pages.why_used: The cited rivals size stations by rated Wh times an assumed loss factor and never give how much a station draws idling with its AC on. Over a weekend that idle draw decides whether a 2 kWh station has a second 700 Wh charge left. This page gives reviewer-measured idle draw and measured AC output for all four candidates, and the spare energy after two charges with the AC switched off between charges and with it left on.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 2 kWh picks can't be compared on their headline specs. Anker's '10,000 cycles' for the SOLIX S2000 is to 60% capacity (6,000 to 80%), its '3,000 W' is peak against a 1,500 W rated output, and only the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 has an independently measured AC discharge. Two reviewers measured 1,910 Wh and about 1,990 Wh, enough for two 700 Wh charges at the 880–935 Wh each that one charge takes.
angles.decides: It confirms the Elite 200 V2. It is the only ~2 kWh candidate with measured AC delivery, 1,910–1,990 Wh, and that covers two 700 Wh charges at 1,760–1,870 Wh with 40–230 Wh to spare. ChatGPT's S2000 pick is unmeasured. At 0.85 of its rated capacity it delivers about 1,709 Wh, which is short of a second full charge. Its 10,000-cycle headline is to 60%, not the 80% the others use. Rated vs peak output doesn't matter for an e-bike charger, which draws 100–300 W, but the table should not set Anker's 3,000 W peak against BLUETTI's 2,600 W continuous.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2's measured AC output (1,910 Wh, StorageReview) gives 2.3 charges of a 700 Wh e-bike pack with a 263 Wh margin over the 1,647 Wh two charges need at an 85% charger floor, that the 2.44 kWh StorageReview measured to recharge it means about 1.05 kWh of wall power per bike charge, or that each 2 kWh rival must deliver at least 80–82% of its rated Wh on AC to manage two charges (the Elite 200 V2 measured 92%).
angles.decides: This confirms the Elite 200 V2 ($899) as the only 2 kWh candidate with a third-party measurement that clears two 700 Wh charges (1,910 vs 1,647 Wh needed). It also qualifies ChatGPT's plain-chat pick. On rated figures the Anker SOLIX S2000 is cheaper today ($699.99 on Anker's store) and lighter (56.3 vs 38.8 rated Wh/lb). It still needs at least 81.9% of its 2,010 Wh on AC, which no reviewer has measured, so it is the light, unproven alternative. The DELTA 3 Max ($879, 20.3 kg) is in the same position and needs at least 80.4%. The AC200L is sold out on BLUETTI's US store today, so it should come off the list of live picks. The Elite 300 ($1,199) needs only 54.6% of its rating, so it is the safe-margin pick.
products: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 200 W Solar kit

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI sells a 560 W alternator charger, Charger 1, for $219 that it says works with all BLUETTI stations, and that it is sold bundled with the Elite 200 V2 for $1,099. It feeds the Elite 200 V2's 12–60 V / 20 A / 1,000 W solar input, so about 1.6 hours of driving puts back one 700 Wh e-bike charge, against the 96 W a 12 V socket gives.
angles.decides: It backs the Elite 200 V2 as the pick. Its main weakness, a thin margin for two charges (1,910 Wh measured against roughly 1,750–1,900 Wh needed), can be fixed with a maker-sold $219 accessory that refills it on the drive at 560 W. That makes a second charge plus camp loads realistic without moving up to the 3 kWh Elite 300. It also gives the page a maker-level caveat: one e-bike maker (Biktrix) says a non-grid source may void the warranty. Shoppers should check their own bike maker's policy before relying on any station.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a power station's inverter uses power just by being on. Measured idle draw with AC on is about 27 W on the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max, 9.5 W on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 and 6 W on the Anker SOLIX S2000. If the AC is left on for a 48-hour weekend, the DELTA 3 Max burns about 1.3 kWh of its 2,048 Wh with nothing plugged in. That is the difference between two 700 Wh e-bike charges and one.
angles.decides: It confirms the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 as the pick and makes the DELTA 3 Max a weaker two-charge choice. Two Bosch 4A charges take about 11 hours of inverter time (700 Wh ÷ 0.88 ÷ 144 W ≈ 5.5 h each). At 27 W idle, the DELTA 3 Max loses about 300 Wh just to inverter overhead in that time. Its 79% measured efficiency already puts it at about 1,618 Wh at the outlet, against the roughly 1,590 Wh two charges need, so it has almost no margin. The Elite 200 V2 delivered 1,910 Wh in StorageReview's test and idles at 9.5 W (about 105 Wh over the same 11 hours). That leaves room for both charges. The page should tell shoppers to switch AC off between charges or turn on ECO / AC timeout. It should also list idle draw as a column, with the Anker SOLIX S2000 at 6 W as the low-overhead option (its 1,500 W AC is plenty for any e-bike charger).

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which small power station and fridge keep insulin cold through a two-day outage". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which small power station and fridge keep insulin cold through a two-day outage?
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages (Willrun and our Nov 3 page) work out runtimes from rated Wh × 85% and Dometic's spec sheet, and Willrun says it did not test. None gives a named lab measurement of the energy a station actually delivers, a measured fridge draw, or GearLab's finding that a 35 °F setting held the inside at 32 °F, which would freeze insulin. This page uses GearLab's 950 Wh, 600 Wh and 8.3 W figures. It also shows that the 8.3 W average sits inside the AC180's 5–10 W DC ECO cut-off.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI AC180's ECO mode can switch off the 12 V DC output when the load stays below a 5–10 W threshold for 1–4 hours. A compressor cooler holding a few insulin pens in a cool room averages about 9–11 W and sits near zero between compressor cycles, so the published runtime holds only if DC ECO is turned off.
angles.decides: It keeps the AC180 plus a 12 V compressor cooler as the pick, but it attaches a setup step the pick depends on. Turn off DC ECO (Setting mode: hold AC+DC for about 2 s with the AC output off), or the 2-day runtime math doesn't apply. It also supports the DC-only setup with a number: the manual's roughly 15 W self-consumption over 48 h is about 720 Wh, which is most of the AC180's roughly 980 Wh usable. A mini-fridge on the AC outlet won't last two days on this unit.

That is one $899.99 box that gets through 48 h with only 4 h to spare. The other route, a Dometic CFX3 25 at its 90 °F rating, needs at least 624 Wh of rated station capacity for two days.
angles.decides: It backs the robust pick: a 1 kWh station on 12 V running a Dometic CFX3 25. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 is the lightest of these at 25 lb and gives about 79 h at Dometic's 90 °F rating, 31 h more than needed, for $1,198.99 together. It also adds a cheaper single-box option, the EverFrost 2 40L at $899.99. But that only clears 48 h at 77 °F with the cooler empty, so in a summer outage it needs a second power source. A 288 Wh station is not enough with the Dometic: the Elite 30 V2 gives about 22 h.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI AC180 user manual has an ECO mode that switches off the DC outputs, including the 12 V car port, when the load stays under a set threshold of 5–10 W for 1–4 hours, while Dometic rates the CFX3 25 at only about 11 W average at 90 °F, so ECO has to be switched off for this pairing.
angles.decides: The AC180 + CFX3 25 pick still stands, but only if DC ECO is off. The manual sets the DC ECO threshold at 5–10 W. Dometic's 0.92 Ah/h at 12 V works out to about 11 W at 90 °F, and the average is lower in a cooler house. Between cycles the compressor draws almost nothing, so with ECO on the 12 V port could shut off in the middle of the outage and nothing would restart it. The page should tell buyers to turn ECO off in Setting mode and run a 48-hour test with ECO off. The 6.5 A rated DC input of the CFX3 25 fits the AC180's 12 V/10 A car port. Dometic includes both a 12/24 V cable and a 120 V cable, so no extra cable is needed.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the AC180 maker's actual auto-off rule. In ECO mode the AC180 switches off its DC outputs, the 12 V car port included, after 1–4 hours below 5–10 W. A 12 V compressor cooler like the Dometic CFX3 25 averages about 11 W, with long stretches near zero between compressor runs. That puts it right at the cut-off, and once the port turns off the cooler gets no power and warms up.
angles.decides: The AC180 + 12 V compressor cooler pick holds only with two conditions. (1) ECO mode is off, or set to its lowest 5 W threshold and longest 4 h duration and then tested: the cooler's ~11 W average is barely above the 10 W top setting, and the manual doesn't say whether ECO judges the average or a continuous low-load stretch. (2) The AC inverter stays off. BLUETTI's runtime formula adds 'about 15W' of self-consumption. If that 15 W applied while running on 12 V, it would add 360 Wh a day: 1,152 × 0.9 × 0.85 = 881 Wh ÷ (265 + 360) Wh/day ≈ 1.4 days, short of the two-day goal. With the inverter off, the page's 3.7-day figure is the right one. The page should tell readers to check that the ECO icon is off and the AC output is off before the outage. It should also have them run the 48-hour test with the cooler on the car port, so any auto-off would show up during the test.

pages.query: power station to keep reptile heat on in a power outage
pages.why_used: The cited reptile-outage pages (animalstart.com, pets.co.uk) give only a 'Wh ÷ watts' formula and name no station figures, and the runtime tables built from them use a flat 85% factor with no idle draw. This page gives each station's measured idle draw (9.5–27 W) and delivered Wh. With a 24–50 W reptile heater that idle draw roughly halves the runtime, and it reorders same-size stations: about 56 h vs about 32 h on a 24 W mat for two 2 kWh units.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much power the station draws for itself while it waits. Jackery lists 18 W standby for the Explorer 1000 v2, and The Gadgeteer gives about 10 W idle for the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. A 24 W heat mat draws about as much as that idle load, so the 1,000 Wh class lasts far less time than its Wh rating suggests.
angles.decides: For low-watt reptile heat (heat mats, and emitters cycling on a thermostat), the station's own draw matters as much as its Wh. On a 24 W mat, the Explorer 1000 v2's listed 18 W standby makes it use 42 W in total, so it runs at most about 25 h, not the 38 h that ChatGPT's method gives. The Elite 200 V2 stays the long-outage pick: about 10 W idle per The Gadgeteer and 1.91 kWh delivered in StorageReview's test, so about 56 h on the same mat. The page should give runtimes as Wh ÷ (heater W + idle W), not Wh × 0.85 ÷ heater W. It should also tell owners to turn off BLUETTI's ECO mode. BLUETTI says ECO turns outputs on and off by itself, and that is a risk when a thermostat drops the load to near zero.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of a small reptile heater's runtime goes to the station's own draw. Jackery lists 18 W standby on the Explorer 1000 v2 and Gidon at The Technology Man measured about 17 W on the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, so with a 24 W heat mat about 43% of the battery heats nothing (18 / (24 + 18)). BLUETTI lists 4.5 W standby on the Elite 30 V2. Anker's default Smart AC mode also turns the inverter off after 15 minutes below 20 W, which would cut a thermostat-cycled emitter during its off period.
angles.decides: For a low-watt mat or a thermostat-cycled emitter, standby draw changes the ranking more than capacity does at the small end. The 288 Wh Elite 30 V2, at its stated 4.5 W, runs a 24 W mat about 8.6 h, against about 5.8 h if it drew 18 W like the Jackery. On 1 kWh stations the Anker C1000 Gen 2 (907 Wh measured, 17 W idle) and the Jackery 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, 18 W standby) both come to about 22 h on a 24 W mat. The pick should say to turn off Anker's Smart AC mode (and the equivalent auto-off on any station) before relying on it with a thermostat. It also confirms the Elite 30 V2 only as a small-mat station.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a power station's own power-saving switch-off (BLUETTI ECO mode, EcoFlow AC timeout, Jackery Energy Saving Mode) cuts the AC outlet when the load stays low or comes and goes. A thermostat that cycles a reptile heater, or a small heat mat, is exactly that kind of load, so the heat can go off partway through an outage unless the owner turns the feature off before the power fails.
angles.decides: This doesn't knock any candidate out, because BLUETTI, EcoFlow and Jackery all let you turn the feature off. It decides whether the plan works at all, so the page needs a 'before the outage: turn off ECO / set AC timeout to Never' step for each pick. It also changes the runtime table. Each station's own draw (AC180 about 15 W per BLUETTI's manual; Jackery 1000 v2 18 W standby per Jackery) is close to a 24 W heat mat's own draw, so the 'heat mat' runtimes are roughly 40% too long. Example: Elite 200 V2 at 2,073.6 Wh × 0.85 ÷ 24 W ≈ 73 h, but ÷ (24 + 15) W ≈ 45 h. That 15 W is the AC180's figure applied to the Elite as an illustration; I didn't find the Elite's own number. Small mats favour stations with a low or adjustable ECO threshold and low idle draw.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for how much power a station uses with its AC outlet on and nothing plugged in. With a 24–50 W reptile heater, that draw cuts runtime far more than ChatGPT's flat 85% efficiency assumes. The Technology Man measured about 19 W on the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2. The Solar Lab measured 16 W on the Elite 100 V2 and 9.5 W on the Elite 200 V2, plus 94% efficiency on the Elite 200 V2.
angles.decides: This confirms the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 as the pick for multi-day heat. It had the lowest measured idle draw (9.5 W, The Solar Lab) and the highest measured efficiency (94%, The Solar Lab; above 93%, about 2,000 Wh, The Gadgeteer). By my arithmetic it keeps a 24 W mat going for roughly 2,073.6 × 0.93 ÷ (24 + 9.5) ≈ 57 h. It also demotes the 288–300 Wh units (Elite 30 V2, Tenergy T320) to 'a few hours only'. The Technology Man measured about 19 W of AC idle on the Elite 30 V2 with Eco mode off, and only 231 Wh usable on AC. That gives at most 288 ÷ (24 + 19) ≈ 6.7 h for a 24 W mat, the bottom-to-middle of our page's 'About 6–8 h', and about 288 ÷ (50 + 19) ≈ 4.2 h for a 100 W emitter at half duty. Shoppers should also be told to turn off Eco/auto-off for AC: it cuts idle draw but can shut the outlet off while the thermostat has the heater switched off. For the 1 kWh class, The Solar Lab's 16 W idle on the Elite 100 V2 limits a 24 W mat to about 1,024 ÷ (24 + 16) ≈ 25.6 h. That supports 'about a day' as an upper bound, not a typical figure.

pages.query: can a portable power station run a gas furnace during a power outage and how do you connect it
pages.why_used: Outage Authority (cited) gives per-model furnace hours and a stale $/rated-Wh ranking (Elite 200 V2 at $1,399; it is $899 today), and no rival states how many 8-hour furnace nights one charge holds, what each station costs per usable Wh, or that the Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit costs the same $1,199 as the bare Elite 300 while holding 45% less usable energy and refilling one night only after about 11 hours of full-rated sun.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's '4,800 W lifting' / '3,900 W Power Lifting' and EcoFlow's '2,200 W X-Boost' headline numbers are resistive-only modes that do not count toward starting a furnace blower motor, and that BLUETTI's Elite 300 and Elite 200 V2 US pages publish no true surge rating at all, while EcoFlow, Jackery and ALLPOWERS publish surge and boost as separate numbers.
angles.decides: A PSC blower needs roughly 1,350–1,800 W to start (PreparedStates quoting DTE), so for 2,400 W-and-up stations (Elite 300, Elite 200 V2, DELTA 3 Max Plus, R4000) the continuous rating alone covers the start and the missing or resistive-only boost number changes nothing; it confirms the 2,400 W+ picks. For 1,800 W-class units (AC180, Elite 100 V2, DELTA 3 Plus) the shopper must not read 'Power Lifting 2,700 W' or 'X-Boost 2,200 W' as surge headroom; only a published true surge (Jackery 1000 v2 3,000 W per Outage Authority; DELTA 3 Plus not confirmed on the maker page today) counts, which keeps the AC180's 'PSC start unverified' flag and argues for the EcoFlow/Jackery units in that class.

The $899 Elite 200 V2 is the value pick per usable Wh ($0.51) if 0.8 of a mild night is enough; the ALLPOWERS R4000 ($0.51 per usable Wh, 1.3 nights) is sold out today.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "power station to run a heated blanket all night". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What's a good power station to run a heated blanket all night?
pages.why_used: The cited rivals turn rated Wh into hours with a flat 0.85 factor, and none has a measured figure for any power station. This page uses OutdoorGearLab's measured usable AC energy (AC180 950 Wh, Jackery 1000 v2 910 Wh, C1000 Gen 2 and Elite 100 V2 890 Wh each) and measured idle draw (The Technology Man: Elite 30 V2 about 19 W; The Solar Lab: C1000 Gen 2 13.8 W, Elite 100 V2 about 16 W), and works out the overnight hours from those numbers.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the BLUETTI AC180 has an ECO mode that switches the AC (or DC) output off when the load stays low for a set time. BLUETTI's manual puts the AC threshold anywhere from 15 to 30 W and the DC threshold from 5 to 10 W, with a delay of 1, 2, 3 or 4 hours. So a blanket on a low setting, or a 12 V blanket, can lose power partway through the night unless ECO is turned off.
angles.decides: The AC180 stays the pick: it is $499 and in stock at BLUETTI today, has 1,152 Wh, and the blanket counts as the resistive load its manual describes. The finding adds a condition to that pick: turn ECO off, or set it to its lowest threshold, before using the AC180 overnight. Thermostat-controlled blankets on low and 12 V blankets on the car port are the loads most likely to sit under 15–30 W (AC) or 5–10 W (DC) for an hour or more. Because the hour figures are rated-capacity arithmetic, a station that shuts off at hour 3 never reaches them. The same check should go in the table for every candidate. I could not source the default thresholds for the AC180, or the energy-saving thresholds for the Jackery 1000 v2, so the page should show that column as manual-stated ranges, not defaults.
products: Jackery Explorer 1000 (manual mirror, model not confirmed as v2)

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out, for a single blanket at the US DOE's typical 60 W, the hours each 1 kWh station runs once its own AC draw is included, or the cost per usable Wh: the BLUETTI AC180 gives 13.1 h at $0.51 per usable Wh and the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 gives 12.4 h at $0.57 per usable Wh, both at $499.
angles.decides: This confirms the AC180 over the Elite 100 V2. They cost the same $499 on bluettipower.com today, and the AC180 runs about 0.7 h longer on a 60 W blanket with a lower cost per usable Wh. Both cover a 10 h night at 60 W, but neither covers 10 h at 100 W (8.5 h and 7.9 h). The Elite 30 V2 runs only about 3.5 h on a 60 W 120 V blanket, so it belongs only with low-draw 12 V blankets. The AC180 is now listed as available, which corrects our page's 'back late Nov' stock note.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the BLUETTI AC180, ChatGPT's 'best overall' pick, has an ECO mode that switches the AC outlet off after the load stays at or below a 15–30 W threshold for 1, 2, 3 or 4 hours. A blanket on low, or one whose thermostat has cycled off, can lose power partway through the night unless ECO is turned off.
angles.decides: It does not change the pick. The AC180 still fits a 120 V blanket overnight. It adds a required setup step: turn ECO off, or set it to the lowest threshold and longest duration, before a night on low. Otherwise a low-draw blanket can lose power within 1–4 hours. Jackery and Anker have similar energy-saving features, but I could not read their thresholds from the makers' documents, so the page should not claim this is AC180-only or say the other stations are exempt.

angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's #2 pick, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, rather than ruling it out. Energy Saving Mode is on out of the box, but the 12-hour timer is longer than an 8–10 h night, and the mode can be turned off. The blanket's low draw while its thermostat is off should not cut power in the middle of a normal night. The bigger runtime hit is the 18 W standby Jackery lists. Over 10 h that is 180 Wh, about 17% of the 1,070 Wh battery. ChatGPT's '≈12 h at 75 W' leaves it out (arithmetic: 1,070 × 0.85 ≈ 910 Wh; 910 / (75 + 18) ≈ 9.8 h, not 12 h). For the BLUETTI AC180 (ChatGPT's #1), the deciding question is ECO mode: whether its delay can be as short as 1–4 h and its threshold above a blanket's thermostat-off draw. I could not open a readable official source for that (see unsourced), so the page should tell AC180 owners to turn AC ECO off for overnight blanket use rather than quote numbers.

pages.query: power station to run a pellet smoker overnight
pages.why_used: Traeger's support page gives the D2's 0.08–0.17 A running draw but never mentions power stations. None of the other pages says that the stations shoppers are steered to switch their AC off by themselves at low load: Jackery's Energy Saving Mode is on as shipped and cuts outputs after 12 h, the Anker C1000 Gen 2 cuts after 15 min under 20 W, and the AC180 cuts after 1–4 h under 15–30 W. Any of these can stop a 10–20 W smoker partway through the night. This page names each station's shut-off rule and the setting to change, and it adds the inverter's own all-night draw to the watt-hours per cook.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the power stations it recommended can switch their AC outlet off by themselves when the load is light, or that a Traeger D2 grill holding temperature draws about 10–20 W. That puts the grill at or below those cut-off levels: the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 turns its inverter off after 15 minutes under 20 W by default (The Technology Man), and the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's Eco mode cuts AC below a 10–40 W level set in the app (New Atlas). Either can stop the auger and fan in the middle of the night unless the setting is turned off.
angles.decides: This mostly adds a required setting rather than ruling a station out. With an Anker C1000 Gen 2, turn off Smart AC Output before an overnight cook. With a BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, turn off Eco mode or set the AC level to its 10 W minimum. Otherwise a D2 Traeger idling at about 10–20 W can lose power and the fire goes out. It also shrinks capacity: The Technology Man measured about 17 W inverter overhead on the C1000 Gen 2, which is roughly 200 Wh over 12 hours, as much as the grill uses. That backs the 1 kWh minimum and makes the 2 kWh Elite 200 V2 safer for 12-hour or cold-night cooks.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the power station's own AC inverter keeps drawing about 10–16 W all night (The Gadgeteer: 10 W on the Elite 200 V2; The Solar Lab: about 16 W on the Elite 100 V2). Against a measured 35 W smoker, that adds 29–46% to an overnight cook. A 12-hour cook then takes about 540–612 Wh from the battery, not the 420 Wh the smoker itself uses. So a 1 kWh station covers about 1.7 overnight cooks and the 2 kWh Elite 200 V2 covers about 3.7.
angles.decides: It confirms that 1 kWh is the minimum for one 12-hour night. The Elite 100 V2 runs one night with about 400 Wh left, not the 2+ nights that 0.85-derate arithmetic suggests. It also argues for the Elite 200 V2 when the shopper wants two back-to-back nights without recharging, and it costs less per overnight cook. Our table's '1' for 1 kWh units stands. For the Elite 200 V2, the sourced arithmetic gives about 3.7 rather than 2–3.

Anker's C1000 outlets shut off only when no plug is detected for 15 minutes, with no wattage rule, so a plugged-in grill keeps power. That makes the Anker C1000 (the card ChatGPT showed at $449.99) the safer choice if the shopper won't change settings. Anker's −20 °C to 40 °C discharge range also covers a cold overnight cook.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which portable power station runs a pellet stove through a 12-hour winter outage". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which portable power station runs a pellet stove through a 12-hour winter outage?
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages work out runtime from rated Wh. Home Battery Report divides rated Wh by the stove's VA, and Power Fallback assumes a flat 0.85 efficiency. None of them gives the AC energy that reviewers measured coming out of these stations. This page builds every runtime from named reviewers' measured output (Notebookcheck: 2,650 Wh from the Elite 300 at about 200 W). It also shows that delivered energy ranged from 78 % to 93 % of the rating, which no flat 85 % rule captures.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many watt-hours these stations actually deliver at a pellet-stove-sized load. Tested at about 200 W, the BLUETTI Elite 300 gave 2,650–2,670 Wh of its 3,014 Wh (about 88 %). The 3,840 Wh Anker SOLIX F3800 gave only 2,980 Wh (78 %). The 4,096 Wh EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 gave 3,790 Wh (93 %). So the 826 Wh gap in rated capacity between the Anker and the BLUETTI is only about 330 Wh of real output, and on measured energy the Elite 300 runs a 200 W stove for about 13.3 h, not 'about 12'.
angles.decides: This backs the Elite 300 ($1,199) as the pick for a stove that runs at about 200 W or less. At that load it delivered about 2,650 Wh, which is 13.2–13.3 h at 200 W. Our page's 'about 12, no margin' at 215 W becomes about 12.3 h on measured energy. It also weakens the F3800 as the 'bigger margin' alternative: measured, it gives about 14.9 h at 200 W, not the 19–20 h its rating implies. The DELTA Pro 3 is the only one of the three with real headroom (about 19 h at 200 W). None of the three base units clears 12 h for a stove like the Harman XXV (2.8 A run, about 322 VA): Elite 300 about 8.2 h, F3800 about 9.3 h, DELTA Pro 3 about 11.8 h. Those numbers treat VA as W, so they are the most each unit could manage. That kind of stove needs an expansion battery.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a station's measured AC-on idle draw (19 W on the BLUETTI Elite 300, 19.5 W on the Apex 300) or works the 12-hour runtime from measured delivered Wh plus that idle draw. Done that way, the Apex 300 drops from Home Battery Report's 12.8 h to about 9.7 h on a Quadra-Fire Classic Bay 1200 (216 VA), and the Elite 300 lands at about 12.0 h with no margin.
angles.decides: This confirms the BLUETTI Elite 300 as the pick for stoves running at or below about 150–200 W. At 150 W with 3 ignitions it gives about 15.5 h, a 3.5 h margin. At a Classic Bay 1200's 216 VA it gives exactly 12.0 h, so a shopper with a 200 W+ stove needs about 2,900+ delivered Wh and should step up a size. The idle and capacity measurements also knock the BLUETTI Apex 300 out of the 12-hour slot for 216 VA stoves (9.7 h), although rated-Wh math gives it 12.8 h. The Elite 200 V2 ($899) covers 12 h only on a low-draw stove like the Quadra-Fire Santa Fe (127 VA).

For a Harman owner, the BLUETTI Elite 300, ALLPOWERS R4000, AC200L, EcoFlow and Anker units are all outside Harman's approved list, so the page should tell Harman owners to check with their dealer first. I could not confirm from BLUETTI whether the Elite 300 takes expansion batteries. angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the UPS Harman lab-tested for its pellet stoves, the APC BE750G, switches to battery in 6 ms typical and 10 ms maximum. That is the only stove-validated transfer time we have. A power station that switches in ≤10 ms is inside it, and the 15–20 ms units are outside anything Harman tested.
angles.decides: This supports the BLUETTI Elite 300, which BLUETTI rates at ≤10 ms, and the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 at 10 ms. Both switch over no slower than the 10 ms maximum of the UPS Harman approved. It is a reason to rank the Elite 200 V2 (15 ms), AC200L (20 ms), AC180 (20 ms) and ALLPOWERS P1800 (20 ms) lower as pass-through units, because 15–20 ms is slower than anything Harman tested. Our current page already lists those switchover times. There is a condition: transfer time only matters if the stove's own control is set to Continue Operation. With Harman's factory quick-shutdown setting, any power station just powers a shutdown. So the page should say: check the stove's power-failure setting first, then pick a unit that switches in ≤10 ms. This is our comparison; Harman publishes no ms limit.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which portable power station runs a full-size refrigerator for 24 hours in an outage". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which portable power station runs a full-size refrigerator for 24 hours in an outage?
pages.why_used: The cited rivals repeat CNET's raw fridge hours (27.40 h, 26.32 h) or estimate runtime with a flat efficiency. None rescales CNET's measured runtimes from its 54–60 W Whirlpool to a typical 585 kWh/yr or a thirsty 679 kWh/yr full-size fridge. Rescaled, both 2 kWh picks fall below 24 h, and the in-stock 1,199-dollar FOSSiBOT F3600 Pro (CNET 44.65 h) beats the 3 kWh units on hours and on price.

Worked backwards, that fridge averages no more than about 51–55 W (about 1.2–1.3 kWh/day). Put the 2 kWh picks on the median ENERGY STAR full-size fridge instead (585 kWh/yr, about 67 W) and they land at about 23–25 h, right on the 24-hour line, not Anker's 32 h.

It moves the safe pick for a guaranteed 24 h to the 3 kWh class (Jackery HomePower 3000 or BLUETTI Elite 300). The 2 kWh units, C2000 Gen 2 and Elite 200 V2, clear 24 h only with an efficient fridge that averages 60 W or less. The footnote is the finding: maker fridge-hours are not comparable with each other or with the shopper's fridge.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which portable power station runs a 13 hp sump pump through a 12-hour outage". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which portable power station runs a 13 hp sump pump through a 12-hour outage?
pages.why_used: The cited rivals work out runtime from nameplate Wh at an assumed 85% and leave out inverter idle draw. RunTimeFit says outright that its hours exclude it, and OutageReadyHQ and The Home Battery Report say they did not test. This page uses named testers' measured usable Wh and idle draw instead. On those figures the PECRON F3000LFP falls to 11.4 h at 25% duty, short of 12, and the DELTA Pro 3 reaches 16.9 h. The page also gives the highest duty each station can carry for 12 hours.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 300's 4,800 W 'lifting' figure covers resistive loads only, so a sump-pump start has to fit under its 2,400 W rating, or that StorageReview drew only 2.67 kWh from its 3,014 Wh pack (88.6%), which puts a 1/3 HP pump at about 13 hours at 25% duty, not the 'about 12 hours' ChatGPT showed.
angles.decides: This confirms rather than overturns. Sized against the real 2,400 W limit, the Elite 300 still clears the 1,300 W start figure RunTimeFit uses for a 1/3 HP pump, and on StorageReview's measured 2.67 kWh it covers 12 hours at 25% duty with margin (about 13.4 h at 800 W, about 16.4 h at 650 W). The page's table should normalise every row to two things: a surge that applies to motors (not a lifting or boost mode), and delivered Wh rather than nameplate Wh. On that basis, stations that list only a 'Max' or lifting figure, such as the F3800 Plus and Elite 300, are judged on their continuous rating.

angles.decides: This changes the pick. With an M53-class pump at 25% duty, the 3 kWh stations (PECRON F3000LFP and BLUETTI Elite 300) last about 9 hours, and the most duty they can hold for 12 hours is about 19%. The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus reaches about 11.3 h. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the only one near 12 h (about 11.8–12 h), but it is currently unavailable. The page should lead with the highest duty each station can carry for 12 h (about 19% for 3 kWh, about 24% for 4 kWh) and tell readers to read their pump's amps off the label. Read literally, 13 hp is about 9.7 kW of shaft power, which is more than any listed portable station's continuous output (the highest here is 6,000 W). So the 13 hp answer is 'no portable station'.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus only the three leftmost NEMA 5-20R outlets give UPS backup. Anker's page marks the TT-30R 'No UPS', caps bypass at 1,440 W while the unit is charging from a 120 V wall outlet, and lists those same three UPS outlets as unusable when a generator feeds the unit. A sump pump left on standby therefore has to go in one of those three outlets, and you have to move it to the TT-30R or L14-30R when a generator is running the station.
angles.decides: This confirms the setup more than it changes the pick. A 1/3 HP pump (about 800 W running in ChatGPT's own tables) fits under both bypass limits, so the F3800 Plus and Elite 300 can each keep it on UPS standby, but only through the right outlet. The resistive-only limit on the Elite 300's 4,800 W figure means its motor-start headroom should be judged against 2,400 W, not 4,800 W. That favours the F3800 Plus (6,000 W, expandable with BP3800 batteries) for wet basements where the pump cycles often. A literal 13 hp pump falls outside every candidate here.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a sump pump draws 0 W between float cycles. A station's ECO or no-load AC shut-off can therefore kill the outlet before the pit refills. BLUETTI's AC300 manual says ECO turns AC off below 30 W over 4 h, and The Technology Man reports the Elite 300's Eco mode turns AC off with no load. If ECO is switched off to prevent that, the inverter's own idle draw (about 19 W, measured on an Elite 300) uses about 226 Wh over 12 hours, and no runtime table counts it.
angles.decides: This doesn't change which station is biggest, but it adds a condition the plan depends on: ECO or AC auto-off must be disabled, or the pump has no power when the float closes. Once ECO is off, idle draw comes out of the budget. For the Elite 300 our 25 %-duty row drops from 11.9 h to about 10.9 h (2,380 Wh usable ÷ (200 W average pump + 19 W idle), using our page's own 800 W × 25 % basis). That pushes it under 12 h, so the 12-hour pick should be the 3.4 kWh-plus ALLPOWERS R4000 or larger (F3800 Plus, S5000). The page needs a 'turn off ECO / set AC timeout to Never' step.

With those figures the PECRON's 3,072 Wh lasts about 11.4 h, short of 12 h, under ChatGPT's own assumption of an 800 W pump at 25% duty. RunTimeFit's '~16 hours' left idle draw out. Notebookcheck measured the BLUETTI Elite 300 at 2,650 Wh delivered at about 200 W, and named-tester figures put the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 at about 17 h and the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus at about 15 h on the same assumption.

The PECRON F3000LFP that ChatGPT recommended loses about 333 Wh to its 37 W idle draw over the 9 hours the pump is off, so it falls short of 12 h at 25% duty with an 800 W pump (about 11.4 h). Even with RunTimeFit's own 650 W pump it reaches only about 13.7 h, not 16 h. On named-tester measurements the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the safe 12-hour choice: Scott Caine measured 3,772 Wh usable and 34 W idle (about 16.9 h), and The Solar Lab ran it at 5,100 W surge for nearly a minute. The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus is next (3,448 Wh, 38 W idle, about 15.3 h). The Elite 300 gets past 12 h on energy, but its 4,800 W lifting rating applies to resistive loads only. Nobody measured a motor start on any candidate, so pump starting stays a spec-sheet question. None of this changes the literal 13 HP reading, which no portable station covers.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "can a portable power station run a 5000 btu window ac overnight while camping". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Can a portable power station run a 5000 btu window ac overnight while camping?
pages.why_used: Home Power Facts and Lights On Lab work out runtimes from a calculated AC draw (347 W from CEER, or an assumed 400–500 W) and from estimated or unattributed usable Wh. This page uses TechGearLab's metered 0.40–0.47 kWh per hour for four 5,000 BTU window units and divides that into usable Wh measured by named reviewers for each station. That fixes the 'calculated, not tested' caveat attached to the earlier version of this page.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the BLUETTI Elite 300's advertised 4,800 W is 'Power Lifting', which is only for resistive loads and is not a startup allowance for motors or compressors. Its real headroom for starting an AC compressor is its 2,400 W rated output, and StorageReview measured 2.67 kWh of usable output from the 3,014 Wh battery. ALLPOWERS's 6,000 W figure for the R4000 is labelled surge.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick and does not change it. Even with no real surge headroom, the Elite 300's 2,400 W rated output is above the 1,000–1,500 W starting draw the rival pages give for a 5,000 BTU unit, so it can still start the AC. The footnote should say: compare 2,400 W (Elite 300) against 6,000 W surge (R4000), not 4,800 against 6,000. If a particular AC is hard to start, the R4000 has more margin. Our page assumes about 2.56 kWh usable for the Elite 300, and the measured 2.67 kWh should replace that. On the measured figure, about 11 h at a 240 W inverter-AC average (2,670 ÷ 240) and about 5.9 h for a conventional 450 W unit running flat out (2,670 ÷ 450). The 'only the 3 kWh class' verdict still holds. The R4000 is shown as out of stock today, so the Elite 300 is the 3 kWh pick you can actually buy.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that refilling one night of AC use from the kit's own panels takes most of a day or more: StorageReview measured the BLUETTI Elite 300 taking 3.49 kWh to recharge after it delivered 2.67 kWh, so its 2×200 W kit needs 3,490 ÷ 400 = 8.7 hours of full-rated panel output, and the 1,200 W solar input still needs 2.9 hours.
angles.decides: Confirms the BLUETTI Elite 300 as the pick on measured numbers: 2.67 kWh delivered covers an 8-hour night at 50% duty (1,820 Wh) with about 850 Wh to spare. It does not cover a flat-out night (3,640 Wh). For a second night on solar, the Elite 300 + 2×200 W kit ($1,699) is not enough. Shoppers need about 1,200 W of panels (the Elite 300's maximum input), or a campground hookup. The R4000 is sold out at the maker today, so it can't be the lead pick.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that GE's 5,000 BTU window AC manual forbids extension cords, surge protectors, multi-outlet adaptors and adapter plugs and wants the AC on its own outlet. Read literally, the AC has to plug straight into one of the station's 120 V household outlets with its own factory cord. That rules out an extension lead to a station sitting outside the camper, and it rules out a TT-30 dogbone adapter. In BLUETTI's US lineup, only the AC200L is named as B300K-compatible, so it is the only BLUETTI on our page that can grow past about 4.2 kWh rated, and it is sold out.

The station has to sit inside the camper, within the AC's own cord length of the window, with the AC alone on one outlet. The Elite 300 and R4000 TT-30 outlets are not a sanctioned way to feed a GE window unit. For a conventional 450 W AC running flat out, which ChatGPT says needs about 4.2–4.7 kWh, the only maker-documented BLUETTI path is the AC200L plus a B300K. That is 2,048 + 2,764.8 = 4,812.8 Wh, about 4,090 Wh usable at 85 %, so about 9.1 h at 450 W. But the AC200L is sold out at BLUETTI US today, and the R4000 is sold out at ALLPOWERS US. That leaves the Elite 300 as the only in-stock 3 kWh pick from these two makers, and it does not cover a conventional AC running flat out all night.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the BLUETTI Elite 300's advertised '4,800 W' is Power Lifting, which BLUETTI's manual limits to resistive loads and does not count as a start allowance for compressors. A fixed-speed 5,000 BTU AC therefore has to start within the 2,400 W continuous rating, and a starting draw of 2 to 3 times about 450 W fits inside that.

The Elite 300 can start a conventional 5,000 BTU unit because its 2,400 W continuous rating is about 1.8 times the top of lightsonlab's 1,000–1,500 W starting range. angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a measured draw for a 5,000 BTU window AC. TechGearLab metered four 5,000 BTU units for one hour each on maximum settings and recorded 0.40–0.47 kWh, which is about 400–470 W. Set against named bench tests of the 3 kWh class (The Technology Man got 2,819 Wh from the BLUETTI Elite 300; Notebookcheck got about 2,650 Wh), that gives only 5.6–7.0 hours of flat-out cooling. Even the 3 kWh class needs the compressor to cycle to last 8 hours.
angles.decides: This confirms the page's line that only the 3 kWh class can make it through a night, and it tightens the claim. With a conventional 5,000 BTU unit at TechGearLab's measured 400–470 W, the best-measured 3 kWh unit (Elite 300) delivers 2,650–2,819 Wh, about 5.6–7.0 hours of continuous cooling. It gets through 8 hours only if the compressor cycles, at roughly 75–85 % run time or less, or with an inverter AC. Every 2 kWh unit with a named measurement (DELTA 2 Max 1,800 Wh, Elite 200 V2 1,910 Wh) gives about 4–4.8 hours at 400 W. The AC180 (950–1,030 Wh) gives about 2.4–2.6 hours. So the picks stay Elite 300 and R4000, and the 2 kWh rows should be labelled 'half a night'. Leaving the AC outlet on also costs about 19 W of idle draw (The Technology Man), roughly 150 Wh over 8 hours.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which 1000 wh power station is quietest while charging". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which 1000 wh power station is quietest while charging?
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages present the DJI Power 1000 V2 and the BLUETTI AC180 as a 37 dB tie and the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 as maker-claim only. None says that The Technology Man's 37 dB readings sit at his room's background level (1 dB above it for the AC180), that nextpit measured the Jackery's quiet charging mode at about 30 dB at about 260 W, or that Notebookcheck measured the Anker C1000 Gen 2 at 45 dB at full speed. This page adds all three, which shows the DJI is as quiet as the room while charging about four times faster than the AC180 in Silent.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the only like-for-like charging-noise pair is from one reviewer, The Technology Man. Using the same 1 m distance, room temperature and full-speed charging on UK mains, they measured about 37 dB for the DJI Power 1000 V2 (over 1,400 W) and about 42 dB for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 (1,600 W). Notebookcheck measured the same Anker at 45 dB at 1 m. Every quiet-mode dB figure on the maker pages either names a different distance and charge rate or names none at all, so those figures cannot be ranked against each other.
angles.decides: This confirms the DJI Power 1000 V2 as the quiet choice for full-speed charging. Under one reviewer's identical setup it was about 5 dB quieter than the Anker C1000 Gen 2 while charging faster than 1,400 W. A second reviewer, Notebookcheck, put the Anker even louder at 45 dB at 1 m. For overnight charging the pick does not change. The Anker's fans switch off at 200 W, which The Technology Man observed directly. By contrast, Jackery's 22 or 30 dB claim and DJI's quiet-mode claim are maker numbers taken under different or unstated conditions, so neither can be ranked against the other.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how long each station's fan noise lasts for one full charge. The DJI Power 1000 V2 took 53 minutes to fill in The Technology Man's test. The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 took 47 minutes at about 42 dB in the same test. At its fans-off 200 W setting the Anker would take about 5.1 hours, and the BLUETTI AC180 at its measured 283 W Silent draw would take about 4.1 hours.
angles.decides: This backs the DJI Power 1000 V2 as the answer for anyone who shares a room with the station. ChatGPT shows it and the AC180 tied at about 37 dB at 1 m, the figures on Dealectric's current page. The DJI reaches that level for about 53 minutes to fill, while the AC180 in Silent needs about 4.1 hours at a 283 W draw (before charging losses), so the AC180 is audible about 4.6 times as long for the same charge. The exception is a shopper who must have no fan sound at all. For them the Anker C1000 Gen 2 set to 200 W is the pick: fans off, about 5.1 hours to full, which fits inside one night. Anker's 600 W 'Silent' setting is not fan-off, according to The Technology Man.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the quiet or slow charging settings it recommends have to be turned on in the maker's phone app. On the BLUETTI AC180, Turbo and Silent are turned on in the BLUETTI app. On the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, both the AC charging speed and the 1,600 W UltraFast mode are set in the Anker app. Without UltraFast, its AC charging on 120 V tops out at 1,200 W.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick and adds a setup condition; it does not change the ranking. For the AC180 and C1000 Gen 2, the quiet result ChatGPT quoted (about 37 dB in Silent; fans off at 200 W) only happens after the owner changes a setting in the app. For the AC180, it also needs the unit paired with the app first. Out of the box, the Anker charges at up to 1,200 W on 120 V. This makes DJI Power 1000 V2 more attractive for shoppers who don't want to use an app, but only if DJI's mode switch is a physical control. I could not confirm that from a DJI page I opened (see unsourced).

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says how each 1,000 Wh unit is switched into its quiet charging rate. The DJI Power 1000 V2 has a physical charging-speed switch on the unit. The quiet or low rate on the BLUETTI AC180, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is set in the maker's phone app; their pages and guides describe no on-unit control. The measured quiet figures ChatGPT quoted (AC180 Silent about 37 dB, C1000 Gen 2 fans off at 200 W) are only reached once the shopper has set the lower rate in the app.
angles.decides: This confirms rather than flips the pick. The DJI Power 1000 V2 is the only candidate where the shopper can choose the slower rate on the unit itself; on the rest the slow rate goes through the phone app. The DJI is also the unit measured at about 37 dB at full speed. For a shopper who wants a quiet overnight charge without depending on an app (an RV with no signal, or a non-technical user), the DJI pick gets stronger. The AC180 and C1000 Gen 2 recommendations need a caveat: their quiet figures depend on first setting Silent or a low AC rate in the app. If that isn't done, the Anker charges at up to 1,200 W by Anker's own spec. Our page does not have the AC180's default rate from an opened source.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that nextpit measured the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at about 30 dB while charging at about 260 W in its quiet charging mode. They also don't say that The Technology Man's 37 dB readings for the BLUETTI AC180 and DJI Power 1000 V2 were only about 1 dB above the background noise in his room, so those readings can't show which unit is quieter.
angles.decides: The Jackery 1000 v2 moves from 'claim only' to 'measured quiet mode'. nextpit got about 30 dB at about 260 W, a rate that would fill 1,070 Wh in roughly 4 to 4.5 h, close to the AC180 Silent mode's 283 W and 4.5 h. That makes it a measured contender for overnight bedroom charging, not just a footnote. The figures still come from different reviewers, rooms and (for nextpit) an unstated distance, so the page should not crown the Jackery quieter than the AC180. It should say that both have measured quiet modes near room noise. For fast charging, DJI Power 1000 V2 stays the pick: The Technology Man measured 37 dB at over 1,400 W, at background level. Two reviewers measured the Anker C1000 Gen 2 at full speed, 42 dB (The Technology Man) and 45 dB (Notebookcheck), and both put it louder than the DJI.

pages.why_used: The cited rival pages (homepowerfacts, outagemath, backupcalc) work out hours as rated Wh × 85% ÷ load, use made-up idle figures and name no tester. This page bases its hours on named tests: Reefs.com measured 11 h 23 min at 13 W on the Elite 30 V2, and named reviewers measured each station's own power draw. That moves the 20 W estimate from about 12 h to about 9 h and shows that the 12 V barrel route gains little on this unit.

The 12 V tip (DC for the router, AC for the modem) therefore makes this unit's overhead worse: for a 20 W router and modem, estimated runtime falls from about 11.8 h to about 9.9 h.
angles.decides: It keeps the Elite 30 V2 as the pick: it has the only small-unit idle figure split by output, and its ≤10 ms UPS claim is unambiguous. The EcoFlow RIVER 3's own figures conflict (StorageReview's spec table says <20 ms, its text says 10 ms), and Jackery's 240 v2 is 20 ms. It also changes the advice for the Elite 30 V2: put the router and modem on the same output type, so only one bank is on. Splitting them between AC and DC turns on both banks and costs about 2 hours at 20 W. One caveat: if ECO mode is on, it may cut AC at low load. I couldn't confirm that from the manual.

They also never say which boxes include such a cable. The Jackery 300D's handle is a 140 W USB-C cable (Jackery store), Anker lists a USB-C cable in the C300 DC box, and the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 ships with AC and car cables only. The facts that matter more for this question are these. The 300D's third USB-C port is only 65 W (C1 and C2 are 140 W), which fills in the port detail ChatGPT told shoppers to 'verify'. BLUETTI says the Elite 30 V2 has 'only 4.5W standby' but does not say in which mode. If that draw ran all weekend it would be 216 Wh, so I would not put it on the page until the mode is sourced. The Anker C300 DC or Jackery 300D is still the lightest way to get 100 W or more over USB-C.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "best solar generator kit for an apartment balcony". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What's the best solar generator kit for an apartment balcony?

PowerStationGearLab says it doesn't test anything, Flowers of Vice's '850Wh usable' is the author's own guess, and Wattfolk and The Gadgeteer test nothing hands-on. None of them gives a kit's measured usable watt-hours or a panel's measured clear-sun output. This page uses OutdoorGearLab's and The Technology Man's measurements to work out how many hours of sun each kit needs to refill, and those hours decide the pick.

angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. The DELTA 3 Classic kit stays the 1 kWh pick, and EcoFlow's US store sells it for $669, less than the $729 Best Buy card ChatGPT showed. On durability, the page should say the makers' numbers can't be compared, not rank them, because only Jackery names an endpoint and it is the looser 70%. For the compact tier, the Elite 30 V2 is a 600 W continuous unit, and its 1,500 W 'lifting' figure covers only kettles and heaters, not motor start-up. The Anker C300 is 300 W continuous with a 600 W surge, so neither compact kit runs a mini-fridge as well as a 1 kWh unit does.

Worked out from maker specs and today's maker-store prices: Elite 30 V2 + 100 W takes 2.9 h at $1.70/Wh, DELTA 3 Classic + 220 W takes 4.7 h at $0.65/Wh, AC180 + 200 W takes 5.8 h at $0.67/Wh, and AC180 + 100 W takes 11.5 h (about 3 days at 4 peak-sun hours) at $0.59/Wh.
angles.decides: It supports the DELTA 3 Classic + 220 W as the pick: it is the cheapest of the kits that refill in under 5 rated-sun hours, at $0.65/Wh and $669 on EcoFlow's US store today, which is less than the $729 Best Buy card ChatGPT showed. It also shows that the AC180 + 100 W kit on our current page needs about 3 sunny balcony days to refill. So we should list AC180 + 200 W ($769, 5.8 h) instead. The Elite 30 V2 + 100 W refills fastest (2.9 h) but costs about 2.6× more per Wh, so it is the small-battery pick for daily top-ups, not for outage backup.

The other limits are also missing: the compact Anker SOLIX C300 accepts only 11–28 V solar through an XT60 plug, does not work with Anker's own PS30 USB-C panel, and does not come with the solar cable it needs.

A renter who picks the DELTA 3 Classic for backup cannot add a battery later, so anyone who expects to need more than about 1 kWh should look at an expandable unit such as the BLUETTI AC180 already in the catalog. Expansion support for the AC180 still needs checking on BLUETTI's page; I only saw a rival page claim it. For the small kits, BLUETTI's 200 W solar cap on the Elite 30 V2 and Anker's 11–28 V limit on the C300 mean neither will run from a larger panel bought later. The C300 also needs its XT60 solar cable bought separately. The page should state these limits rather than change the pick.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a folding panel's cells are wired in series behind usually three bypass diodes, so a railing bar or baluster that shades one cell switches off about a third of the panel, or that one reviewer measured a nearly 70% drop with one of four sections of a 200 W kit panel shaded.
angles.decides: It doesn't change which product ranks first, because every kit ChatGPT showed uses a standard series-wired folding panel. It does decide whether the plan works on a given balcony. A panel hung behind or along a railing, where one cell is shaded, loses roughly a third or more of its output, not a small fraction. That makes a 200–220 W panel on a shaded balcony perform more like a 100–140 W panel. So the page should say: put the panel where no bar shadow crosses it, or look for a half-cut-cell panel, where a shaded cell costs only a sixth of the panel. For a shaded balcony this argues for the bigger panel (DELTA 3 Classic + 220 W or Jackery 1000 v2 + 200 W) over a 60–100 W kit, because the bigger panel still has usable watts left after the loss.

That advice comes from ChatGPT's answers and from our page's $210–280 third-party 200 W panel suggestion. If the panel's Vmp is under 28 V, Anker's 8.2 A cap applies. At about 20 V that cuts delivered solar power to roughly 164 W, about 18% below the panel's 200 W rating. The cheaper parts then buy less charging speed, unless the shopper picks a panel with Vmp of 29 V or more or wires two low-voltage panels in series (still under 60 V Voc). For the BLUETTI AC180, the manual's 12–60 V window and 'Voc no higher than 60V' warning mean at most two 12V-class panels in series. Three in series would go over 60 V. Footnote for the table: a station's 'max solar input W' is reachable only at the voltage and current the panel actually supplies.

So for this model, buy Anker's matched panel (as a kit or separately) or a high-voltage third-party panel, not a cheap low-voltage one. angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the AC180's solar input is capped at 10 A (500 W, 12–60 V, DC7909 port). Because watts = volts × amps, the panel string has to run near 50 V to reach the full 500 W, and its open-circuit voltage still has to stay under the 60 V limit. Adding a second panel in parallel, the way Trek4Tech suggests, raises the current but not the voltage, so it hits the 10 A cap.

Two panels in parallel are still held to 10 A, so the second panel adds little. To get toward the 500 W input, the panels have to go in series, at about 50 V with an open-circuit voltage under 60 V. BLUETTI's 2×200 W kit is $65 cheaper than the same parts bought separately ($1,232 vs $499 + 2 × $399 = $1,297, read today). A third-party panel also needs an MC4-to-DC7909 cable. This supports our page's verdict: the kit is the safe default, and a third-party panel saves money only for a buyer who checks the 10 A and 60 V limits. pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "best solar generator with panels included". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What's the best solar generator with panels included?
pages.why_used: Lights On Labs, StormWatts and SolutionEnergy work out refill hours from rated panel watts and say they didn't test anything. PowerSized quotes only two measured usable-capacity figures, has no measured panel output, and has no cost per usable Wh. This page sets each kit's lab-measured usable energy (StorageReview, OutdoorGearLab) beside OutdoorGearLab's measured panel watts and today's maker-store price per usable Wh. It also points out that the BLUETTI panel OutdoorGearLab tested is an older model, not the SP200L that ships in BLUETTI's kits.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the Anker SOLIX PS200 panel in the C1000 Gen 2 kit has a 57.6 V open-circuit voltage against the station's 60 V solar limit, so the 600 W input can't be filled by wiring PS200s in series (two would reach 115.2 V). A second panel has to go in parallel. The station's input also splits into two bands: 11–28 V capped at 8.2 A, and 29–60 V at up to 14.5 A.
angles.decides: This confirms that the C1000 Gen 2 + PS200 kit is a sound value pick out of the box: the 48 V panel runs in the 29–60 V band, so the 8.2 A low-band cap doesn't hold it back. It also qualifies the '600 W, 1.8 h' upgrade path. PS200s added later must be wired in parallel, not in series, and the C1000 Gen 2 can't take an expansion battery. A shopper planning to add solar should budget for a parallel lead or pick a 12–24 V-class panel pair wired in series. A single 12 V-class panel would charge in the 8.2 A band. It doesn't overturn the pick, but it's the one Anker detail the rival pages are missing.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 limits solar input to 8.2 A at 11–28 V and allows 14.5 A only at 29–60 V. Its bundled PS200 bifacial panel is a 48 V, 4.16 A panel, so it sits in the full-current band. A typical 18–20 V 200 W panel would land in the 8.2 A band and be cut to roughly 150–165 W. Two PS200s can't be wired in series (96 V is over the 60 V input limit), so more panels have to go in parallel.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's repeated 'best value / compact' pick, the Anker C1000 Gen 2 + 200 W kit (ChatGPT showed $799.99–$859.99). The panel Anker bundles (48 V, 4.16 A) uses the station's 14.5 A band, so the full 200 W rating reaches the station. The same station sold alone and paired with a cheap 12 V-class panel would lose about 20–25% to the 8.2 A cap. So buy the Anker bundle, not the station plus an outside panel. To grow it, add up to three PS200s in parallel (3 × 4.16 A = 12.5 A ≈ 600 W); never wire them in series. A side note for winter home backup: the C1000 Gen 2 will not charge below 32°F and has no self-heating. PowerSized already covers the same limit for the AC180, so this is not new.

pages.why_used: Every cited Soundcore page gives the AeroClip 2's 8 h/32 h and the C50i's 7 h/28 h with no codec or volume conditions, and none says the C50i also plays LDAC. Soundcore's own support tables show that with LDAC on, the AeroClip 2 falls to 5 h at 50% volume (3 h at 100%) and the C50i drops multipoint. This page is the only one with that fully maker-sourced battery and codec fact, which removes LDAC and battery as reasons to pay for the AeroClip 2 and leaves the call microphones as the reason.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the AeroClip 2's 8 h rating is measured with AAC at 50% volume and drops to 5 h with LDAC on (3 h at 100%), which is less than the C50i's 7 h. Soundcore's own C50i FAQ also lists LDAC (SBC/AAC/LDAC) and says dual connection is off while LDAC is on, so LDAC does not set the AeroClip 2 apart.
angles.decides: This confirms the C50i as the pick for music and everyday use and narrows the AeroClip 2 case to calls only. Both ChatGPT answers that give winners credit the AeroClip 2 for music partly because of LDAC, and the table one gives it a 'modest' battery win. Soundcore's own figures say the C50i also does LDAC. With LDAC on, the AeroClip 2 runs 5 h at 50% volume against the C50i's 7 h (the C50i figure is at Soundcore's standard test codec, not LDAC). In call mode, the gap is 5 h (AeroClip 2) vs 4.5 h (C50i). The AeroClip 2's real edge stays the 4 mics + 2 VPU call pickup and the 10 min = 4 h fast charge (vs 2 h). That is what the $100 gap at list price ($169.99 vs $69.99 on us.soundcore.com) pays for.

Calls cost $8.50 per rated call-hour on the AeroClip 2 and $2.22 on the C50i, and the AeroClip 2 gets only 0.5 h more talk time per charge.

A lost C50i means buying a whole new set for $39.98, while a lost AeroClip 2 bud costs $79.99. It also shows that the AeroClip 2's extra price buys mic quality, not much battery. On a call-heavy day it gets 5 h per charge against 4.5 h, so both need the case after about one 4.5–5 h stretch of calls. The extra $130 should rest on call clarity alone.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the $40–70 C50i supports LDAC too, using the same SBC/AAC/LDAC codecs as the AeroClip 2. Soundcore's own C50i FAQ also says that turning LDAC on switches off dual connection (multipoint), and LDAC is Android-only, so iPhone users get AAC on both.
angles.decides: This backs the C50i as the value pick and removes one of the AeroClip 2's claimed music advantages. LDAC is the same on both. An iPhone owner gets AAC from either model. An Android owner who wants LDAC on the C50i gives up two-device connection while it is on. The AeroClip 2's real hardware differences are the call microphones, IP57 and a wireless-charging case, the last per two named reviewers. LDAC should come out of the AeroClip 2's advantages on our page. We should also fix our C50i Bluetooth cell, which currently reads '6.0, multipoint' with no LDAC.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how the two call systems work or what that requires of the wearer: on the AeroClip 2, 2 VPUs (voice pickup units) pick up the wearer's own voice instead of filtering out the noise around it, rated for 80+ dB surroundings, and its mic sits where the battery housing meets the C-bridge, so Anker says each bud must be on its correct ear and not swapped left/right during calls; the C50i's 2 AI mics only filter background noise.
angles.decides: This supports the pick ChatGPT already made rather than changing it. The AeroClip 2's extra $100–130 mostly pays for a different way of picking up the voice (VPUs on Anker's Thus chip), not for better music. iPhone owners get AAC, not LDAC, so for them the music argument mostly goes away and calls are nearly the only reason to pay more. Anyone who doesn't take calls in loud places should buy the C50i.
