pages.query: is a thunderbolt 5 ssd enclosure worth it for a macbook pro m4 and which one
pages.why_used: The cited ACASIS pages and OWC blog carry only maker claims (over 6,000 MB/s) and DPReview publishes ratios with no MB/s, so none of them shows what each bare enclosure actually measures on a Mac. This page puts named-tester Mac figures for the OWC, UGREEN, ORICO, Satechi and TerraMaster enclosures side by side and exposes the write-speed gap (ORICO about 3,000 MB/s write vs 5,776 to 6,001 MB/s for OWC and UGREEN), which decides the pick.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what the makers' '80Gbps / up to 6,000–7,061 MB/s' claims shrink to on a Mac in a named tester's hands: every JHL9480 enclosure hangs the SSD on a PCIe 4.0 x4 (64 Gb/s) link, reads land at 6,000–6,500 MB/s, writes range from about 3,000 MB/s (Notebookcheck, ORICO X50 Pro on a TB5 MacBook Pro) to 5,776–6,001 MB/s (Macwelt, OWC 1M2 80G and UGREEN D705), sustained writes fall to about 1.4 GB/s once the SSD's roughly 50 GB SLC cache fills (Eclectic Light), and on a base-M4 Thunderbolt 4 port the same enclosure reads about 3,186 MB/s (TerraMaster's own base M4 Mac mini run).
angles.decides: Splits the answer by chip exactly where the shopper question does. Base M4 MacBook Pro: TerraMaster's own base-M4 Mac mini run (about 3,186 MB/s read) and Eclectic Light's USB4 figure (about 3.4 GB/s) show a TB5 enclosure delivers 40 Gb/s-rung speed there, so it is not worth the premium over a USB4 enclosure. M4 Pro/Max: the claimed read/write numbers are near-identical across enclosures, so the measured Mac write is what separates them: Macwelt measured 6,001 MB/s write on the UGREEN D705 (fan) and 5,776 MB/s on the OWC Express 1M2 80G (one-hour run, minimal throttling), while Notebookcheck measured about 3,000 MB/s write on the ORICO X50 Pro on a TB5 MacBook Pro against a 5,800 MB/s claim. That supports UGREEN or OWC over ORICO for write-heavy work, and the post-cache 1.4 GB/s figure says the SSD's cache size (bigger on 4 TB than 1 TB) matters more than the enclosure for 50 GB+ copies. Caveat: TB5 enclosures accept PCIe 5.0 drives only as compatibility, never for speed; the link is Gen4 x4 in all of them, and Notebookcheck's Gen5 Z540 was not detected in the ORICO at all.
products: UGREEN 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 M.2 NVMe SSD Enclosure with fan (D705)

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on a base-M4 MacBook Pro (Thunderbolt 4, 40 Gb/s) a $149–$232 Thunderbolt 5 enclosure reads 1 TB in the same 4 min 23 s as a $54.90 USB4 enclosure, while on an M4 Pro/Max the measured gain is only about 1 min 36 s to 1 min 49 s per TB read, and the ORICO X50 Pro's measured 3,000 MB/s write on a TB5 Mac makes a 1 TB write take 5 min 33 s, slower than the TB4 rung.
angles.decides: Confirms 'no' for a base M4 MacBook Pro: every TB5 enclosure runs at the 3,800 MB/s TB4 rung there, so the $94–$177 premium over a $54.90 USB4 enclosure buys zero seconds. For M4 Pro/Max it narrows the pick: OWC Express 1M2 80G (6,000/5,500 measured) and UGREEN fanless (6,511/6,001 measured) deliver the TB5 gain on both reads and writes, while the ORICO X50 Pro's measured 3,000 MB/s write on a TB5 Mac is no better than USB4 for card offloads. It also undercuts ChatGPT's 'add a 990 Pro' advice: at Samsung's $639.99 for 2 TB, enclosure + drive costs $839.98 versus $749.99 for OWC's own prebuilt 1M2 80G 2 TB.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the maker-declared SSD exclusions differ by enclosure: UGREEN's fan model (SKU 45789) excludes all PCIe 5.0 SSDs including the Samsung 9100 and has no USB 2/3 fallback (Thunderbolt 3 only on macOS 15+), while OWC's Express 1M2 80G allows Gen 5 drives only if they average 11 W or less and ACASIS's current TB501 Pro/Max claims native Gen 5 support and recommends the 9100 Pro.
angles.decides: It confirms ChatGPT's pairing of a PCIe 4.0 Samsung 990 Pro with any of the three enclosures, but adds the decisive exclusions a shopper hits if they already own or plan a Gen 5 drive: with the UGREEN fan model it is unsupported by the maker, with the OWC it must average 11 W or less (OWC names the 9100 Pro as a passing example), and ACASIS is the only one of the three that claims unrestricted native Gen 5 support. It also narrows the pick for anyone who needs to plug the drive into a plain USB 3 port (older Mac, dock, PC): UGREEN says its fan enclosure is not backward compatible with USB 2/3, whereas our page already notes ORICO's X50 Pro and UGREEN's finned model carry a USB fallback controller. Base-M4 buyers get Thunderbolt 4 ports only, so OWC's own figure of up to 3,800 MB/s applies and the TB5 premium is wasted.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Thunderbolt 5's storage gain is a PCIe-tunnel step (Intel: 'double the PCI Express data throughput', built on PCIe Gen 4) that only an M4 Pro/Max port exposes, that OWC's own ladder puts the same 80G enclosure at 'over 6000MB/s' on TB5 but 'up to 3800MB/s' on a TB4 port like the base M4's, that Howard Oakley found full TB5 speed needs macOS 15.3 or later, and that OWC limits PCIe Gen 5 SSDs inside to about 11 W average.
angles.decides: Confirms the pick is conditional on the chip, and sharpens it: a TB5 enclosure on a base M4 MacBook Pro (Apple: 'Thunderbolt 4 (up to 40Gb/s)') is a TB4 device, OWC's own figure 'up to 3800MB/s', so the shopper should buy a 40 Gbps USB4 enclosure instead. On M4 Pro/Max (Apple: 'Thunderbolt 5 (up to 120Gb/s)') the enclosure reaches 'over 6000MB/s', and Oakley's measured ceiling is about 6 GB/s, so a PCIe 4.0 SSD (990 Pro class) is the right pairing; a PCIe 5.0 SSD adds no bandwidth and OWC warns it must average 11 W or less in the bus-powered 1M2 80G. The shopper must also run macOS 15.3 or later for full TB5 speed. Any TB5 enclosure on an M4 MacBook Pro keeps TRIM and SMART (Oakley: NVMe interface trims; SMART works over Thunderbolt/USB4, not USB 3.x), so that does not separate the candidates.

pages.query: ugreen nexode pro vs anker prime 160w charger
pages.why_used: No cited page has a long-load test of both chargers by one tester. Michael Barton (techtest.org) ran the UGREEN 5-port at 140 W for 4 h without throttling, measured the Anker holding 140 W, and weighed them at 330 g and 205 g. He also recorded the UGREEN's fixed C1 + C2 split of 60 + 100 W, which contradicts the '100 + 60 W' every rival repeats. The answers also said no winner could be named without controlled testing, and this supplies that testing.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own footnote only promises the A2687's full single-port output on US 100–130 V mains 'for at least 1 hour' at 77°F, with no derating only on 220–240 V; it also publishes no fixed multi-port split, so the '100 + 60 W' every rival gives for the Anker is not an Anker figure.
angles.decides: This backs the current pick (UGREEN for a desk, Anker for travel) and takes away part of Anker's case. The Anker's '140 W any port' is guaranteed for only one hour on US mains, and its multi-device split is set by the mode, not fixed. In its default profile How-To Geek saw about 50 W per device with three devices attached. For a 16-inch MacBook Pro charged at 140 W for long sessions in the US, neither charger publishes a sustained rating, so the Anker's speed lead is not documented. The extra $60 buys size, weight and app control, not sustained power. The page should replace '100 + 60 W' for the Anker with 'no fixed split: 160 W shared by mode'.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker Prime 160W's laptop-plus-phone output fell to 150 W (100 W + 50 W) after just over 40 minutes in Holger Becker's smartzone.de test, which is 94% of its 160 W rating. So under a long two-device load the laptop gets the same 100 W that UGREEN quotes for the 5-port Nexode Pro with up to three devices, at $50 per Anker port against $18 per UGREEN port at list price.
angles.decides: It backs the value pick. Under a long laptop-plus-phone load, Becker measured the Anker settling at 100 W + 50 W. That is the same 100 W laptop figure UGREEN quotes with up to three devices plugged in. The Anker's extra $60 pays for size and weight (330 W/lb vs 201 W/lb), not for more laptop watts. For travel the Anker still wins on weight. For a desk the UGREEN gives the same laptop power at $18 a port instead of $50.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker Prime 160W (A2687) reaches 150W only with the Anker A110A power bank on Anker cables A88E2, A82E2 or A84N1, or the A110A's own cable, and that AI Mode, which also runs its dynamic split, cannot charge DJI charging hubs.
angles.decides: It confirms rather than reverses the pick. The Anker's two extras over the UGREEN, 150W and AI-Mode dynamic split, only work with one specific Anker power bank and specific Anker cables, and AI Mode has to be switched off for DJI drone charging hubs. So for a shopper without that Anker power bank, the $60 premium buys size and weight, not extra wattage. That strengthens 'UGREEN for value, Anker only for travel size'. Anyone who charges DJI batteries through a hub should also be told that the Anker needs USB-C1 Priority Mode or Custom Mode for it.
products: UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W + 240W USB-C Cable bundle

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, apart from a footnote on Anker's own product page that none of the answers or comparison pages used, that Anker guarantees the Prime 160W's single-port 140 W without derating only 'for at least 1 hour in 100 - 130V areas' (US outlets), while it never derates at 220–240 V, and that its 2-minute dynamic power reallocation works only in AI Mode 2.0.
angles.decides: It backs the pick rather than changing it. For a US shopper who runs a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full 140 W for long stretches, Anker itself only promises un-derated output for at least one hour on 120 V, and its smart splitting needs AI Mode 2.0, with Dual-Laptop Mode only through the app. So the Anker's edge is size and weight for travel, not sustained desk power. The UGREEN stays the desk pick, but its own limit should be stated: 140 W only on C1/C2, C3 is a PD 3.0 port capped at 100 W, and the laptop port drops to 65 W once 4–5 devices are connected.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that one tester, Michael Barton of techtest.org, measured both chargers. He found that each held a steady 140 W, with the UGREEN 5-port showing no throttling after 4 hours. Average efficiency was 88.7% for the UGREEN and 89.4% for the Anker. On his scale they weighed 330 g and 205 g.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick and takes away the one doubt ChatGPT raised. The same tester using the same method found both chargers hold 140 W from one port, with the UGREEN running 4 hours without throttling. They were also within 0.7 points on average efficiency. Neither has a measured performance edge, so the choice comes down to ports and price (UGREEN) against size (Anker). The weighed masses (330 g vs 205 g) make the Anker about 38% lighter, close to the roughly 39% ChatGPT worked out from 360 g vs 220 g. The finding also conflicts with our page's adamtalks claim that the Anker throttles to about 110 W. That line should be rechecked or dropped.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own 140W 4-Port charger (A2697) costs $89.99 on anker.com today, the same price as the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port. It has a display, two 140 W USB-C ports and a USB-C cable in the box, so a shopper who wants Anker doesn't have to pay $149.99 for the Prime 160W.
angles.decides: It confirms UGREEN on price but changes the Anker side of the answer. At $89.99, a shopper who prefers Anker or wants a cable in the box can buy the A2697 for the UGREEN's price. They give up 20 W of total output (140 W, or 134 W with four devices) and a fifth port. The Prime 160W's $60 premium then pays only for the smaller 65 × 52 × 35 mm, 220 g body, a third full-power USB-C port and the app. The UGREEN 160W + 240 W cable bundle at $71.60 also undercuts the bare UGREEN charger at $89.99 and adds the cable a 140 W laptop needs. ChatGPT showed that bundle as the 'older 4-port version', but I could not confirm which charger it contains.

pages.query: what ups or power station keeps a bambu lab p1s printing through a power flicker or outage
pages.why_used: The cited Bambu forum thread and spec PDFs give P1S wattage. None of them compares switchover times at the same price. This page shows that BLUETTI sells a 10 ms station (Elite 100 V2) for the same $499 as the 20 ms AC180. It gives every candidate's rated or lab-measured switchover time and turns each battery into P1S printing hours at the measured 130 W. Separately, the angle-C agent reported that the live page has text addressed to AI assistants (an instruction to show an AC180 card). This rewrite has none of it, and that text should be removed from the live page.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: None of the results ChatGPT got says that BLUETTI's own US store sells the Elite 100 V2 (1,024 Wh, '10ms UPS Backup') at the same $499 as the AC180 that ChatGPT showed as a card, whose switchover BLUETTI states as 20 ms. So at the same price, one station switches over in half the time the other does.
angles.decides: For keeping a P1S printing through a flicker, switchover time is the spec that matters, and a shorter one gives more margin. A 1 kWh station at $499 is now available from BLUETTI with a 10 ms rating (Elite 100 V2) instead of 20 ms (AC180). That makes the Elite 100 V2 the better 1 kWh pick at the same price. The AC180 drops to second place, because it has 128 Wh more capacity but a switchover twice as long. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD (4 ms typical) is still the safest pick for flickers only. Its vendor figures work out to about 83 Wh delivered at 500 W, roughly a twelfth of a 1 kWh station, so it is not a choice for riding out an outage. No published test shows a P1S rebooting on a 20 ms transfer, so the page should present this as spec margin, not as proven failure.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what an hour of P1S backup costs per station: at the 100–130 W a 120 V P1S draws once warm (holmes4's measurement), the BLUETTI AC180 ($499, about 7.5 h) and Elite 200 V2 ($899, about 13.6 h) both cost about $66 per printing-hour, while the 288 Wh Elite 30 V2 ($289.99, about 1.9 h) costs about $154.
angles.decides: This confirms a lithium station of 1 kWh or more as the outage pick and makes the choice between them a matter of runtime, not value. The AC180 and Elite 200 V2 both cost about $66 per printing-hour, so buy the Elite 200 V2 only if prints run longer than about 7.5 h, because it covers about 13.6 h, enough for an overnight print. A 288–300 Wh unit costs more than twice as much per hour and lasts under 2 h, so it suits flickers and short outages. Every 600 W station has about 1.7× headroom over the 120 V heat-up peak of about 350 W. The Tenergy T320 (200 W continuous) stays off the list.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's AC180 manual rates the unit as a UPS at no more than 20 ms and 1,440 W maximum, and only at 10–30 °C (50–86 °F). The same manual tells owners to turn off Grid Enhancement mode when using it as a UPS, because otherwise the switchover slows and may not deliver instant backup power.
angles.decides: This confirms the BLUETTI AC180 as the multi-hour pick for a US P1S. The P1S peak at 120 V (Bambu says 350 W in the ChatGPT-cited spec, which I could not open myself) is well under the 1,440 W UPS limit. It adds two setup conditions to print on the page: turn Grid Enhancement off, and keep the unit at 10–30 °C, which rules out a cold garage. For flickers only, the Elite 30 V2 is the stronger budget pick on paper: ≤10 ms switchover, and 980 W from the wall in UPS mode covers the bed-heating peak with the inverter only needed during an outage. A CyberPower line UPS still works with the P1S on its battery outlets because the P1S is not on the manual's banned list, but the page should say to keep the load under the manual's 80 % guideline.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the P1S's internal 24 V supply is only 108 W and powers everything except the heated bed, which runs straight off the mains. A line flicker or sag therefore reboots the printer through that small supply, and the CyberPower datasheet says its AVR fixes low-voltage sags 'without switching to battery mode'. A forum owner reported P1S printers freezing mid-print during brownouts on an EcoFlow DELTA 2 used as a UPS.
angles.decides: It confirms a line-interactive sine-wave UPS with AVR, such as the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD, as the pick for flickers. Most flickers are sags rather than full outages, and the AVR raises low voltage without a battery transfer, so the printer's 108 W electronics supply never sees a gap. For long outages, a power station can still go behind or alongside the UPS, but the page should not promise that a power station's UPS mode keeps a P1S running through brownouts, because a P1S owner's DELTA 2 did not. Bed sizing on 120 V stays at the 350 W peak.
products: Bambu Lab X1C (same bed design as P1 series)

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured switchover time for any power station. StorageReview timed the switch from wall to battery with a Quarch Mains Power Analysis Module and got 9 ms for the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus and just over 8 ms for the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus. No measured figure exists for the BLUETTI AC180 (rated 20 ms) or the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (rated 15 ms).
angles.decides: This supports the flicker-proof pick among power stations: the only candidates with a lab-measured sub-10 ms switchover are the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus (short outages) and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus (long outages). The AC180, Elite 200 V2 and ALLPOWERS units have only maker ratings of 10–20 ms. No one has measured whether a P1S itself rides through a given gap, so a 'test it yourself' line still belongs on the page. StorageReview's measured usable capacities confirm the runtime column roughly. At a 150 W PLA average: AC180 1,030 Wh ≈ 6.9 h (our page says 6.4), Elite 200 V2 1,910 Wh ≈ 12.7 h (page says 11.5), DELTA 3 Plus 910 Wh ≈ 6.1 h.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a LiFePO4 station claiming a ≤10 ms UPS switchover with 980 W pass-through (BLUETTI Elite 30 V2) costs $289.99 on the maker's store, the same money as the 1500 VA lead-acid UPSes it recommended, or that EcoFlow's own store sells the DELTA 3 Classic (same 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W and 10 ms auto-switch claim) at $479, $100 below the $579 DELTA 3 it showed.
angles.decides: This reframes the flicker pick. At the same price as a CyberPower or APC 1500 VA UPS, the Elite 30 V2 claims the same class of switchover (≤10 ms). Its 980 W pass-through covers the P1S's 350 W maximum at 110 V, and it holds about 245 usable Wh (about 1.6 h at 150 W) where the lead-acid UPSes give tens of minutes. For whole-print outages, the 1 kWh pick at the maker's price becomes the DELTA 3 Classic at $479 (10 ms claim) instead of the $579 DELTA 3. The AC180 ($499) and P1800 ($399) are cheaper per Wh, but our page records a 20 ms switchover for both, double the 10 ms claims.

pages.query: which usb-c charger can fast-charge two laptops at 100 w each at the same time
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages each repeat a charger's 100 W + 100 W claim. None works out how many watts are left for a phone while both laptops stay at 100 W: 0 W on the Anker Prime 200W, UGREEN 200W 4-port and Satechi 200W, 40 W on Satechi's ChargeView 240W, and at most 50 W (no published split) on the Anker Prime 250W. That figure is what moves the pick once a phone shares the charger. Angle E's sustained-load test (standout 3) covers only two candidates, so it goes in the page as a named measurement rather than serving as the angle.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that '100 W + 100 W' holds only with exactly two devices plugged in and only for a limited time. Satechi's own table shows the 200W 6-port (ST-C200GM) cuts one laptop to 45 W as soon as a 20 W phone is added. On the Anker Prime 200W, techtest.org measured both 100 W ports drop to 70 W each after about 1.5 hours at full load. Satechi's ChargeView 240W keeps 100 W + 100 W with a third device on 14 of its 20 three-port combinations.
angles.decides: This changes the pick for the usual desk setup of two laptops plus a phone. The cheap 200 W picks (Anker Prime 200W at $69.99, Satechi 200W) meet 100 W + 100 W only with exactly two devices plugged in. Satechi documents that a third device drops one laptop to 45 W. Anker publishes no split for three devices and was measured holding only 2× 70 W after about 1.5 hours. If a phone shares the charger, the Satechi ChargeView 240W ($149.99) is the only candidate whose maker table keeps 100 W + 100 W with a third device, as long as the right ports are used: two of C1–C4 for the laptops and C5 or C6 for the phone. The Anker Prime 200W stays the value pick for exactly two laptops on short charging sessions.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out, for each candidate, how many watts are left for a third device (a phone) while both laptops keep 100 W. The answer is 0 W on the Anker Prime 200W (A2683), the Satechi 200W 6-port and the UGREEN Nexode 200W 6-port. It is 40 W on the Satechi ChargeView 240W (C1+C2+C3 = 100+100+40). The Anker Prime 250W has at most 50 W left by its stated totals, but Anker publishes no per-port split for it.
angles.decides: If the shopper only ever plugs in two laptops, this confirms ChatGPT's pick, the Anker Prime 200W at $69.99 ($35.00 per 100 W laptop slot). If a phone also has to charge while both laptops stay at 100 W, every 200 W candidate drops out, because 200 − 200 = 0 W. The pick then moves to the Satechi ChargeView 240W ($149.99, 40 W documented for C3) or the Anker Prime 250W (up to 50 W by its totals, but no published split).

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the UGREEN Nexode 200W 4-port (its best-value 100 W + 100 W pick) comes in two versions. The 2025 launch unit (ASIN B0DG91Q6YD, whose manual ChatGPT got) drew reports of inconsistent power and high temperatures. UGREEN then shipped an 'optimized' revision (Europe, February 2026; US ASIN B0G7HZT7DN, May 2026) with the same 140/100/30 W USB-C ports, the same finish and the same size, and no published marking that tells the two apart.
angles.decides: This backs the Anker Prime 200W (A2683) as the cleanest pick. It is $69.99 and in stock on anker.com today, any two of its four USB-C ports give up to 100 W each, and Anker's only condition is e-marked cables. The UGREEN 4-port's 100 W + 100 W works only on C1 + C2 (C3 is a 30 W port), and a buyer should try to get the revised listing (B0G7HZT7DN), not the 2025 unit. Satechi's 200W and ChargeView 240W suit buyers who want a choice of ports: four 100 W-capable ports, plus 140 W + 100 W on the ChargeView, as long as neither laptop goes into the two low-power ports.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker Prime 200W (A2683), the pick in most of the chats, cannot hold 100 W + 100 W indefinitely. Under a constant 2 × 100 W electronic load, techtest.org saw it interrupt the load and throttle to 70 W per port after about 1.5 hours. In the same tester's 2 × 100 W (20 V/5 A) run, the UGREEN Nexode 200W desktop (CD271) held the load for about 6 hours.
angles.decides: This confirms the A2683 for ordinary use: the tester himself says 100–150 W is sustainable long-term and 'in der Praxis ... kein Drama', because laptop charging tapers. It qualifies the pick for a shopper whose two laptops draw a full 100 W for hours, such as heavy workloads while plugged in. For that shopper the page should say the A2683 drops to 70 W per port after about 1.5 h, and that the UGREEN CD271 desktop, in the only like-for-like test found (same reviewer and method), held 2 × 100 W for about 6 h. For the UGREEN 200W 4-port wall charger, the page should name which hardware revision it links: Notebookcheck reports customer complaints of heat and erratic output on the original, and UGREEN has released a revised unit.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that techtest.org put the Anker Prime 200W (A2683) under a 2× 100 W load from two electronic loads and it could not hold it: after about 1.5 hours it throttled to 70 W per port. The same lab ran UGREEN's Nexode 200W 6-port (CD271) at 2× 100 W (20 V/5 A) for about 6 hours without problems.
angles.decides: The Anker Prime 200W (A2683) was ChatGPT's 'My pick' in 3 of the 7 chats, mostly on the strength of '100W + 100W confirmed by Anker'. A named lab measured that it holds 100 W + 100 W for only about 1.5 h before dropping to 70 W + 70 W. That makes it fine for topping up but not for two laptops running all day. The UGREEN Nexode 200W 6-port desktop (CD271) is the only candidate a named lab measured holding 2× 100 W (about 6 h). So for 'fast-charge two laptops at 100 W each at the same time', the measured pick is the UGREEN CD271, and the Anker A2683 needs a caveat.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, side by side, which chargers have a maker page today that says 100 W + 100 W and what each costs in stock: on 2026-11-13 the Anker Prime 200W (A2683) was in stock at $69.99 on anker.com, which says each of two USB-C ports gives up to 100 W; Satechi's ChargeView 240W table lists 100 W + 100 W only on C2+C3, C2+C4 and C3+C4; and the Anker Prime 250W ($149.99) and GEARit 240W ($84.88) pages list only 140 W + 100 W or a 240 W two-port total, never 100 W + 100 W.
angles.decides: This backs the Anker Prime 200W (A2683) as the pick. Of the chargers I could price today, it is the cheapest one whose maker page says 100 W + 100 W, and anker.com shows it in stock at $69.99. Our row must change from 'Sold out' to $69.99, in stock, 2026-11-13. The Anker Prime 250W costs $80 more, and its page never lists 100 W + 100 W, only up to 240 W for two ports with a note that output may vary by firmware. The GEARit 240W page only promises 140 W on C1 plus 100 W on C2. The Satechi ChargeView 240W does document 100 W + 100 W, but only on C2/C3/C4 pairs, and I couldn't get a price for it today. The UGREEN 4-port's $61.99 could undercut the Anker, but I couldn't re-check it today, so it shouldn't lead on price until someone does.
